# Design review 5 — playability and 3D models

This review judges the build at commit 853cad2 (branch `claude/nifty-knuth-519jg0`) against five goals: is it **fun**, is it **playable**, does it **teach through play**, is it **easy to understand**, and are the **3D models** good. It is written for a future coding session to execute: section 4 is the fix list, section 5 the order to do it in.

**How this review was done.**

1. **Research.** Two research passes produced `RESEARCH_ART.md` (art direction from the concept art and toon references) and `research-external.md` (Good Job!, Human: Fall Flat, game-feel and teaching references). They were distilled into the rulebook [RULES.md](RULES.md): 80 checkable design rules (DR-01 … DR-80) on top of the AGENTS.md hard rules, each with a check and the known open items from reviews 3 and 4.
2. **Reviewers.** 42 reviewers ran in the real game through the capture helper: 28 room × dimension reviewers (10 rooms; *play*, *teach* and *models* per room, lobby and Arcade Rush with two), 6 cross-cutting reviewers (props gallery, characters, cable, HUD/UI, camera & rendering, progression) and 8 completeness ("gap") reviewers added after a coverage pass (stuck items & soft-locks, quality-2 retake, re-check list, juice & audio, toon pipeline, world reactions, snap/grab/target, meta/settings/errors). Every reviewer scripted its own playthroughs, took and looked at screenshots, and wrote findings with file:line evidence, a fix and a verification.
3. **Adversarial verification.** Each finding was handed to a separate verifier who tried to refute it: re-reading the code, re-running the repro (scripts in `tools/verify-<key>/`, shots named `verify-<key>-…`), and correcting the proposed fix where it was wrong (shown below as **Verifier correction**). Verdicts: CONFIRMED (reproduced), PLAUSIBLE (code supports it, not fully reproduced), REFUTED (dropped).
4. **Completeness pass and merge.** This report loads every `data/<key>.json`, drops refuted findings, and merges duplicates across reviewers (same root cause, same file or same model) with an automatic similarity pass followed by a hand-made merge map (`tools/report/merge.mjs`), keeping all evidence and the highest priority.

**Counts.** 741 findings raised → 4 refuted → 737 kept (712 CONFIRMED, 25 PLAUSIBLE) → merged into **378 fix-list entries**: 2 × P0, 158 × P1, 218 × P2. By category: teaching 86, clarity 81, playability 48, fun 45, model-detail 40, visual-bug 36, overlap 27, art-style 15. 3435 screenshots are in [shots/](shots/).

**Taking the screenshots again.** A Vite dev server must run at http://127.0.0.1:4173. The helper is `mockups/review5/tools/cap.mjs`: `import {launch} from '../cap.mjs'; const g = await launch('<level>', {fullfx:true});` then `g.advance(sec)`, `g.walk(x,z,r)`, `g.key('KeyE')`, `g.act(name,arg)` (bench buttons), `g.orbit(dx,dy)`, `g.zoom(dy)`, `g.survey()`, `g.snap()` (state JSON), `g.audit()` (start overlaps), `g.shot(name)` → `shots/<name>.png`, `g.crop(name,{x,y,width,height})`, `g.page` (raw Playwright), `await g.close()` (returns console/page errors). Run from the repo root: `node mockups/review5/tools/<key>/<script>.mjs`. Level ids: lobby (bare URL), playground, meeting, lunch, arcade, arcade-rush, garage, qfn, observatory, spectrum; `?manual` makes time advance only on advance/walk; `query:'norim'`, `query:'practice'`, `?lowfx` as needed; `SWIFT=1` forces software WebGL. Every reviewer's scripts are kept in `tools/<key>/` and `tools/verify-<key>/`, so any shot cited below can be retaken by re-running the script whose name prefixes it.

## 1. Verdicts

**Fun.** **In moments yes, across the campaign not yet.** The cable floors deliver the Good Job toy: strain reads white → yellow → orange → red with jitter and twang, the overstretched slingshot launches crates, swing doors slam, coworkers pop "!", and Lunch is the richest physical room in the game. But the clean route of every room hides these toys — the Playground clean spec wins in 5 s with zero props moved and the Q prompt never appears (R5-089), the slingshot prompt shows when there is no energy and the plug never recoils (R5-081, R5-092), and the bowling-pin bonus is earned by walking (R5-083). After job 02 the cable disappears: all six station rooms are a short carry followed by a button menu, with no cable, no chaos route, no physical bonus, and a thrown delivery that does not count (R5-079, R5-085). Grading gives an A to almost everything, including standing still for 3 minutes in Arcade Rush (R5-078). And the payoff is mis-framed: the win push-in crops Pip or misses the thing that now works in nearly every room (R5-077), the Arcade success beat is off the bench camera (R5-080), the Garage robot reboots facing away (R5-082), win and all sign-offs share one jingle and hitstop/flash exist only for the cable plug-in (R5-093, R5-094, R5-095).

**Playable.** **On desktop with keyboard and mouse, yes: every level can be finished, and no script logged a console or page error.** One soft-lock remains: in the Meeting the power strip (or coupler, or second reel) can be thrown into the sealed server closet and lost for good, because nothing respawns (R5-002). The other P0 is platform: on a phone every bench camera crops its own controls, so QFN and Spectrum cannot be finished by touch (R5-001). Below that, controls are fragile: R restarts the job instantly with no confirm, also from a bench (R5-004), while its keycap on the result and fail cards does nothing (R5-007); bench keys leak into floor verbs (R5-161); WASD at the Garage bench quietly un-fits parts (R5-014); P at the Arcade bench switches the bench off while the prompt invites it (R5-006); no gamepad input reaches any bench and touch cannot orbit (R5-015, R5-016). The camera hides Pip behind every tall fixture because only pillars fade, and the shell-wall cutaway fails near corners (R5-003, R5-005). Draw calls run 3–6× the budget in every room and first-time players are always on render quality 0 (R5-026, R5-143).

**Teaches through play.** **The truthful core is there, but too much of the teaching is a menu pick with a live oracle, and several details teach the wrong thing.** What works: the Garage's beads circling the diode loop after shutdown, Lunch's thin cable visibly warming and per-cart needles, the Meeting load adding up on one breaker. What fails: answers are found by sweeping with the result shown live (Arcade meter, Spectrum LINK, Observatory "Enter · Log" oracle, Garage one-socket-per-part; R5-028, R5-048, R5-037); messages and cards print the method or the answer (R5-065, R5-049, R5-289); and failures are sentences, not world events — the Meeting trip has no cause cue (R5-039), the Observatory latch and motor do not exist (R5-044), the Garage stop line has no physical consequence (R5-055). Truth errors to fix: the Playground has no switch and its reel is the "source" (R5-031, R5-046); breakers trip instantly (R5-041); any intact cable in the puddle shorts (R5-061); decoupling is explained as travel time (R5-070); PTCs re-arm while powered (R5-184); a popped LED "runs hot and dies early" (R5-034); pulses do not track current (R5-047); invisible bands are shown in visible hues unlabelled (R5-050). The curriculum spikes at Lunch (about 7 ideas, the only fail states) and then resets to new domains with no reuse (R5-069).

**Easy to understand.** **The start of each room reads; the middle often does not.** Objective cards are short and mostly agree with the prompt at spawn. Then: card and prompt disagree at key moments (R5-105), step 2 ticks before step 1 (R5-107), carry prompts name the wrong verb (R5-008), the marker is a pale depth-tested cone with no off-screen indicator and rides on the carried item instead of the destination (R5-103, R5-109). The job-yellow language that should mark job items is spent on decor in every room (R5-101), and the "parts" clutter recipe puts grabbable reels and splitters into rooms with no cable (R5-104). Station benches carry 45–100 words with every value shown two or three times (R5-102) and labels are 4–10 px against the 14 px rule (R5-242). Several states are misnamed: a door-cut cable is "burned", a missed beam is "TOO WEAK", the Garage says "reset the FUSE" when there is no reset (R5-110, R5-116, R5-111). Bonus stars are unexplained and two are pre-lit at t=0 (R5-112).

**3D models.** **A solid kit with good hero pieces, let down by a long tail of props that read as something else, unfinished backs and art-direction drift.** Good: the chair, box, desk, mail cart, mop bucket, the Garage robot and the improved Playground lamp; toon outlines and the chunky silhouette mostly hold. Weak: beanbags still read as macarons or buns (R5-149), the Meeting coffee machine is a black cube (R5-151), bowling pins are cones, floor lamps are mushrooms, the wedge and bridge are knife-edge extrusions, fixtures have bare single-colour backs (R5-336), signs are floating single-sided planes (R5-311), carried items tilt on edge at head height (R5-138), Pip's ridge reads as a fin and the Arcade tester is still a realistic human (R5-337, R5-371). Physical truth is off: the cable runs through Pip (R5-139), cuboid colliders stop round props rolling and 6 of 9 levels start with interpenetrations (R5-293, R5-292). Art direction: floors are too bright in six rooms (R5-154), clutter palettes break their colour families (R5-158), neither toon ramp shows 3 bands (R5-376) and the new rim light has no measurable effect (R5-372).

## 2. Design rules

The rulebook is [RULES.md](RULES.md) (80 rules, DR-01 … DR-80, plus the AGENTS.md hard rules). "Entries" is the number of **merged** fix-list entries (section 4) that cite the rule; "Findings" is the number of kept reviewer findings before merging (a rule broken the same way in ten rooms is one entry but ten findings). One entry can cite several rules. Sorted by entries.

| Rule | Entries | Findings | Rule text |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| DR-47 | 62 | 55 | Every device shows its state on the device itself: on, off, tripped, overloaded, warming. Examples are the lamp lit, a flashing breaker reset, a gauge needle, a sad-food icon. All read at the game camera. |
| AGENTS 10 | 55 | 58 | AGENTS.md hard rule: Electricity is truthful at the level taught. |
| DR-28 | 52 | 54 | Failure shows its cause in the world first (a spark, scorch, flicker or groan at the faulty part), then one sentence names the physical cause. |
| DR-62 | 38 | 43 | Detail meets a minimum. |
| DR-26 | 36 | 33 | The mechanic is the concept. Every electrical idea is taught by a physical act (routing, plugging, chaining, flipping, docking), never only by picking a value from a list or reading. |
| DR-42 | 35 | 32 | The job card's current step and the key prompt agree. The prompt and marker point at the current step's object, not the nearest prop or a later step. |
| DR-37 | 35 | 29 | Hidden rules are shown by the world before the player can fail them. |
| DR-19 | 32 | 32 | Every key prompt is a real action at that moment, and the key does what the prompt says. A key never toggles something off while the player is trying to retry. |
| AGENTS 2 | 31 | 28 | AGENTS.md hard rule: Play by doing, with a minimal text HUD (objective card plus a one-line key prompt). |
| DR-70 | 31 | 31 | Nothing interpenetrates at rest. `g.audit(0.02)` reports zero overlaps at start on every level, and decor (shelves, racks, box stacks) has colliders so the audit can see it. |
| DR-61 | 27 | 32 | Every prop passes the silhouette squint test at the game camera, using the cue table in ART R7: beanbag, sofa, bookshelf, box, vending machine, supply cart, lamp, plant, cable. |
| DR-11 | 26 | 27 | Success and failure moments are juicy and keep Pip in frame. They have flash, sound and a short hitstop, and the win push-in frames Pip together with the working machine. |
| DR-38 | 23 | 27 | Grades and bench tiers reward understanding, not trial and error. "Reliable" and "elegant" tiers need the right margin, not a lucky value, and brute-force cycling through parts costs credits. |
| DR-34 | 22 | 24 | The wording is physically right everywhere: in code strings, docs, the card and toasts. |
| AGENTS 4 | 20 | 9 | AGENTS.md hard rule: The cable is the star: finite length, wraps, strain white → yellow → orange → red, slingshot. |
| DR-50 | 20 | 17 | One name per thing, one spelling everywhere. The card, prompt, bench, docs and result card use the same noun ("practice", "power strip", "reel"). |
| DR-22 | 18 | 16 | Controls are consistent across rooms. |
| DR-63 | 17 | 23 | Every model has a finished back and underside, because the player orbits. Gauges, screens and signs have housings, never bare boards or open-backed planes. |
| DR-43 | 16 | 14 | Pip, the held item and the current goal are the three highest-contrast shapes in the frame. |
| DR-39 | 16 | 16 | Goals say *what*, never *how*. Objective cards name an object and a place, never the tool, the method or the part value. |
| DR-48 | 16 | 18 | All text the player must read is at least 14 px cap height at 1440×900, on HUD, bench and signage. |
| DR-72 | 15 | 11 | Nothing floats. Every sign, decal, poster and badge is mounted on a wall, board, door or prop face, 0.5–1 cm off it. |
| DR-18 | 15 | 11 | Grab selection prefers the job item. When a required item is within 0.4 m of reach of the nearest junk prop, E or F takes the required item. |
| DR-46 | 15 | 9 | Cable state reads without text. |
| DR-66 | 15 | 20 | Lighting is restrained. |
| DR-17 | 15 | 19 | No false affordances. A grabbable prop that looks like a job item (a reel, splitter, plug or cable) only appears where it is part of the job, or it looks clearly different. |
| AGENTS 7 | 14 | 12 | AGENTS.md hard rule: Forgiving interaction: a plug that looks in snaps in, and stuck items respawn. |
| DR-02 | 13 | 16 | Chaos is never a failure. Only a mistake in the taught concept can end a job early, and it always offers a one-key retry. |
| DR-31 | 13 | 16 | Every displayed number is the simulation's own value, and the bench lets the player predict before testing: inputs (V, R) show before power, results after. |
| DR-07 | 13 | 17 | Each grading axis is tuned per room. A clean run can earn an A on every axis. Standing still or pure wrecking can't earn A on all three. |

Other rules cited: DR-12 (12), DR-16 (12), DR-41 (12), DR-05 (12), DR-44 (11), DR-67 (11), AGENTS 6 (11), DR-03 (11), DR-10 (11), DR-71 (10), AGENTS 9 (10), AGENTS 5 (10), DR-27 (10), DR-40 (10), DR-32 (10), DR-77 (10), AGENTS 8 (9), DR-79 (9), DR-04 (9), DR-45 (9), DR-25 (8), DR-13 (8), DR-58 (8), DR-29 (8), DR-09 (8), DR-20 (7), DR-14 (7), AGENTS 3 (7), DR-36 (7), DR-54 (7), DR-69 (7), DR-06 (6), DR-51 (6), DR-53 (6), DR-49 (6), DR-56 (6), DR-59 (6), DR-01 (5), DR-15 (5), DR-78 (5), DR-52 (5), DR-73 (5), DR-21 (4), DR-30 (4), DR-75 (3), DR-74 (3), DR-24 (3), DR-33 (3), DR-65 (3), DR-57 (3), DR-35 (2), DR-08 (2), DR-60 (2), DR-64 (2), DR-55 (2), DR-68 (2), DR-23 (2), AGENTS 1 (1), REGRESSION of L6 side effect (1), DR-76 (1).

**The pattern.** The most-cited rules are about *teaching truthfully through the world*: AGENTS 10 (electricity truthful at the level taught), DR-47 (every device shows its own state), DR-28 (failure shows its cause in the world first), DR-26 (the mechanic is the concept), DR-37 (hidden rules shown before you can fail them) and DR-38 (reward understanding, not trial and error). Next come *clarity of the text layer* — DR-42 (card and prompt agree), DR-19 (a prompt is a real action), DR-34/39/50 (wording, what-not-how, one name per thing), DR-40/41/48 (text budget, each value once, 14 px) — and *model finish* — DR-62 (minimum detail), DR-61 (silhouette squint test), DR-70 (no interpenetration), DR-63 (finished backs). Some rules have few entries but each entry is large: DR-12 (camera hides Pip) and DR-24 (performance) are each essentially one merged root cause found in every room (see R5 entries in batches B3 and B8). Hard rules most at risk: AGENTS 4 (cable is the star — absent in 6 of 9 doors), AGENTS 5/6 (chaos shortcuts and Good Job grading), AGENTS 8 (orbit camera with occlusion fade), AGENTS 7 (forgiving interaction: no respawn exists).

## 3. Rooms

Each block quotes the reviewers' own notes per dimension (reviewer key in italics), lists key screenshots, the re-check of earlier reviews (R3A/R3B/R4A/R4B and the RULES "Known" lines), and the fix IDs that touch the room. Notes are the reviewers' words; where they disagree with a verified finding, the finding (section 4) wins.

### Lobby (`lobby`)

Reviewers: `lobby-models`, `lobby-play`.

#### Fun

> *lobby-models:* As a hub the lobby has no fail state and needs none, but there is very little physical fun. There are 15 props in a 600 m² room. A plant and a coworker get knocked over when you walk into them, and that's the only slapstick (the plant at (-5,-1.2) toppled on a straight walk to a door, visible lying in lobby-models-27 to -29). There's no cable anywhere, so the game's star mechanic is missing from the first walkable room (DR-05). The meta goals ('Light every wing', medals) are the hub's reward loop, but the lamps that show them are nearly off-screen and the medals are tiny, so finishing a job doesn't change the lobby in a way the player notices. Making progress physical and visible at the default camera, plus a small plug-in toy at reception, would make returning to the hub feel rewarding.

> *lobby-play:* What works: the lobby is quick and snappy. Spawn to the farthest door is about 3.2 s, any door to any other 3.0–4.0 s, and a door to the loaded job about 1.4 s, so there is no dead walking (DR-09 passes). Chaos is responsive: grabbing the red chair and throwing it (Q) at reception sent it over the desk at 8.4 m/s, popped the receptionist's '!' alarm bubble within 0.5 s (DR-04 passes) and counted damage, and a thrown mug also alarmed. Doors swing open on a springy overshoot as Pip nears, light spills onto the floor, and the interior-mapped portal shows real parallax and a thumbnail of the destination room (lobby-play-11, -30). That is charming and the best thing in the room. What doesn't: the hub is mostly empty floor with 15 props and no cable, so the game's star mechanic is missing from the room players see most. There's no chaos goal and nothing happens on its own in the first 30 s. Entering a door is an instant reload with no walk-in or fade, and coming back resets Pip to spawn with no wing-lamp ignition, so the progression payoff ('a wing lights up') never plays on screen. Done doors are hard to tell from undone ones at the default camera.

#### Playability

> *lobby-models:* Doors work. Walking to a door's `at` point opens it with a nice spring, the prompt names the job, and E enters. The locked Rush door gives a clear prompt and a rattle. Zero console or page errors across the four scripts (start, survey, orbits, done state, norim, phone, title). The problems:
> - The directory board hides Pip completely on a 180° orbit and Pip's head passes through it (DR-12).
> - The Workshop arch invites walking through but traps Pip against the bench at (7.0,4.25).
> - On a phone, the survey shows only 3 of 9 doors (DR-21).
> - About 592 draw calls for 15 props (DR-24).
> - Scripted straight walks also stalled against the desk (to (0,-5.6)), which hints that the desk plus board block a natural line toward the middle back doors. A human will walk round, but a clutter-free aisle should exist.

> *lobby-play:* Navigation works and nothing soft-locks: all 9 doors are reachable, the locked Arcade Rush door gives a clear prompt and unlocks once the Arcade has a result (verified by seeding localStorage, lobby-play-31), the front edge has an invisible wall at z 9.5, a crate carried to a door just drops on E and a second E enters, the Workshop picker launches practice, and Esc closes it without opening pause. audit(.02) returns [] and every script closed with zero console or page errors (DR-80 passes). The big playability problem is the door leaves. They swing toward the camera and cover Pip completely at all three side doors (and on phone), and half-cover him at back-wall doors, right at the moment of choosing. The reception board and desk also hide Pip from a reverse orbit because the lobby registers no occluders. On a phone, both the start view and the Tab survey show only 3 of 9 doors and the target is off-screen. The Workshop picker doesn't block game input: WASD walks Pip away and Tab toggles survey behind it. The Workshop's 1.6 m radius steals E from the beanbag beside it. Performance is 60 fps but 663–693 draw calls for 15 props.

#### Teaching

> *lobby-models:* The lobby teaches no electronics by design: it's a hub with no fail state. The only teaching-adjacent elements are the job order on the directory board (which reads in zig-zag order, 00/02/03R… then 01/03/04…, so it doesn't convey a progression) and the lock on Arcade Rush ('finish 03 first'), which communicates the order well through the prompt, though the on-door LOCKED plate is hidden behind Pip. A lit wing-colour lamp strip per completed job, plus a reception 'plug the lamp' toy, would let the hub reinforce the core loop-and-switch idea without text.

> *lobby-play:* The hub teaches no electronics, by design. A missed opportunity: a small 8 m hub reel that lights the HQ sign would let the first act in the game be the cable act (length, plug-snap) before the Playground, and would satisfy AGENTS 4 in the hub.

#### Clarity

> *lobby-models:* Door titles are readable at zoom 9 to 18, but they auto-shrink: 'Overheating Arcade' and 'Cable Playground' render at about half the cap height of 'Lunch Rush', about 6 px at the default camera. Side doors carry their name twice. The objective marker is a small pale triangle, about 14 to 18 px, above the next door's number plate (lobby-models-01, -43). It points correctly but is easy to miss (DR-44). The first frame shows only the six back doors: the side doors are cut off or under the job card. The Workshop uses 'practise' while the code and URL use 'practice', and the HUD stays live behind its picker. At spawn there's no misleading prompt (L2 improved), but at reception the only prompt is 'Grab the mug' for a stray floor mug.

> *lobby-play:* The prompt pill is good: it names the door and number, the best grade, and what a locked door needs ('Locked: finish 03 · Overheating Arcade first'). There's no stray 'Grab the cone' prompt at spawn any more. Signage, which the hub depends on, doesn't read at the game camera: door names are 5–8 px cap height, numbers, LOCKED and medals 4–6 px, and side-door blade signs about 4 px and partly hidden under the job card. Each side door has two crossed signs. The objective marker is a pale 20 px unoutlined cone inside the door frame and gets lost easily, with no off-screen arrow. The lobby's one rule ('Every door is a job. Pick one.') is defined as the level tagline but never shown; the card reads only '00 · Cable Playground' with nine dots and three unexplained grey stars, whose wording never appears anywhere in the hub, and one bonus duplicates another. The pause card shows a meaningless damage and cost tally, 'Circuit Crew Hq', and a Jobs button that reloads the lobby. 'Practise any station' uses jargon and lists only 5 of 9 jobs. The title still has the unclear HQ badge and the faint gamepad glyph.

#### Models

> *lobby-models:* Lobby models get mixed marks. What works:
> - The doors are the strongest fixtures in the game's hubs: chunky wing-coloured frames, a glossy leaf with a colour panel, number plate, knob and threshold, and an interior-mapped portal that shows a real corridor with the destination room at its end when you look at it from the front (lobby-models-13, -18, -22).
> - The shell walls (wainscot, rail, wallpaper, thick cap) and the wood plank floor (median luma 181) read well. Outlines are present, and Pip's darkest pixels are about luma 49.
> - The chairs (5-star base, armrests) and kraft boxes (tape, flap seam, label) pass the squint test.
> - g.audit(.02) returns []. That's only because most broken parts are decor without colliders.
> 
> What's wrong:
> - The side-door blade signs added for L1 now cut through the door titles and lintels, hang off the wall, and float after the cutaway.
> - Door leaves swing out through Pip.
> - The directory board is a floating, collider-less, non-fading black slab whose plates overlap and z-fight.
> - The 'wing lights up' lamps sit on top of the wall, almost out of frame.
> - The medal floats 17 cm off the wall.
> - The Workshop arch is a dead end with blocks clipping the bench.
> - The beanbag still reads as a lilac macaron or coworker.
> - The cooler and reception lack detail, and the pendants hang from the sky.
> 
> At game camera most props are detailed enough. At close-up the reception and Workshop fall under DR-62's 6 cues.

> *lobby-play:* Not this reviewer's dimension. In passing: the directory board's back is a bare black slab floating behind the desk with no support (lobby-play-43). The blade-sign bracket stops short of the wall. The portal corridor shader reads well. Pip, chairs, plants and coworkers read cleanly at the game camera. Floor luma is 165–177, inside DR-54's 140–185.

### Playground (`playground`)

Reviewers: `playground-models`, `playground-play`, `playground-teach`.

#### Fun

> *playground-models:* The core toy works and feels good. The cable's strain ramp (white, then yellow, orange and a thick red) reads beautifully at the game camera (shots -43, -49, -50). The slingshot prompt appears at the limit, and the lamp payoff (glow, pool, confetti, Pip cheering) lands. The clean solve took 10.2 s and earns A/A/A. Two things undercut the fun in model and art terms. First, the six 'pins' are recoloured traffic cones that Pip bowls over just by walking, so the strike bonus and confetti fire without the cable (shot -33). The slingshot's designed reward is free, and the pins don't look like pins. Second, the slingshot run itself flung nothing visible in my scripted overstretch (fastestProp 0 after 1.5 s, shots -51/-52), and the centre of the room is thin, so a fling has little to hit. Pushing a 24 kg bookshelf over by walking (shots -22, -23, -61) is a nice accidental slapstick moment. Coworkers, though, have no colliders, so the most obvious comedy target (bonking a trainee) can't happen.

> *playground-play:* What works: the cable itself is a joy. Strain reads white → yellow → orange → red along its length, with jitter, twang arcs and a buzz at the limit (shots 13, 22, 23), and the overstretched slingshot launches the crate row with shake and sound (shots 24–25). Coworkers pop '!' when a taut cable sweeps past them or a crate lands nearby (shots 30, 54). Pip can topple a 24 kg bookshelf by walking into it, and the win beat (bloom on the lamp, confetti, Pip cheering, the rising result tag) is warm (shots 16–17). What doesn't: the room's best toys are hidden from someone who just does the task. The clean spec route wins in 4.98 s with zero props moved and peak strain 0.91, so the Q prompt never appears. The pins, the advertised slingshot target, were knocked down in 0 of 5 straight slingshot attempts but fall over when you walk or drag the cable through them (they sit on the open lane), so the strike doesn't reward the cable. Grading (default 120/10/300) hands out AAA for anything. Crates don't wrap the cable, so the 'obstacle course' is decoration and routing is one pillar decision. Net: fun if you go looking, flat if you follow the card.

> *playground-teach:* The slingshot remains the best toy, and the tension tagline lands. Overstretching makes coworkers alarm with '!' bubbles, props fly (fastestProp 44 m/s), and damage and cost tick on the HUD (shots 19–21). The scripted slingshot from tests/routes.spec.ts knocked a plant and a chair, not the pins (pinsDown 0 in runs D and E), so the bowling bonus needs a deliberate aim. That is fine for a bonus, but the spec comment's 'front row of boxes' no longer matches where the cable lies. The win itself is a confetti burst that happens too fast to enjoy the lit lamp. A 1–2 s 'it works!' beat before the card would make the payoff land and double as the teaching moment.

#### Playability

> *playground-models:* Controls and the route are fine: walkTo reached every fixture, and the clean route needed no detour. The camera is the main problem:
> - Bookshelves (1.8 m) and the supply cage never fade and hide Pip (shots -17, -21).
> - When a pillar does fade, it leaves its cap and plinth floating (shots -18, -20).
> - The side-wall stub fills the frame at low orbits (shot -16).
> The plug starts under Pip's feet, so the first frame shows no job item. Pip walks through coworkers. 778 draw calls is three times the budget even in this light room. g.audit(.02) at start reports only 3 overlaps, all paper sheets 3 cm inside beanbags. It cannot see fixed-vs-fixed overlaps such as the two pallets at (8.2,8.2) and (8.9,8.4), decor-only interpenetrations (poster vs window mullion, target ring vs lamp base, double socket), or the coworkers. g.close() returned [] for every script: no console or page errors.

> *playground-play:* No soft-locks found. Every run reached its end state, and all scripts closed with zero console or page errors (DR-80 pass). The plug can always be re-picked within 1.75 m (dropped mid-route, after a slingshot, at the room's front lip), plug-in snaps from 1.6 m with a clear 'F Plug in' and a ready-glow on the F button, and the switch can be pressed before power (it latches, so plugging in later wins at once). Problems: tall clutter, especially the five 1.8 m bookshelves from the shelf recipe, hides Pip because only pillars fade (shots 37, 45). A faded pillar leaves an opaque cap floating over Pip (shot 41). Running into the crate/chair cluster with the plug stalls Pip and costs damage. On a phone the survey crops off the lamp and the card covers the strain meter (shots 49, 50). There is no dead time; the opposite problem is that the whole job lasts about 5 s. The desktop survey shows the whole room (shot 02, DR-21 pass at 16:10). Restart is a page reload with autostart.

> *playground-teach:* Controls behaved as prompted in every state I drove: F pick up, F plug, E switch, Q slingshot, F drop. No console or page errors in four scripts (every g.close() returned []). When Pip is stuck short on a wrong route, the only prompt is 'Q Let go to slingshot the cable'. A learner gets told the chaos option, not that the route is too long. Consider letting the strain HUD meter or the reel spool pulse instead. Draw calls are about 780–950 (P2 finding). The plug-snap radius (2.2 m from Pip) is forgiving and worked first time at the spec point. A strain ≥ 1.12 plug-in rejection (game.ts:205) exists, but I couldn't reach it near the socket (max observed strain about 1.045), so I don't report it.

#### Teaching

> *playground-models:* The wordless how-to board on the side wall (reel → cable → plug → socket → lamp) is excellent and exactly the 'play by doing' language the room needs (shot -14). Three model problems weaken it:
> - The socket on the poster is a recognisable socket, but the real target is a blank dark box. It has no face or slots, its geometry is duplicated, and the plug's pins come out of its back.
> - There is no switch model at all: 'Switch the lamp on' means pressing E at the bare post base, so the room never shows that a switch closes the loop.
> - The practice wall's five sockets, one glowing green, accept nothing and give no feedback, which teaches the opposite of 'a plug that looks in snaps in'.
> Adding a visible switch box with a toggle and pilot light, a proper socket face with a pilot LED, and a conduit linking socket → switch → bulb would make the loop visible without text. Making the practice wall a working warm-up (an LED lights) would teach plugging before the real job.

> *playground-play:* The room aims to teach cable feel (length, wrap, strain) and that a switch closes a loop. Cable feel is partly taught. Strain colour, the HUD reel bar and the pull-back are clear when you reach the limit, but the clean route never reaches it, and light props don't wrap, so length and route lessons are thin. The loop is not taught at all: the reel isn't connected to any source, the lamp has no visible switch, and nothing shows open vs closed beyond the final light-up. The idle hint (35 s) streams cyan 'current-like' dots from Pip to the socket on an open circuit, the misconception the game should avoid, and the dots run through crates. Truthful parts: the cable turns gold and pulses only once the lamp is actually on; the lamp only lights with both plug and switch; F at the socket requires the plug to be near.

> *playground-teach:* The Playground teaches cable feel well, and it does so through play. The 19 m reel over an 18.9 m clean route makes length a real constraint. A wrong route round pillar-b stalls Pip with a red cable and twang arcs at the biting corner (shot 17). The world shows why without printing it. That part meets DR-26 and DR-28.
> 
> The electrical idea the room claims ('a switch closes the loop') is not taught by any act or object:
> - the switch is an invisible radius at the lamp base;
> - its state lives only in the prompt pill;
> - the lamp lights only inside win(), under confetti;
> - the current pulses are one-way and buried in the hose;
> - the reel itself is shown as the source of electricity.
> 
> The one prompt that addresses order ('needs power first') teaches sequential reasoning. Nothing electrical can fail (5 A / 3 A / 1 A), so the room can be solved by obeying three prompts without learning anything about circuits.
> 
> What is truthful already: the simulation is a series condition (the plug AND the switch must both be closed, in either order). The pulses only run on a closed, live loop. The game also distinguishes 'plugged in' from 'on'. The fixes are almost all in presentation, plus one in sequencing (the dwell and win decoupling). Recommended order:
> 1. Visible switch with lever state.
> 2. Circuit-driven lamp with a 1.2 s dwell before the win.
> 3. Visible wall supply feeding the reel.
> 4. Two-lane loop pulses that can actually be seen.
> 5. Non-electrical idle hint.
> 6. Fix the prompt wording.
> 7. Separate the live tint from strain yellow.

#### Clarity

> *playground-models:* The colour language is muddied in the tutorial room. Job yellow (#ffc94d) appears on:
> - a trainee blob;
> - a clutter splitter that prompts 'Grab the splitter';
> - the cage reels;
> - the yellow lane lines and tape.
> A second grabbable reel (brown) sits by the practice wall. The yellow lane lines form a rectangle around the room rather than leading to the socket (decor.ts:86, whose comment says they 'lead from the reel to the lamp socket'). The objective marker is unoutlined and pierces the post and Pip's hat. The spool's remaining length is hidden because the reel's flange faces the default camera.
> What works: the HUD card and one-line prompt stay minimal. The strain meter and cable colours agree. The win card clearly shows which axis earned the A.
> Values (re-measured): floor median luma 207 at the start (target 140–185; ART F7 still open, not regressed). Pins 225 and the slack cable 219 sit only 13–20 luma off the floor. Outline darkest-2% on the box stack is about 104 (DR-56 wants ≤ 70; global toon.ts:77). With ?norim (shot -35) props still separate from the floor (box 157, chair 103, cone 171 vs floor 207), so the rim light is not what carries readability here.

> *playground-play:* At start the card and prompt agree ('Pick up the reel's plug' / 'F Pick up the plug', DR-42 pass), with 9 words on screen (DR-40 pass), and the grab reticle and marker sit on the plug. After that, clarity drops. The lamp and socket are off-screen for most of the drag, with no edge indicator. The lamp is a low-contrast grey pole, while the brightest 'socket' in the room is a green-glowing decorative one on the practice wall. A second grabbable cable reel, a job-yellow splitter and yellow reels in the cage are false affordances. The yellow wall lines look like a path to the lamp but run 30 m round the walls, and following them strands Pip with only a 'slingshot' prompt. 'Switch the lamp on' points at a bare pole with no switch. The bonus goals are three roughly 10 px stars, two pre-lit, worded only on the result card (not on pause as the code comment says), and they call the white cones 'pins' while the prompt says 'cone'. The marker shares the lamp shade's yellow and reads as its light beam.

> *playground-teach:* The card plus pill is short and readable. Problems:
> - At the lamp the marker camouflages as a second lampshade.
> - At the plugged socket the pill offers 'Grab the plant'.
> - The connected-cable gold is the same hex (#ffd451) as the 70–85% strain band.
> - Spare reels and splitters from the 'parts' recipe muddy which reel matters.
> - The how-to poster is wordless and good in spirit, but it starts at the reel; it should start at the wall.
> - At the start view the lamp (the goal) is off-screen. Acceptable, since step 1's marker is on the plug, but the survey shows the lamp as a tiny post that reads poorly as a lamp until it is lit.

#### Models

> *playground-models:* Strong models at both the game camera and zoom 9:
> - cardboard boxes (rounded, flap seam, tape, label: 4+ cues);
> - task chairs (5-star base, casters, gas lift, armrests);
> - cones;
> - bins with paper balls;
> - windows with blinds and city view;
> - the hazard pillars;
> - the how-to board;
> - Pip's overalls, belt and boots.
> Everything is MeshToon or MeshBasic (no Standard or Phong; DR-57 passes), and round parts have 24+ segments.
> Weak or buggy:
> - beanbags (still brown bread loaves; P5/F5 open);
> - pins (white cones);
> - socket (blank box, built twice);
> - the missing switch;
> - the anchor reel (no stand, flanges sunk into its base plate, winding hidden from the camera);
> - the lamp (black puddle base, oversized glow);
> - pallets (flat slabs that overlap each other);
> - cage reels (floating, read as a red ball);
> - the water cooler (2 cues);
> - plant pots (no rim);
> - bookshelves (identical, saturated candy-bar books, books taller than the posts);
> - Pip's helmet ridge (cat ears);
> - the 20 cm hose cable (as thick as the plug).
> Systemic: every dynamic prop sits about 2.7 cm below the visible floor (the floor collider top is at −0.025), the 'graph' poster is hung over a window, sprint dust shows as ink rings, and the cable clips through Pip and through props.

> *playground-play:* Within this dimension: the lamp now has a pole, arm, shade and bulb that blooms (the R2 'black bowling ball' is fixed), but it lacks a switch and reads small and grey from the game camera. The socket is a plain dark box. The pins are modelled as white traffic cones, not bowling pins. The hazard pillars are clean. Kraft beanbags still read as bread loaves (P5 still open, shots 01, 05). The floor remains bright: about 194–207 luma in the start shot, above the 140–185 target (DR-54 still failing). The cable clips through crates (light props don't wrap) and enters Pip through the legs from behind (P3 still open).

> *playground-teach:* The lamp post and socket are simple, but they read in the toon style. The socket is built twice (game.ts:88 and decor.ts:92), and the plug's prongs come through its back. The plug reuses the Meeting coupler mesh. There is no lamp cord from the socket to the post, so the loop's last leg is invisible. The win glow washes Pip out. The reel drum and spool read well at zoom 9 (shot 03).

### Meeting (`meeting`)

Reviewers: `meeting-models`, `meeting-play`, `meeting-teach`.

#### Fun

> *meeting-models:* The comedy set dressing is strong: coworkers with personalities and accessories, a lounge with sofa, ping-pong and beanbags, the boardroom audience, and slapstick-ready loose props (14 cartons, 32 mugs, bins and chairs all scatter when Pip sprints through, meeting-models-52/-53). The payoff moment, the projector going from no-signal to a glowing chart with confetti, is the right idea, but the window mullions and blinds drawn across it, plus Pip missing from the win push-in (QA 10 still open), take the shine off. Making the coworkers sit the right way round on their chairs is also a cheap fix that makes the whole office read as alive rather than glitchy.

> *meeting-play:* What works: the core cable drag in Big Meeting is genuinely fun. The cable goes visibly white → yellow → orange → red as it pays out across the office (shots 13, 14, 15, 17), the HUD length bar fills in step, and pushing past the limit at a sprint makes coworkers pop '!' bubbles and drags chairs out of the pods (shots 17, 68). That is exactly the Good Job slapstick the brief asks for. The plug-in and the trip have punchy audio and a shake. Unplugging the kettle makes the whole boardroom groan, and borrowing the coffee reel makes the coffee corner groan (shots 25, 65); both are good comedic beats, and the coffee one is the best 'sneaky' moment in the game. The deadline clock and the impatient boardroom after 4:00 are a nice pressure layer that never fails the player.
> What hurts:
> - The win shot leaves Pip out.
> - Grading is trivially A for every route, wrecking included, so the clean and chaos routes have no scoring identity.
> - Letting go (Q) has no target or payoff in this room, and no bonus rewards chaos.
> - The strip-first order creates lots of back-and-forth walking before the fun starts.
> - Coworkers have no colliders, so the most obvious slapstick (bumping blobs, bonking them with thrown mugs) can't happen.
> DR-03: on the tidy path, nothing funny happens in the first 30 s unless the player throws things. Throwing a bin at a pod did alarm 5 coworkers (via the cabinet impact), but throwing the light strip produced no reaction.

> *meeting-teach:* The trip is a decent comedy beat: groans, '!' bubbles in the boardroom (shot 14) and appliances dying. But it lands mostly off-camera, and it is over in one frame, so the 'hum, then CLACK' drama is lost. A 2 s rising hum with a buzzing strip and flickering kettle would make it both funnier and truthful. Choosing who loses their tea (or moving the heater to another circuit to avoid the groan) would give the player a small, readable decision instead of an obligatory toggle.

#### Playability

> *meeting-models:* From a models standpoint, the camera works in most of the room: the floor reads, pillars fade, and the survey shows all walls at 1440×900 (meeting-models-02). Things that interfere with play: the lounge pendant fully covers Pip's head at zoom 9 and isn't an occluder; steam puffs up to 1.5 m wide sit over the kettle and boardroom glass; sprint-walking through the desk aisles knocks chairs, monitors and the box raft about (expected physics comedy, but the 14-box raft doubles as an obstacle wall next to the printer). There were no console or page errors in 9 script runs. snapshot().drawCalls reported 1236 at the start with fullfx; that counter includes the outline and post passes, so it isn't directly comparable to the ~175 LR15 figure, but it is worth a lowfx re-measure against DR-24.

> *meeting-play:* No P0 soft-lock found. Every route the specs describe works through the capture driver: sprint overstretch won at 0:29, the clean coupler route at 0:39, and the coffee reel worked. I tested these wrong moves:
> - plugging in before placing the strip: works, with the prompt '(the power strip is still missing)', and the strip can be placed later;
> - carrying the reel to the plug first: silently ignored, which is recoverable;
> - resetting without unplugging: re-trips forever, but is recoverable;
> - switching on before power;
> - throwing the strip away: it lands reachable;
> - shoving glass panes;
> - idling past the deadline: no fail.
> The reach radius (1.65 m) is generous, so no required item wedged out of reach. Respawn still covers only items above 2.1 m.
> The occlusion sweep at the bookshelf, the vending machine and the server closet (4 yaws, low pitch) kept Pip visible in all 12 shots, and the interior-wall fade from QA 5 holds. Problems found:
> - R is an instant, unconfirmed restart next to E/F;
> - the phone survey crops the room to the middle third;
> - Pip walks through coworkers;
> - the placed strip is still grabbable and prompted;
> - appliance targeting uses find(), not nearest;
> - 1237–1422 draw calls.
> Timing: in the drive script, strip placement takes about 10 s; the strip carry (21 m) and the return (22 m) are each about 5 s at walking pace, under DR-09's 8 s, but the clean route crosses the same aisle five times.

> *meeting-teach:* The full clean solve (strip, reel, coupler and second reel via F at the cart, plug, switch, trip, unplug, reset) worked through the capture helper in about 33 s of game time, with no console errors in any of 3 runs. The early-switch path and the pre-emptive-unplug path also complete.
> 
> Playability issues:
> - the appliance prompt picks by array order (the heater is hard to select);
> - the strip can be lifted after plug-in.
> 
> I found no soft-locks in the load beat: a reset is always available, and replugging appliances toggles freely.

#### Teaching

> *meeting-models:* The one electricity beat (a load budget on a strip) is modelled as a strip lying next to a black box that everything plugs into. So the physical picture of "three loads summed on one strip" is missing: no plug heads in the strip's outlets, no empty outlet after unplugging the kettle, and the reset on the wrong object. The gauge does move through the green, yellow and red zones (4.5 A → yellow, trip → red), but it floats in mid-air and shows from frame one, before the strip exists in the doorway. The kettle reads as a toilet roll, so "unplug the kettle" is hard to act on by sight. The coffee machine's 30 m reel isn't connected to the machine by any cord, so the sneaky route's meaning ("borrow the coffee machine's power") is carried only by the prompt text.

> *meeting-play:* The room now has a real electricity beat: the kettle (2.5 A) and heater (2 A) already load the 5 A strip, and the projector's 1 A tips it. That is truthful at the level taught (loads add, the breaker trips on the total and stays off until reset), and the meeting-strip.ts header documents it well. But the beat is taught almost entirely by the text prompt 'Unplug the kettle'. When it trips:
> - the card keeps saying 'Switch the projector on';
> - the marker stays on the projector;
> - the only offered action is 'Reset the strip', which loops;
> - the load gauge, the one physical cue, floats in the doorway and is unreadable at the game camera.
> The star cable contradicts the lesson: it carries no pulses while feeding 4.5 A to the kettle and heater, and stays gold while tripped. A coffee-reel edge case leaves the strip live with no cable. Cable length and routing (wraps around pillars, the strain colours, the spool) teach well by doing. The coupler-before-reel rule is still not readable from the parts, and the plug is literally a coupler model.

> *meeting-teach:* Partly. The idea is real and the core act is physical: you unplug an appliance and press the strip's reset. Several things are truthful at this level: loads add, the trip comes from the total, the strip stays off until reset, and resetting while still overloaded trips again (I saw trips:2 in practice). The appliances visibly go dark when it trips. Their cords run to the strip and can be read. The order of draws (kettle > heater > projector) is right.
> 
> But the concept doesn't decide anything the player reasons about:
> - the trip is effectively forced;
> - the gauge has no units, no per-appliance share, and reads full while no current flows;
> - the trip happens on the same frame as the switch press, so the switch looks like the cause;
> - removing either appliance works;
> - the prompt names the fix ('Unplug the kettle'), so trial and error plus prompt-following wins every time;
> - nothing rewards predicting the overload. I verified that unplugging first gives a 0-trip win, but no star or grade notices.
> 
> Truth issues:
> - an instant trip at 1.1x (real breakers use an inverse-time curve);
> - a live male plug pushed into the strip's sockets (reversed supply, a suicide cord);
> - pulses don't show on the reel while it carries 4.5 A, yet idle dots flow on an open circuit;
> - a kettle that never switches off;
> - the clean route is a daisy chain.
> 
> The highest-leverage changes, in order:
> 1. a 2 s overload dwell with the needle past the line;
> 2. a stacked per-appliance load bar on the strip with a limit line;
> 3. a gauge that reads 0 plus a ghost needle while tripped;
> 4. a 'Don't trip the strip' bonus;
> 5. a second boardroom circuit so 'spread the load' becomes the elegant apply-the-idea solution.

#### Clarity

> *meeting-models:* The palette and object families work against clarity. Job yellow (#ffc94d) is on 32 desk mugs, a beanbag, desk lamps and the lounge pendant, while the job items themselves are an orange strip and a teal coupler. The coupler is literally the plug model in another colour, and on the teal mail cart it disappears at the default zoom. At spawn the plug is the same yellow as the reel flange. In the boardroom, the electrical topology (reel → strip → projector, kettle, heater) is not visible: every lead ends in the generic black socket box that half-covers the strip, and the reset light appears on the box. The grab cue meant to answer "what will E take?" is broken (rotated upright). The deadline clock, blinds, server-closet glow and the no-signal to slide screen swap do read well without text.

> *meeting-play:* The objective card plus one-line prompt stays within the ~25-word budget (the start shot has about 20 words). The progress dots and stars read well at 1440×900 and on the phone (shot 46). Strain colours read without text, and the HUD length bar is clear. Clarity problems:
> - The card and prompt disagree at the start ('Pick up the plug' vs 'Fetch the power strip'), after placement ('Grab the power strip'), and at the heater ('Unplug the kettle').
> - 'Grab the thing' appears for the vending machine and the glass.
> - The marker has no outline and no off-screen indicator, and sits on Pip's helmet when the target is at Pip's feet (shot 04).
> - The idle hint dots point at the door during the strip step.
> - The sprint trick is unhinted, and the stall prompt pushes the player to let go instead.
> - Three identical yellow reels (anchor, mail cart, coffee) follow three different rules.
> - The lounge beanbag uses job yellow.
> - The result card's bonus lines are small (about 12 px), and the card doesn't say which axis earned the A.

> *meeting-teach:* The objective card is clear for steps 1 and 2. The strip snap prompt ('Set the power strip down by the door') works, and 'Plug in (the power strip is still missing)' is a good guard.
> 
> The failure moment is the weak spot:
> - the card and marker keep pointing at the projector after the trip (M11 is still open);
> - the trip effects are hidden behind Pip at the default camera, and no sentence names the cause;
> - the start prompt says 'F Pick up the plug' while the card says to fetch the strip (DR-42, still open);
> - after plugging in, the prompt invites 'E Grab the power strip', which silently cuts power.
> 
> The gauge floats in the doorway and isn't visibly tied to the strip.

#### Models

> *meeting-models:* The Big Meeting is the most complete-looking room. The overall model language matches the concept anchor: chunky rounded desks with keyboards, mice, pen cups and cable tails, five-star task chairs on casters, a ten-variant desk dressing, monitors with live screen textures, pillars with base, rail and cap trims and posters, server racks with hot LEDs and cable spaghetti, a framed whiteboard with scribble, a mail cart with posts, a parcel shelf and a push bar, and two-tone walls with windows, blinds and a sill. Outlines are dark ink: the darkest 2% of edge pixels measured 41–47 luma on the box and plant crops, which passes DR-56. Floor luma at the game camera is 148–182 (DR-54 OK), and ?norim (meeting-models-44) is nearly identical to the default, so the rim light is restrained. Where it falls short is layout and assembly more than missing polygons. The worst is that every pod chair is rotated 180°, so the 20 seated coworkers sit inside their backrests, and two boardroom blobs face away from the table. The win image has window frames and blinds drawn across the projector slide, and a poster mounted on a window. The load gauge floats in the doorway. The grab cue stands vertically. A plant sits inside a collider-less decor stack. The start-state audit reports 51 shallow overlaps (monitor/paper ×32, cabinet/box ×18, cart/reel). Every prop rests 2.5 cm under the visible floor because the floor collider top is at -0.025. Several key fixtures are 2–3-part placeholders: the coffee machine, water cooler, printer, projector, kettle, ping-pong table and socket box. Repetition (a 14-box raft that reads as a pallet, 18 identical cabinet+box units) undercuts the hand-made Good Job density. Beanbags still read as blobs or buns (DR-52/F5 open).

> *meeting-play:* Secondary for this pass:
> - The kettle on its side table, the fan heater and the coiled cords are readable and charming at zoom 9 (shot 77). The heater is a fairly plain box with a grille, about 3 cues.
> - The strip prefab is good (four sockets plus a red reset) but is hidden under the leftover socket box once placed.
> - The load gauge has no housing or mount and floats.
> - The coupler is a plain teal block.
> - Coworker blobs, desks, pillars and cabinets hold up well at zoom 9 and in orbit.
> - Coffee steam is soft now but still reads as a large pale balloon at zoom 9 (shot 85).
> - The plug rises into Pip's raised left mitt beside the helmet at high strain (shot 16), close to DR-65.
> - The dropped second reel sinks into the anchor reel, which has no collider (shot 32).

> *meeting-teach:* Within my teaching scope:
> - the strip model is readable (orange body, four sockets, red reset cap that pops up pulsing);
> - the projector has no switch or LED, so its state is invisible;
> - the gauge has a flat black slab back and floats in the doorway;
> - the kettle's 'on' halo is a big white translucent sphere;
> - the plug and the coupler share one mesh with brass pins (prefabs.ts:101), so the coupler doesn't read as a joiner.
> 
> The seated plug on the strip reads as a dark block on top, not inserted (shots 04, 22).

### Lunch (`lunch`)

Reviewers: `lunch-models`, `lunch-play`, `lunch-teach`.

#### Fun

> *lunch-models:* From the models side, the room's physical comedy is helped by the bots, swing doors and splitters. It is hurt by sparse clutter: 137 props, half of them paper and mugs, with a big empty wood corridor and no lounge or beanbag clusters. That leaves little to knock over on the routes, and the climax (lift and tray) looks unfinished. Fixing the lift cage, rope and conveyor extension makes the win moment read as a machine doing its job.

> *lunch-play:* What works: Lunch is the richest cable floor so far, and its individual beats are good, physical toys.
> - The swing door flaps open as Pip walks through and slams shut behind him.
> - Mopping shrinks the puddle you're standing in.
> - Two cleaner bots patrol a painted loop and drag the mop around (it ended up at (12.35,0.39)).
> - Powering the feed post has a clear payoff: the cable lights with pulses, the oven window glows, and the storeroom lights up to reveal the capacitor cart (c07).
> - Docking the cart gives a satisfying spark and plug sound.
> - The dolly drag feels weighty.
> - Throwing the doorstop at the lunch crowd raised two '!' alarm bubbles (x06, DR-04 passes).
> - The strain colour runs white → orange → red along the thin cable (x03), so the build-up reads.
> 
> What hurts:
> - The cable's signature slingshot has no payoff. The room is barely longer than the reels: max strain is 0.99 at the east wall, and release moves 0 props.
> - There is no fling target or chaos bonus. All three bonuses are 'don't fail' bonuses.
> - Prop density is half the Meeting's.
> - The fridge timer ends the job at 2:00 for anyone who explores or messes about. That is the opposite of Good Job's promise.
> - The win shot drops Pip.
> - The grade is effectively always A.
> 
> Timing: the bot's clean solve is 91.8 s of simulated time. The longest leg is the 11.5 s cart push, followed by up to 15 s of locked watching at the end. A person will need roughly 3-6 minutes.

> *lunch-teach:* The physical comedy is intact: door pinches, bots dragging plugs, the dolly-hauled thick cable, smoke from the oven, groaning crowds. The full solve is a satisfying chain, about 95 s scripted and 3–6 min for a human. The best fun beat, though (the lift lurching up on borrowed charge), is invisible, and the win shot frames confetti on a lift top without Pip or the cap cart. Experiments are taxed by 25 m walks to reset cart A, and a reset restarts every enabled motor, so the same trip repeats. That makes failing feel like a chore rather than a joke. Seeing the surge (telltale needle, winch jerk, cap cans dumping) would make the failures and the success both funnier and more instructive.

#### Playability

> *lunch-models:* Two model and physics issues affect play directly. First, supply cart A tips onto its side (55.9°) from an ordinary walk past and never rights itself; the respawn rule only fires above y 2.1. Second, decor without colliders lets Pip walk into benches, plants and under the lift car. Draw calls are 1257 at start and 1303 in survey (fullfx), and 1309 in lowfx, versus about 175 in PROGRESS. Most of that is unmerged shell-wall window parts on game.root, plus a lamp cord rebuilt every frame. Host fps is still 60, but the DR-24 budget is blown.

> *lunch-play:* The clean route works end to end (s2-clean: won at 91.8 s, zero console errors on every run). Breaker trips and shorts are recoverable with a cart reset, and the retry click is fast (0.7 s).
> 
> Problems found by playing:
> - (P0) The doorstop can be thrown behind the conveyor, which is unreachable and never respawns. Without it the door can't be wedged and the job can't be finished without a restart.
> - (P0) Pip gets pinned between the wedged right leaf and the doorstop on the natural return path from the lift room. Movement keys do nothing and only a jump frees him.
> - The dolly parks in the doorway and stalls later legs. This happened in three runs.
> - E near a cart unplugs a working feed when nothing is tripped. A double-tap on reset kills the fridge feed.
> - 'E Grab the doorstop' appears at the wedged door, and one press cuts every cable through it.
> - The R keycap on Retry and replay does nothing, while R in play reloads instantly.
> - The fridge, pendant lamps and half-walls hide Pip at zoom 9.
> - At phone size the survey shows only a third of the room.
> 
> Performance: 60 fps at 1440×900 on the host GPU. snapshot().drawCalls is about 1230 for Lunch and about 1150 for Meeting, but since src/game.ts:451 now counts every pass (composer and outlines), the PROGRESS table's ~175 is no longer comparable. Re-baseline the table with tools/perf.mjs rather than treating this as a Lunch regression.

> *lunch-teach:* Every scripted state was reachable through the capture helper: start, survey, thin-cable scorch, water short with a re-trip on reset while wet, lift kick trip, the intended solve to the A result card, the lift-then-conveyor trap, spoil at exactly 120 s, and burn at 90 s after baking. Close() returned no console or page errors on any run. Retry from the fail card is instant. Side notes for other reviewers:
> - snap().drawCalls read 1243 at the start with fullfx (LR15 claimed about 175; possible regression, perf reviewer to confirm).
> - My scripted walks stalled at the closed door and at the lift divider (expected).
> - Pressing E near the wedged door picks the wedge back up, which re-closes the door (DR-18).

#### Teaching

> *lunch-models:* The models carry some teaching well: the bake dial on the oven, the fridge thermometer and sad-food icon, the floor conduits showing the post's fixed wiring, the cart gauges, and the scorch and warning badges. But the start-up-kick lesson is undercut: the winch never visibly pulls the lift (no rope, no drum spin), and the capacitor cart has none of a capacitor's visual cues and no socket. The physical story 'feed → cart → winch → lift' therefore isn't drawn. The capCord only appears once docked, and there is nothing at the inlet.

> *lunch-play:* (Not my main dimension; noted where it overlaps clarity.)
> 
> The in-world load story works well, with no text needed:
> - The thick-versus-thin rating is taught by a thin cable visibly warming.
> - The breaker budget shows on each cart's needle.
> - The capacitor is wired inline: the feed goes into the cart and a short dark cord runs to the winch (c17, LR9 readable).
> - The hard-wired feed post's conduits are drawn on the floor (v06, LR13 partly addressed).
> 
> Weak spots:
> - The fridge 'thermal storage' idea is never surfaced before it fails.
> - The conveyor-before-lift ordering, the kick sum, is invisible.
> - A door-cut is mislabelled as burning, which mixes up a mechanical cut with heat.
> - Bars still have no unit hint (LR12).

> *lunch-teach:* Lunch Rush has the strongest teaching backbone in the game, and most of its electricity is right at the level taught. Loads on one supply add up against a limit. An undersized cable cooks even when its supply's protection doesn't trip, which is true and a great lesson (E-7). A motor needs a short start-up surge above its running draw. Stored charge at the load supplies that surge, so the supply and cable only see the steady draw. Motors that start together add their surges, so you start them one at a time. Thermal mass lets a fridge ride through an outage. The capacitor is mandatory: the 9-bar kick is over any cart's 5 whichever cable you use, and the thick cable can't help because the limit is the cart's. So the surge is genuinely the mechanic that decides success.
> 
> The problem is that almost none of this can be seen. Loads, budgets and ratings appear nowhere in the world (finding 1). The capacitor never shows charge or discharge (finding 2). Kicks happen in one tick, the needle shows full scale on a dead circuit, and nothing happens at the motor (finding 3). Pulses don't scale with current (finding 9). Four faults share one icon, and there is no cause line (finding 8).
> 
> The result is that the room is solved by trial and error plus badge and prompt following. The player learns 'blue cart goes by the lift', not 'stored charge carries the surge'. Truth bugs that would mislead a learner:
> - Breakers that trip instantly at 1.2–1.8×. Real B-curve MCBs don't trip at all in 1 s at those levels. Reframing the carts as battery power carts with an overload cut-out makes the whole room truthful at no puzzle cost.
> - Any intact cable in water counts as a 'short'.
> - The capacitor starts full and charges for free.
> - Linear, 6-second cable cooking.
> - The doc verbs 'absorb' and 'eats'.
> There is one real moment of applying the idea: once you know the lift kicks, choosing thin versus thick for the kitchen and the start order of the motors. It needs the surge made visible before it can count as applied understanding.

#### Clarity

> *lunch-models:* Model-side clarity problems: the job-yellow colour is reused by 9 clutter crates and 12 mugs, and the clutter also has teal and white crates. That dilutes 'yellow means job item' right next to the wedge, bridges and storeroom. A dark socket box near the lift and the cap cart's missing socket give false or missing affordances. The storeroom 'darkness' is a tinted lid that still shows every crate, while the lamp shade pokes through bright, so the can't-grab-in-the-dark rule isn't sold by the visuals. The kitchen counters are office desks with keyboards, so the serving pass doesn't read as a kitchen.

> *lunch-play:* The scene itself is quite readable.
> - On-device state reads well: the needle gauges on the carts, the oven bake dial, the thermometer on the fridge and the sad-food badge over it (f02), the red bolt badge at a cut or short (n02), and the pulsing reset button.
> - The fail cards are icon-only and legible: the spoiled bowl or the oven, the thermometer, and the progress chain.
> - The 1440×900 survey shows the whole room.
> 
> The text layer fights the scene, though:
> - The very first prompt ('F Pick up the thin cable end') contradicts the card ('Wedge the door…'), and following it causes the first failure within 4 s.
> - The card still prints method text (LR8 still open: 'with the doorstop', '(or bridge it)', '(oven and lamps)').
> - The card skips the conveyor while the HUD chain highlights it.
> - A cut cable is called 'burned'.
> - The winch offers 'Switch on' with no feed.
> - Six job-yellow clutter crates compete with the yellow doorstop.
> - The marker reads as a floor tag, and south-wall items fall under the action bar.
> 
> A new player could probably work out the door, the mop and the post from the marker. They couldn't work out the fridge timer, the conveyor-first order or the capacitor before failing.

> *lunch-teach:* The card and prompt are the only words allowed, and in the two most instructive failures they actively mislead. The 'feed post' and 'leak' steps tick done when a scorching or shorting cable is merely plugged in, and the card then says 'Keep the oven on' while the oven is dead (shots 13, 16). The lift step ticks even when the breaker trips seconds later (trap run, T-37). The fridge, which can fail the job at 120 s, is never a step.
> 
> Other naming problems: 'Repair the burned cable' is shown for a door-cut cable. The carts are named A and B in prompts but carry no letters. The fridge bonus is '80%' of a unitless thermometer. 'Bars' are undefined. The kitchen-lamp cord is the same cream colour as a thin cable and stretches infinitely out of the post.
> 
> What reads well:
> - The HUD chain (oven → belt → lift with progress rings) and the thermometer.
> - The cart-coloured dial bezels.
> - Socket rings that pulse while you hold a plug.
> - The orange then black cable when overheated.
> - The puddle badge placed at the leak.
> - The sad-food icon and puffs before a spoil.
> - Icon-only fail cards that are clear and retry instantly (R).

#### Models

> *lunch-models:* Overall the Lunch kit is in the right style family. It uses chunky rounded boxes (rbox/RoundedBox), toon ramp shading, ink outlines on props and fixtures, and a warm office palette. Several fixtures read well at the game camera: the oven front (window, knobs, bake dial, socket plate), the fridge (magnets, handle, live thermometer), the kitchen feed post (yellow block, bolt glyph, socket, floor conduits to the oven and storeroom lamp), the conveyor (scrolling belt, legs, teal strip-curtain flaps), the swing doors (upright, portholes, kick plates), the cleaner bots, the mop bucket (wringer, bail, mop), the wedge (rubber ribs), the bridges (ink top strip), the splitters (socket face, power lamp) and the thick-cable dolly. Confirmed fixed: the bookshelf book colours vary per row, the vending machine faces +z, and the doors stand upright. g.audit(.02) returns [] at start. At .005 it lists only 9 paper-on-desk contacts of about 1 cm, which is benign. Console and page errors were [] in every run.
> 
> The weak spots are concentrated in the last third of the job and in decor that has no physics:
> - The lift reads as a floating table, Pip's head goes through it, and nothing connects the winch to it.
> - The tray floats across a 3 m gap.
> - A stray dark socket cube sits under the lift.
> - The capacitor cart doesn't read as capacitors and has no inlet.
> - Decor furniture has no colliders (benches, plants, chairs, rack), so Pip and the blobs interpenetrate them, and the audit can't see it.
> - The rack has an upright through two crates and is built twice.
> - Posters sit over windows and on each other.
> - The vending machine, cooler, pots and the oven's back are under-detailed, and the supply-cart gauges are bare boards from behind.
> - Supply cart A tips over when Pip simply walks past.

> *lunch-play:* (Not my dimension; noted in passing.)
> - The fridge back is a featureless white slab when orbiting (lunch-play-03).
> - The vending machine's back is a plain red block (03). The front now faces +z (LR2 fixed).
> - The baked tray is tiny and hard to read at the game camera (b01).
> - The cable passes through the open door leaf (d04).
> - The cyan crowd blob at (5.1,9.1), yaw 2.2, shows its back to the default camera (c01; LR3 partly open).

> *lunch-teach:* Not my dimension. The capacitor cart's four blue cans read well as electrolytic capacitors, and the supply carts read as power carts. Neither model carries state: the cap LED is static, and the carts have no letters and no budget pips. Those additions are specified in findings 1 and 2.
