### Arcade (`arcade`)

Reviewers: `arcade-models`, `arcade-play`, `arcade-teach`.

#### Fun

> *arcade-models:* Seen through the models, the arcade's set dressing is charming from the default camera. The neon sign, candy cabinets with tells (dance pad, claw balls, Game Boy, coin hopper), working cabinets with lit screens and the warm bench pool all give it a clear identity. Each signed-off cabinet lighting up its marquee, with a glow and confetti, is a good small payoff (shot -43). The fun is hurt by the room being inert. There is no cable, nothing chaotic is designed in, and the only physical beat is the tray carry, which looks broken because the tray tilts on edge (-32b). The win push-in lands on a black 'ALL FIXED' monitor instead of the row of revived machines (-74). The kid play-tester bounces and cheers nicely, but it is a human peg figure. A blob kid queue, as R4B suggested, would fit both the fun and the art rules.

> *arcade-play:* What works:
> - Popping a block is the best moment in the room: a crack, candy debris and a puff of smoke, and the bench cuts out.
> - The tripped PTC fuse glows red and visibly cools back to yellow; it reads well and it's physical.
> - The candy block colours and the big ✓ stamp give the bench a pleasant toy feel.
> - Signing off rings a bell and lights a back-wall cabinet, which you can see from the room camera.
> 
> What doesn't:
> - The room is a long hallway to a keypad. Fetching the tray takes about 8 s at sprint. After that, about 95 % of play happens in a fixed bench camera that can't be orbited or zoomed.
> - The things that should be funny are all off-screen at the bench: the kid hopping or slumping, the TILT! marquee, the serviced cabinet's lamp, and the back-wall cabinets lighting up.
> - Nobody in the room reacts to the trips and pops; `alarmed` stayed 0.
> - There is no cable, no designed chaos route and no physical bonus. Throwing the tray at the bench is not accepted, and chaos in the room (tossing a cone) costs grade.
> - Cabinets 3–5 share one answer (470 + 470 Ω), so the last two jobs are repeats.
> - Overall the arcade is pleasant but not a Good Job-style comedy room. The best fixes are to bring the payoff into frame, accept a thrown tray, and add one cable or chaos act in the hall.

> *arcade-teach:* The juice is good when you can see it. The fuse sparks, the marquee shows TILT!, a popped block sprays candy debris across the bench and floor (arcade-teach-14), and the kid's arms go up on a pass (arcade-teach-33). But that kid and the serviced cabinet are outside the bench camera, so the main reward reaches a seated player as a purple progress bar. The smoke and halo effects also cover the board and meter in the most dramatic frames. The room still has no designed chaos shortcut, and the cable is absent (DR-01, DR-05, both known). The 3 s play test does not drag: the five play tests total about 15 s. Pressing P during the test, which the prompt invites, cancels it, which makes it feel like dead time.

#### Playability

> *arcade-models:* Models create real camera problems. The 1.35 m storeroom half-walls and the 2.16 m cabinets are not occluders, so Pip disappears behind them on the tray route and among the right-wall cabinets (-50, -24, -52). At diagonal orbits behind a corner, neither shell wall cuts away and the camera shows only the outside of a 3 m wall (-81). The draw-call count has regressed to about 1500 (A13 was 1181), because the 12 cabinets and the 221-mesh bench are built into game.root unmerged. The host holds 60 fps, but low-end hardware won't. Note for anyone rerunning the captures: in ?manual mode the cutaway and fade lerps advance only once per render call, so shots need several advance(1/60) calls to settle (my scripts do 20). Unsettled single-advance shots can show false wall occlusion. g.audit(.02) reports 6 beanbag–paper overlaps from the lounge clutter recipe. No console or page errors in any script (all close() returned []).

> *arcade-play:* On desktop the clean route is solid:
> - The clutter lanes keep the storeroom run and the bench approach clear, with no stall in any of my walks.
> - The tray is reachable, and it can be recovered from behind the bench via the right end.
> - Dropping the tray from behind the bench counts.
> - The audit shows 0 overlaps, there were no console errors in any of the 14 runs, and the frame rate held at 60 fps (but with 1422 draw calls).
> - Fuse cool-down is 2.5 s and the play test is 3 s, so there is no dead wait over 3 s.
> 
> Blocking problems:
> 1. Phone portrait can't finish the job (P0). The sign-off stamp and two bins are off-screen and the bench has no touch buttons. In landscape the HUD covers the lever and the stamp.
> 2. P is a toggle while its prompt reads 'Fuse cooling' or 'Play test'. The natural retry turns the bench off, which is exactly the DR-19 failure.
> 3. R at the bench reloads the level without a confirm.
> 4. Space, Tab and Q also leak through at the bench.
> 5. The prompts invite graded mistakes: 'P Power on' appears on three cabinets that start broken.
> 6. Brute force is free: the meter is live, swaps under 0.6 s are never counted, and parts are billed only at sign-off.
> 7. Smaller issues: Pip walks through coworkers; the storeroom half-wall hides Pip; a thrown tray doesn't count.

> *arcade-teach:* The solve is reliable. solve.mjs and fail.mjs both complete, g.close() returned no errors, and the win fired at about 50 s of game time. The tray, the bench entry and the act() flow all work. Two prompt bugs hurt play: the prompt reads 'P Play test' while P powers off and wipes the soak, and a stale hover prompt shows 'F Flip the LED' through the whole hopper job and replaces 'Enter Sign off' after a pass. The PTC re-trips every 2.65 s while left on, which is noisy, although the player can still fix the chain while it cycles.

#### Teaching

> *arcade-models:* Two model issues weaken the teaching. The LED BASICS poster's formula and polarity strip is hidden behind the prize shelf (-19b), and the serviced cabinet's ribbon cable ends in mid-air on the bench (-36b), so the physical link that says 'this board is the cabinet's LED circuit' is missing. The bench itself teaches well through its models: candy-coloured blocks with real colour bands and values on top, brass bus bars for side-by-side pairs, an LED with a cathode flat that rotates when flipped, a PTC fuse disc that glows red and cools, hot blocks that go orange and red and smoke, and a transistor and coin wheel for the hopper. It is still the best close-up in the game (-36…-42, -78). The block pop has no physical 'pop off the board' (A6), and its smoke covers the meter at the moment the toast explains P = I²R (-41).

> *arcade-play:* The underlying model is truthful and well commented (logic.ts:1-17). The PTC self-reset, 'over-rating runs hot and dies early', series-adds and parallel-shares, the across-the-LED trap and polarity are all acted out with physical blocks, which is a real improvement on R4's rack menu.
> 
> The teaching is undercut in three ways:
> 1. The live meter plus free fast swaps let players tune by watching the bar rather than predicting with I = (V − Vf) ÷ R.
> 2. Cabinets 3–5 have the same 940 Ω answer, so battery life and base current don't change what the player does.
> 3. The toasts and story print the formula and part of the answer ('Only 0.3 V is left over…', '(I = (V − Vf) ÷ R)'), against 'say why, never how' (A8 still open).
> 
> Powering the start state just to look is counted as a mistake. That punishes the diagnostic habit the room should encourage (A7 still open).

> *arcade-teach:* What works: the arcade has the truest and most mechanical teaching of the station rooms. The chain socket makes series and parallel a physical act: blocks end to end add, and side by side they share, joined by brass bus bars. The board's printed traces make the ACROSS slot read as a parallel path. The 'across limits nothing' trap fails at once with a correct, cause-first sentence. The maths in read() is right: I = (V − Vf)/R_total with 1 Ω of wiring, the current split in a pair, the resistor across the LED carrying vf/rp, and battery life = mAh/I. The Rhythm pad is the one cabinet where the player has to apply an idea (no single block works, so they have to try side by side). The pinball's 220 Ω answer is the textbook one.
> 
> Where it falls short:
> - Tuning and truth. The PTC behaves like a bimetal breaker. Blocks pop at 1.77× within 1.7 s, although real resistors are qualified to take 6.25× for 5 s. 20 mA is treated as a cliff, although 5 mm LEDs are rated for 30 mA continuous. LED HEAT shows a 45 °C 'limit'. The Rhythm design rests on 0.3 V of headroom, which real Vf spread breaks.
> - The transistor job. It looks like the LED jobs with a different target number. The collector and motor circuit are never drawn, the meter says MOTOR FULL and PASSED while the verdict says 'too dim', and the ★ zone rewards the least overdrive, which is the opposite of good switch design.
> - Learning by trial and error. The bench is live while blocks change, sweeping is free (fail.mjs: 470→100→220 in 0.3 s steps cost nothing), and four of five cabinets have dozens to hundreds of elegant chains. A player can win by watching the bar rather than using V − Vf, and the meter never shows V − Vf as a live number.
> - Grading. Simply observing the broken cabinets as found scores 6 mistakes.

#### Clarity

> *arcade-models:* The tray (#ff7eb6) uses the exact clutter pink, and job-yellow #ffd84d is scattered over clutter boxes, beanbags and chairs, so the job item doesn't stand out without the marker (-01, -10). A grabbable cable reel next to the tray in a cable-less room is a strong false affordance (-12). The floating STOREROOM plaque reads from the default yaw but vanishes edge-on and from behind (-15, -83). At the game camera the 'OUT OF ORDER' marquee text is a few pixels tall (-49b); the broken/fixed state reads only through dark vs lit marquee and screen. That works, but broken cabinets have no other cue such as sparks, tape or a flicker. The bench monitor text is crisp at the bench view.

> *arcade-play:* Good:
> - The start view is readable. The tray glows on a dark counter in a clearly signed storeroom, and the marker cone points at it.
> - The bench parts are legible: the value-coloured bins, the A/S/D/X pads printed on the board, and the reversed-LED '+' marker moving.
> - The LIGHT bar's band and ★ zone are a clear target.
> 
> Weak:
> - While carrying, the marker follows the tray in Pip's hands, not the bench.
> - The bench shows about 100 words with values repeated three times. The monitor labels are about 9 px.
> - At the start, the panel shows the pinball spec before it matters, and covers the middle of a phone screen.
> - Keys aren't on the parts: no 1–4 on the bins, no P or POWER on a lever that looks like an arcade joystick, no Enter on the stamp.
> - E means 'stand up' and F means 'flip' at the bench, against their meanings elsewhere.
> - The card's step 2 ticks out of order if you sit before fetching the tray.
> - Prompts describe states ('Fuse cooling') rather than what the key does.
> - The LED halo, then a smoke ball, hide the monitor at the Claw failure, exactly when the player needs to read it.

> *arcade-teach:* The board itself reads well (arcade-teach-23): rails, wire links on the empty pads, the + and − on the LED, and the ACROSS slot wired between the rails. The reversed LED shows its red '+' on the ground side. The text load at the bench is still heavy. The card, panel ask, story, rows, toast with formula, meter and footer come to about 70 words in arcade-teach-13. The current appears three times (meter tile, bar label and panel), and the ask twice (card and panel). Formulas are printed in failure toasts. The tier copy contradicts itself: 'PLAY TEST PASSED ✓' appears alongside 'too dim', and a motor shows FULL alongside 'too dim'. 'too dim' is even used for a motor's base current. The meter's small caps (LIGHT, LED HEAT and so on) are about 9 px, which is known under DR-48.

#### Models

> *arcade-models:* What works: the bench is chunky and rounded, with a clear supply → fuse → chain → LED → across layout. The candy resistor blocks are excellent (rounded body, colour bands, brass caps, value tag). Cabinets read as arcade uprights from the front, with marquee, tilted screen head, deck buttons and coin door. Desk, monitor, cart, bins, plants and the floor lamp are fine at the game camera. Outlines are present on all toon props, and the scene uses only MeshToonMaterial (667) and MeshBasicMaterial (109), with no Standard or Phong materials (DR-57 passes). What fails: cabinets have blank backs and 1.5 m² flat sides. The claw tell merges into its cabinet (the glass swallows the deck and screen). The handheld floats in front of its cabinet. The pinball reads as a side table. The change machine and prize shelf are slabs. Beanbags are macarons. The kid is a human. Cardboard is pastel. Office task chairs stand in for arcade stools. The storeroom stock bricks look like tray blocks. The serviced cabinet clips 4 cm into the bench. There are 6 point lights (+1). The carpet's median luma is about 103, below the 140–185 band. Pip's helmet 'cat-ear' ridge (DR-64) is still visible in crops -32b and -34; that belongs to the Pip owner.

> *arcade-play:* (Not this reviewer's main dimension; noted while playing.)
> - The bench, bins, candy blocks with real colour bands, PTC disc, LED with a cathode flat, and the TO-92 and coin-wheel motor are detailed enough at the bench camera.
> - The back-wall cabinets have distinct props on each one (pinball table, dance pad, claw box, handheld, hopper) and finished backs (shot 75).
> - The play-test kid is still a realistic human child (DR-60, shots 41 and 72).
> - The STOREROOM plaque floats in mid-air.
> - The cabinet ribbon cable ends loose on the bench.
> - The tray is carried tilted.
> - The pastel clutter (pink and teal crates, macaron-like beanbags) and the confetti carpet stay busy at the game camera (shots 01 and 02), but the bench still reads as the focal point in the survey.

> *arcade-teach:* Not my dimension. Incidental notes: the candy blocks with real colour bands and brass end caps read clearly. The LED's unlit dome is drawn too white (tint 0.55), so the red pinball LED looks like a white LED. The TO-92 transistor shows only B and E and there is no collector. The motor is a grey can parked beside the meter with no wiring. The play-tester is still a realistic human kid (DR-60, known).

### Arcade Rush (`arcade-rush`)

Reviewers: `arcade-rush-play`, `arcade-rush-teach`.

#### Fun

> *arcade-rush-play:* What works: the core bench loop is readable and snappy once learned. With a known answer a cabinet takes about 5 s (2 s to read, 1–7 keys, a 2 s play test), the meter, the LED glow and the ★ zone make a hit feel good, and the 'Elegant ★' toast with the bell is a tidy beat. Something physical happens in the first second if the player wants it (I threw a cone at 1.2 s, fastestProp 7.9 m/s, so DR-03 passes).
> 
> What doesn't work:
> - **The grade:** an idle 3 minutes grades A and records a best A, because the time axis is always 180 s ≤ 190. Cost punishes throughput: 32 elegant cabinets grade C on cost.
> - **Variety:** generated cabinets are LED-only single faults collapsing to about nine answers. There's no escalation, no queue or stakes, and the physical cabinet never changes.
> - **The payoff:** the kid, the cabinet and the confetti are all outside the bench camera, so the payoff of every loop is a text pill.
> - **The clock:** it hard-cuts an order at 1.8/2 s.
> - **Chaos:** throwing the tray onto the bench is punished (damage 1, cost 10, not accepted). The room has no cable, so AGENTS 4 has nothing to say here.
> 
> The mode currently feels like a timed quiz bolted onto a room, not a Good Job rush.

> *arcade-rush-teach:* The tempo of the core loop is good. A scripted clean player can fix about 40 cabinets in 126 s, and a 2 s play test with a bell and confetti per cabinet gives a pleasant rhythm. But the mode has no stakes: the grade is always A (zero cabinets earned a gold A, a star and a bonus), the cost axis punishes fixing more, and nothing escalates over the three minutes, so there is no reason to replay for mastery. The tray fetch at the start eats the clock with no fun or learning. Tying the grade to cabinets fixed, first-try accuracy and an escalating fault mix would turn it into a real practice game.

#### Playability

> *arcade-rush-play:* Clean route: spawn → tray → bench takes about 6.5 s of game time, and the lanes are clear. The tray can't be wedged (thrown into the storeroom corner and against the shelf, it stays reachable and the prompt finds it), and the audit is clean (`g.audit(.02)` = []). No console errors in 9 scripts.
> 
> Problems:
> - **Phone:** the bench is unplayable at 390×844. Two bins and the sign-off stamp are off-screen, there are no touch controls and the badges are keyboard keys (P0, A12 still open).
> - **R at the bench** reloads the run instantly. Space jumps Pip while seated.
> - **Live swaps:** every swap with the power on trips the fuse, because lifting a block leaves 'wire only' for more than 0.15 s, so the trip bonus is unattainable for experimenters.
> - **Prompt:** 'P Power on' on a broken start counts a mistake and a trip immediately (A7 still open).
> - **Occlusion:** the storeroom shelf hides Pip and the tray with no fade.
> - **Performance:** draw calls are 1416, 1491 and 1178 against a budget of 250.
> 
> Leaving the bench mid-soak is forgiving (the soak continues), and Enter before the pass is safely rejected.

> *arcade-rush-teach:* The rush plays without errors: every g.close() returned [], and the shift ends on the clock as specified. The friction points are these. Powering on to look is punished as damage on half the cabinets (a free look is needed). The fuse cool-down is a locked wait of up to 2.5 s after the chain is already fixed. The clock runs during a redundant tray carry. The hover-hint prompt can hide the sign-off key. The LED-pop smoke ball briefly covers the LED and meter. All of these are cheap code fixes in station.ts and logic.ts.

#### Teaching

> *arcade-rush-play:* Not my primary dimension, but noted. Rush reuses the station's truthful model (I = (V − Vf) ÷ R, series/parallel, the PTC fuse), and the elegant zone rewards least current. Stories that name the fault ('went in backwards', 'fitted a block across') and 'backwards' starting with the correct chain remove the diagnosis. The answers become a lookup table after about 5 cabinets. The stale trip toast teaches a false cause (100 Ω 'trips' 9 V). Brute force is effectively free, since mistakes never affect the always-A grade, so DR-38 fails in Rush.

> *arcade-rush-teach:* Arcade Rush gets the core relation right. I = (V − Vf)/(R + 1 Ω), series sum, parallel combine and polarity all check out in logic.ts. The chain socket is a real mechanic: the player stands blocks in positions, and the CHAIN Ω tile plus the LIGHT band with its ★ zone are visible before power, so prediction is possible. As a drill, though, rush mostly fails to make the player apply the idea. About 35 % of cabinets need no resistor choice: 14 % can be signed off as found, and 21 % are a flip-only ★. The stories print the diagnosis ('block across the LED', 'went in backwards'). Free hot-swapping with an instant meter makes hill-climbing beat computing: a random guess is reliable a quarter of the time, and eleven answers cover everything. Heat (P = I²R against ¼ W and the 60 % rule) never binds in rush, so half of the Arcade lesson goes unpractised. Several player-facing texts contradict the physics or the visuals, and these are the most damaging for learning: 'too bright, smells warm' when the fuse trips (67 % of hot cabinets); 'runs hot and dies early' on an instant LED pop; 'barely glowing' at 7 mA beside a brightly lit LED; a PTC that re-arms while powered; and an overdriven LED that renders paler than a correct one. The fixes are concrete: stories derived from read() and symptom-only, a free first look, latching PTC with power-off reset, first-try scoring, and an escalation that brings in heat and battery cabinets.

#### Clarity

> *arcade-rush-play:* The objective card (3 dots, current step) and the one-line prompt mostly agree with the state.
> 
> Problems:
> - **Feedback lag:** the card lags about 0.8 s at sit-down. Toasts outlive the arrangement they describe: a 100 Ω board shows TRIP with 'Nothing in the chain limits the current', which misleads.
> - **Hidden damage:** bench mistakes don't show in the HUD damage tally until the result card.
> - **Clocks:** the ring measures 240 s while the clock counts 180 s, and the panel repeats the seconds.
> - **Result card:** it still leads with a meaningless 3:00 A row, with orders served as a caption.
> - **Key hints:** bins, lever and stamp have no keycaps, so the 12-key layout is learned by hovering.
> - **Word count:** about 40–45 words outside the monitor at the bench: card, panel story and rows, prompt, Esc chip, board legends.
> - **Floating sign:** the STOREROOM sign still floats.
> 
> A new player can tell 'carry the tray' from the marker cone and the card, and 'sit at the bench' from the prompt. But they can't tell from the scene that powering a broken board costs them, or that swapping live is a trap.

> *arcade-rush-teach:* The bench reads well at a glance: a big supply label, colour-coded candy blocks with real bands, a clear ★ zone on the LIGHT bar, a TRIP tile and FUSE COOLING. The main clarity failures are these. The prompt is overridden by a stale hover hint ('D Empty: plain wire' through trip, pop and sign-off). 'P Fuse cooling' labels P as something it doesn't do. Values are tripled between the side panel and the monitor, while the Vf input sits in about 9 px footer text. The success feedback (the play-test kid, the cabinet lamp, TILT) is off-camera, so outcomes are learned from a bar and a toast. Results use the 'Orders served' noun, unlike the rest of the room.

### Garage (`garage`)

Reviewers: `garage-models`, `garage-play`, `garage-teach`.

#### Fun

> *garage-models:* The physical payoff is the right idea. Carrying the robot onto a rolling road and then watching it drive a painted delivery lane around the room is a real Good Job-style toy moment. At the default zoom the drive reads well: the robot shows its face while driving, the wheels spin and the route loops past the clutter (garage-models-76). But the fun is undercut in three places.
> - The win camera frames an empty bench and stand instead of the arriving robot and green dock lamp (garage-models-77/78).
> - During the drive, a player at zoom 9 sees almost none of it.
> - The robot is one of three identical bots, with no visible fault before you fix it.
> 
> The arc and dizzy reboot are good slapstick ideas, but they happen edge-on to the bench camera or bleach into a white blob. Chaos is still limited to knocking crates, cones and bins about. The bins visibly tip over just from Pip walking (garage-models-10, -12), which is nice incidental physics. There is no designed chaos shortcut in this station room.

> *garage-play:* What works: the garage has the best 'see the physics' moment in the game. An empty PULSE makes the white-hot arc jump the switch, sparks fly, the robot on the stand wobbles, and cyan beads stall at the switch. A diode makes the beads keep circling the little motor-and-diode loop and fade, which shows the concept on the copper (shots 14, 18). The robot driving its painted lane to the dock is a charming payoff, and the scope trace drawing across is satisfying. The first spectacle (the arc) arrives about 15 s in for a clean player.
> 
> What doesn't: the fun sits on a 1 m square of bench, mostly too small to see. The reboot faces away from the camera, the pass celebration is a tiny 'Elegant' toast, and nobody in the room reacts to the bang. Around the bench, the 22 × 16 m room with 111 props has no reason to touch anything. There's no cable, no chaos shortcut (a thrown robot doesn't count), no physical bonus, and the drive ends with 9 s of watching. When the robot bulldozed Pip 4 m down its lane there was no reaction at all, which wastes free slapstick. Grading gives A regardless of how many fuses you trip. Clean solve about 39 s of play (46.5 s with my camera checks), plus about 9.5 s of drive.

> *garage-teach:* Carrying the robot onto the stand is a nice physical opener. Its stand snap is generous (2.6 m) and readable. The PULSE → arc/beads → scope loop has a satisfying rhythm, and the final drive around the garage (knocking over a bin on the way) is charming.
> 
> But the room has no chaos route (DR-01) and no cable act (DR-05).
> 
> The success beats are flat:
> - TEST advances the job before its five cycles play, so there is no 'passed' moment.
> - The payoff drive doesn't stop at a line or start under load, so it doesn't celebrate the lessons.
> - The win camera frames Pip at the empty bench rather than the robot at the dock.
> 
> The R4B 'Kickback' redesign ideas that would add slapstick were not built: a knife switch, the robot coasting into shelving, dragging the ground cable.

#### Playability

> *garage-models:* The intended route works end to end with the spec's coordinates: pad → (3.4,-4) → (2.5,-4.4) drop, which snaps within 2.6 m; then (2.9,-1.1) → bench E. All 3 jobs pass at tier 3 and the room is won at about 25–29 s game time. There were zero console or page errors in 5 runs.
> 
> Friction found:
> - Pip vanishes behind 2.2 m cabinet columns and behind the bench scope, because none of them fade (garage-models-38, -41).
> - A clutter cabinet column and crates crowd the stand's back.
> - One walk stalled against the decor robot's solid at (8.4, -5.2) (b-close log).
> - The prompt says 'Work at the bench' before the robot is placed.
> - Draw calls are about 1156.
> 
> g.audit(.04) is clean. g.audit(.02) reports only the two stacked cabinet+box pairs, at (-1.6,-4.91) and (-8.21,3.21), depth .02.

> *garage-play:* The clean route is smooth and short: about 2 s from spawn to the robot, about 3 s to carry it around the bench's right end, and about 2 s to sit. The clutter lanes keep the robot route and walking route clear; every walkTo arrived with no stalls. g.audit(0.02) is empty, and there were zero console errors across 5 scripts. The robot can be thrown, re-grabbed, dropped on wheel stacks and recovered; I found no soft-lock. A wedged robot stayed reachable, because the nearest grab tolerance is generous. The real problems:
> - A/S/D at the bench remove fitted parts, which matters because players reach for WASD.
> - The carried robot tips on its side beside Pip's head.
> - At phone size the bench tray and battery are cut off and the toast covers PULSE.
> - Tab, Space and R leak through at the bench.
> - Pip disappears behind the bench and scope at the stand.
> Mouse play works well: hover enlarges parts and sockets, and clicking picks, fits and flips. The fuse self-resets, so there's no dead end after a short.

> *garage-teach:* The clean route from the spec plays end-to-end with zero console errors in three runs: carry, stand snap, bench, 3 jobs, drive, won. Esc leaves the bench. PULSE is refused (with a toast) until the robot is on the stand. The fuse self-resets in 2.5 s. Nothing soft-locks: every fault is recoverable by flipping or removing a part, and parts can't be lost because they live on the bench.
> 
> The only dead control is 'P Fuse cooling'. Grading is too loose:
> - time 420 s vs a ~22–45 s solve;
> - a PULSE experiment costs a bonus.

#### Teaching

> *garage-models:* The bench model itself teaches well spatially:
> - copper traces on a green PCB;
> - a battery, PTC fuse, motor can, NODE test point, MOSFET and controller;
> - three dashed 'drop a part here' sockets;
> - a blue star-ground wire that appears when the lever is flipped (garage-models-62);
> - current beads that keep circling the motor+diode loop after the switch opens (garage-models-59).
> 
> That last one is a truthful, visible picture of flyback current, and it is the best teaching visual in the room. The model-side weaknesses all hide the very cue being taught:
> - The arc whitens the switch it is about (garage-models-70/72).
> - The robot's red-eye reboot faces away from the bench camera.
> - The TEST cycle lamps sit behind the buttons.
> - The harness that 'wires the robot to the bench' starts under the parts tray and ends in a wheel, not at the motor or a connector.

> *garage-play:* (Secondary for this key.) The model is truthful and the shutdown visualisation is excellent. But the act is mostly a menu pick: each part fits only one socket, and the prompt names the socket key. So 'where protection goes' (the topology the sockets are named after) is never chosen, and cycling 1–5 + P brute-forces each job without penalty. Job 2's failure ('too slow for the stop line') has no physical consequence: the robot doesn't coast past a line, so the idea lives only in a millisecond number. Job 3's ground-route idea is hidden behind a tiny lever while the prompt points at the parts tray.

> *garage-teach:* The model is the strongest physics in the game, and it holds up:
> - An implicit L·di/dt node solver with diode thresholds and MOSFET avalanche.
> - The closed-form diode decay is unit-tested.
> - A diode + 24 V zener packaged as one 'CLAMP' (so the old hidden 'zener only works flipped and in series' rule from R4B is gone).
> - A truthful set of 'this doesn't help' guardrails: the RC snubber can't absorb ½LI² (1 µF would need about 212 V), and the bulk cap gives the coil no path.
> - A backwards diode really is a battery short through the on MOSFET; a backwards unidirectional TVS really does conduct like a closed switch; the reversed electrolytic vents.
> - Failure toasts now state causes, not fixes. The logic.test regex guards this, except the scope string 'Fix the backwards part, reset the FUSE'.
> 
> The beads that keep circling the motor through the diode after the switch opens are exactly the right picture of 'the coil's current needs a path'.
> 
> The problem is that the player never has to use any of this. Placement is fixed per part and the socket glows. Orientation defaults to correct. The tray order matches the job order. The ground fix is the only remaining lever. So a 'press the next key' player gets A/A/A in 22 s.
> 
> Three truth issues:
> - The stop-line story (1 ms of current deciding where a robot stops) gives a wrong magnitude. The real lesson is relay or brake-coil release time (Pickering: zener ≈ ⅓ the diode's release time).
> - The air arc across a MOSFET is wrong: avalanche dumps ½LI² into the die as heat (Nexperia AN10273).
> - A 4 ms motor spin-up is about 1–2 orders too short.
> 
> The beads speed up 1.8× at turn-off, circle the wrong loop in the 'stuck' case, and a slow-stop TEST plays the reset animation. All three contradict the text.

#### Clarity

> *garage-models:* Clarity suffers mostly from colour. Job yellow '#ffc629' is in the garage clutter palette, so yellow crates, yellow cabinet columns, yellow mail carts, a yellow chair and a yellow reel surround the yellow job items and the yellow marker (about 2.8% of the play-area pixels at start). The job robot is visually identical to the decor robot next to it. The marker is a pale translucent un-outlined cone that rides on the carried robot instead of pointing at the stand. False-affordance reels, a splitter and a cable dolly invite 'Grab the splitter' in a room with no cable. Bench labels are 7–8 px at 1440×900. On the plus side, the bench view is uncluttered and the scope trace is large and legible.

> *garage-play:* The objective card is concise and the bench reads cleanly at 1440×900. The board's left-to-right battery → fuse → motor → node → switch → controller layout, the dashed '+' empty sockets, the glow on the legal socket and 'Robot not on the stand' on the scope are all good no-text cues.
> Problems:
> - The marker rides on the carried robot instead of showing the stand.
> - The prompt calls the robot 'the cart', and there are two identical-looking teal robots and a yellow 'cart' by spawn.
> - '1–5 Change the parts' misleads in job 3.
> - 'P Fuse cooling' and 'reset the FUSE' name non-actions.
> - Failing panel values aren't red.
> - The toast text is long (about 45 words for about 16 s) and repeats every number (77 V three times).
> - The step-2 dot can tick before step 1.
> - Job-yellow clutter and leftover cable reels add noise around the one yellow-lidded job item.

> *garage-teach:* What works:
> - The board is a clean, legible schematic-in-3D: battery → fuse → motor → node → switch → ground, with named socket posts and a yellow probe lead to the scope.
> - The scope's red 'resets above 50 V' and green 'brake: off ≤ 1 ms' bands give the player a target to read the trace against, which is very good.
> - The prompt chain ('P Pulse the motor' → '1–5 Change the parts' → 'Enter Test') is consistent.
> 
> What doesn't:
> - About 75 words at the bench, and the same number appears three times.
> - Board labels are about 10 px.
> - The fuse state lives in a stale scope message and a frozen 'cooling 2.5 s' row, with a 'P' prompt that does nothing.
> - The reboot consequence is mostly off-screen: the robot's face is edge-on and the stars sit behind the TEST STAND plaque.
> - Job 3's 'long shared ground wire' is never drawn.
> - After a fix the scope leaves the view that showed the failure.

#### Models

> *garage-models:* Strong models:
> - The delivery robot (robotMesh) has about 8 cues: spoked wheels, a dark chassis with yellow bumpers, a glossy teal body, a cream cargo bin with a yellow lid and handle slot, a head with a dark face screen and glowing eyes, and an antenna lamp. It reads at the game camera and looks charming when its face is visible.
> - The bench board is detailed and honest.
> - The roller door and the tyre stacks read correctly.
> - The mop bucket, coolbox and chairs are well built.
> 
> Weak models:
> - The floor lamps read as yellow flags (open zero-thickness cone).
> - The rolling road is four stubby tombstone rollers.
> - The TEST STAND sign is a one-sided plane that vanishes from behind.
> - The wall chargers are blank cream plaques with no cable.
> - The parcel shelves have only front posts.
> - The bench cabinet front and back, the scope back, the tool-chest back and the side-cabinet backs are large blank faces.
> - Cardboard boxes are one size with an identical tape+label layout in five colours, including teal, yellow and grey-blue, which read as plastic tubs.
> 
> Outlines are present and dark enough on most props (darkest-2% luma about 20–30 on cabinets and the robot; Pip about 56). Floors remain near-white (median 214–226, both rim and norim), so contact shadows and value separation are weak. The teal lounge rug at (-6.8, 4.4) is an office prop out of place in a service garage; a rubber anti-fatigue mat would fit better. The Pip helmet ridge ('cat-ear' fin, DR-64) is still visible from behind and at the win (garage-models-15, -66); that is a cross-room Pip issue.

> *garage-play:* (Seen while playing.) The robot model is cute and readable on its pad. The bench board, scope cabinet and test pod read well. Issues:
> - The carry pose (tilted robot at head height, pierced by the marker).
> - The face points +x, so the bench camera never sees the eyes.
> - The decor robots duplicate the job robot's look.
> - The 'TEST STAND' plaque floats on a thin post behind the stand.
> - The arc bloom washes out the SWITCH label for about 0.5 s (DR-66 known).

> *garage-teach:* Out of scope for this teaching pass. In passing:
> - The harness board, parts and scope read well at the bench camera.
> - The PTC fuse disc is tiny (about 14 px) and glows filament-red.
> - The diode band is about 6 px.
> - The arc's bloom washes out the SWITCH and the ACROSS SWITCH socket.
> - The robot's face points +x, away from the bench.

### QFN (`qfn`)

Reviewers: `qfn-models`, `qfn-play`, `qfn-teach`.

#### Fun

> *qfn-models:* From the models side: the slapstick potential is there. Cabinet towers tip, chairs fall when Pip walks through, and the crate carry is physical. The win, though, frames the back of Pip's hat in the corner (shots -50 to -52), and the room's machines never react to the boards being shipped. A conveyor into the reflow oven or a stack light turning green would make shipping a board feel like production. Currently the only feedback is a green slab appearing on the side table.

> *qfn-play:* What works: the bench puzzle is fun. It plays like Flow Free with real stakes. Dragging a track cell by cell with rising ticks, the bell when a pad of the same net is reached, and the 'VDD is joined' chime are satisfying. Par turns each board into a small optimisation puzzle, and CHECK is free, so experimenting doesn't cost grades, unlike the arcade. Board 3 escalates nicely (the crossing that becomes possible with a via, the chip cooling as thermal vias go in). The crate pickup gives a ring burst and a satisfying clunk. What's missing: the room part lasts about 5 s (crate at t≈1 s, bench at t≈5 s). After that 120 props, the pick-and-place, the oven and the AOI are only scenery, with no cable, no chaos route and no physical bonus. The one natural chaos act (throwing the crate at the bench) is ignored and counted as damage. The success beats are flat: the next board appears in the same frame and the finished board becomes a slab on the side table. The win push-in frames Pip cut off at the bottom-left corner behind the result card (qfn-play-36). Throwing the crate at a coworker does trigger the '!' bubble (qfn-play-90), so the slapstick systems work in this room. They're just never invited.

> *qfn-teach:* Routing still plays like a satisfying Flow-Free puzzle. Pads chime when a net joins, parts drop in with a clatter, the send-back groans with the crew alarm, and par invites a replay. The room around it (reflow oven, pick-and-place, inspection box) is scenery: SHIP just stacks a board on the side table, with no bring-up test, LED, oven or tombstoning payoff (review 4's 'Bench + Oven' is still not built). So the success and failure moments for decoupling and heat are a toast, not an event. Adding a 2–3 s bring-up test (LED stutters or throttles for tier 1, steady for tier 2/3) would add both fun and teaching.

#### Playability

> *qfn-models:* At the game camera, 2.2 m cabinet towers (two cabinets with a box on top) sit 2.3 m in front of the bench stand. Pip is reduced to a hat during the crate hand-off (shot -85), and fully hidden near the crane (shot -24). That cause, only pillars fading, is cross-room. A level chair inside the clean lane gets knocked over on every spec route. Performance holds 60 fps on the host GPU, but at 1201 draw calls the scene is fragile on weaker hardware.

> *qfn-play:* The clean route is short and clear: spawn → crate (2.3 m) → bench (about 10 m), all in a clutter lane, with no dead walking (the longest leg is about 2 s). The crate never wedged in five throw tests (pnp, aoi, rack gap, side table, over the bench): it always landed at floor or tabletop height and stayed reachable, because job items win grab priority within reach. Problems: (1) P0 on a phone: CHECK, SHIP, TURN, LAYER and VIA are off-screen and have only keyboard fallbacks, so the job can't be finished on touch. (2) The prompt 'Set the crate on the bench' shows in places where E drops the crate on the floor. (3) A cabinet+box clutter stack in front of the bench hides Pip at the default camera. (4) Moving a two-pin part by its big coloured ends draws a track. The grab body is a 30 px sliver. (5) There are 1197 draw calls at the start camera. (6) Room damage and bench mistakes share limits.damage=1. Modeless input itself (drag body to move, click again to turn, drag from a pad to draw, tap a track to cut, V mid-stroke) works through the real pointer and is a big improvement on review 4's nine modal tools. Undo and the refusal toasts ('C1 would sit on U1', 'short') make mistakes cheap.

> *qfn-teach:* No soft-locks or console errors in either run (g.close() returned []). The full clean solve reached won with three boards shipped and 0 mistakes, and the A/A/A result card showed Pip in frame (qfn-teach-38). One hidden rule remains on board 3: layer-2 tracks must start on a via. In my first scripted run, a layer-2 GND track that started inside the exposed pad was refused because the EP vias weren't there yet. A player who draws on L2 first gets 'Start a layer 2 track on a via…', which explains it, and mid-stroke V helps, so review 4's item is partly fixed.

#### Teaching

> *qfn-models:* The bench models do the teaching well: tracks as chunky copper, decoupling loops that glow and race beads, the chip heating up, and thermal vias. The room models teach nothing yet. The posters' captions are illegible at the game camera. The machines (PnP, reflow, AOI) could show the real production pipeline the boards go into: placement, then solder, then inspection. As built, they are scenery that doesn't read as those machines. A QFN package model with lead tabs would also address R4A's 'nothing about the QFN package itself'.

> *qfn-play:* (Not my primary dimension.) Placement-before-routing and one-layer-can't-cross are learned by doing. Decoupling is measured on real copper paths, and thermal vias in parallel use an honest formula. But the chip's heat shows with no power, and the loop beads look like current on an unpowered board (DR-29/30 territory for the teach reviewer).

> *qfn-teach:* The QFN bench is still the strongest 'concept is the mechanic' station, and most of its logic holds up. One copper layer really can't cross, and the pen refuses with a reason (shorts are prevented at the gesture, not graded later). Connectivity is a real breadth-first search over copper. The decoupling loop is measured on the actual copper path from cap to the chip's pin pair. Vias really change layer. The thermal model is a correct parallel-conductance formula with visible diminishing returns: 135 → 105 → 88 → 77 → 70 °C for 0 to 4 vias, from the run log. The lesson breaks in four places. (1) The *why* of decoupling is wrong: the note and the constant-speed beads teach 'current takes time to travel', not 'loop inductance makes the supply sag' (logic.ts:274, station.ts:228-230). (2) Thermal vias work even when they land on nothing on layer 2. Three of the four vias in the hand-made reference land on bare laminate, and my broken run still reached 70 °C. (3) The chip is red-hot before it is powered. (4) Board 1's stated lesson (pin order decides connector placement) can't be experienced: the header routes from any edge (qfn-teach-30). Because shipping a tier-1 board has no consequence, reliability is learned as 'push the panel numbers into the green'. A player can succeed by trial and error: move C1 until the loop row says ≤ 4, add vias until the chip row turns green. That is still doing, not reading, but the understanding sits in the toast text. The numbers to retune: a 70 °C chip limit teaches an ambient rating as a junction rating; use 1.6 W and 100 °C, which keeps 4 vias. 'Cheaper to make' for shorter tracks names the wrong cost driver. CHECK is free and only a tier-0 SHIP counts as a mistake, which is good (DR-02).

#### Clarity

> *qfn-models:* The job crate is a recoloured clutter carton named 'crate' like every box. The grab cue and 'Grab the crate' prompt land on a kraft junk box at (−7.6, 3.8) (shots -20 and -71). Job yellow, and the yellow-with-ink-stripes language, is used by the crane, a cart 2.3 m from the hand-off table, a chair, a stock bin, reel flanges, the PnP posts and pendants. A 'parts' recipe drops a cable reel and a yellow splitter by the bench in a room with no cable. Floor luma of 196–201 makes the pastel props almost the same value as the floor, a difference of 0–10 with norim. The bench camera frame is legible, but the near-edge connector covers the board title plate, a regression of R3A N7.

> *qfn-play:* The room reads well. The yellow taped spot, the STOCK sign and the marker lead to the crate, and the bench is mid-room under its own light. At the bench the board is well framed at 16:10 and the net colours match the chips in the panel, but the HUD around it is heavy: about 60–80 words, and the board name three times (card, panel header, world plate). The prompt says 'Draw from a pad' while the real first task is placement. Pin tags and key letters are 5–10 px. The ratsnest dangles to invisible parts before the crate arrives and doesn't follow a dragged part. Job yellow is spent on a cart, a chair, splitters and 'locked' connector caps (which mean the opposite of 'grab me'). The marker floats 1.5 m above the crate and lands on Pip's hat at the bench step. Board 3's chip glows 'over temperature' before anything is wired. The send-back toast states the cause ('J1 must sit on a board edge with its mouth facing out'), but red rings cover every pad, not J1. Could a new player solve it from the scene alone? Board 1's 'mouth out' rule and board 2's 'cap hugs its pins' rule need the panel sentence or a failed check first. Board 3's 'start a layer-2 track on a via' is still only discovered through a refusal toast.

> *qfn-teach:* The bench framing, keycaps, dashed ratsnest and live net checklist read well, and the modeless input fixed in review 4 holds (5 buttons: TURN, LAYER, VIA, CHECK, SHIP). Clarity problems that hurt the lesson: the ok and too-long loop glows both wash to pale stripes over red and blue copper (additive blend), and a failing loop row renders in neutral ink, not red. Notes cite 'U1 pin 8/pin 7' but the chip shows no pin numbers. Asks, the job card and the SHORT LOOP poster print the method ('caps hug their pins', 'use layer 2 and vias'). The send-back cue (rings on every unjoined pad) doesn't point at the part the toast names (J1's mouth). The thermal vias become invisible once placed. The panel's ask plus rows is about 40 words, which is within the bench-monitor allowance but long.

#### Models

> *qfn-models:* Most of the QFN room's model problems are about identity and placement, not broken meshes. g.audit(.02) at start is clean: only three 2 cm cabinet-and-box resting contacts. Materials are clean too: 516 MeshToon and 108 MeshBasic, with no Standard or Phong. There are 3 point lights, under the DR-66 cap of 4. The best models in the room are the bench-board parts: the dark QFN body with its printed name, pin-1 dot and net-coloured pin tags; SMD and through-hole pads in net colours; 2-pin parts with net-coloured caps; and a connector shroud with a mouth chevron. The hot-chip lerp and glow, the layer-2 x-ray and the thermal vias read very well from the bench camera (shots -40 to -49). Pip, the coworkers and the cartons are on-style: toon ramp, outlines, chunky. The room's fixtures are where it falls short. The pick-and-place reads as a yellow arch over a table. The reflow oven reads as a lavender sideboard. The AOI reads as a photocopier with a monitor sunk into it. The board rack is a solid cream block that hides its own boards. The stock bins read as soap bars. The bench is a plain slab with blank back and ends. On top of that, the clutter is office kit: desk pods, filing-cabinet towers, bookshelves of candy-bar books and cones. It comes in pastel mint, lilac and periwinkle instead of kraft and neutrals, and is parked against the machines (a bookshelf 0.3 m in front of the PnP, another 0.1 m off the oven, a cart under the crane). Small overlaps include the AOI monitor sunk 12.5 cm, the PnP beam through its glass hood, feeder reels buried 8 cm, shelf reels floating 3 cm, crane stripes poking 5 mm, and a coplanar seam between the bench and side-table tops. Draw calls are 1201 against the 250 budget, because every part is its own mesh.

> *qfn-play:* (Not my primary dimension.) Bench pucks are chunky and readable, and the QFN body is a clean ink tile. Shipped boards on the side table are flat slabs with no detail. The parts crate is a plain prop box tinted yellow, with no job-item stripes or icon.

> *qfn-teach:* Not my dimension. Incidental notes: the bench parts read cleanly at the bench camera. The QFN body's transparency plus the heat glow makes a pink wash over the exposed pad while dropping vias (qfn-teach-18).

### Observatory (`observatory`)

Reviewers: `observatory-models`, `observatory-play`, `observatory-teach`.

#### Fun

> *observatory-models:* The win push-in frames the bench and gallery but not the dome, so the one celebratory change (the stars brighten) happens off screen, and Pip is clipped at the left edge. Confetti and the result card work. The room offers little physical comedy beyond knocking over lamps and shelves.

> *observatory-play:* What works: the room is handsome and cosy. The night dome with the brass telescope, the receiver mast and the spectrum gallery give it a strong identity. Within the first 2 s you can grab a chair and throw it (fastestProp 6.7), and throwing a box at the gallery astronomer gets the '!' alarm (alarmed 1), so DR-03 and DR-04 pass. Throwing the motor cart 9–11 m across the room is a genuinely funny, valid way to finish step 1. At the bench, the Morse trace and the decoded line cleaning up ('CQ ## #E ?IP' → 'CQ CQ DE PIP') is a real toy moment, and the job 2 'ringing at 1 mH, settles at 10 mH' discovery is satisfying.
> 
> What hurts: the room is scenery. Its only verb is a 2–4 s cart carry, and then all three jobs are clicks on a bench. There is no cable (AGENTS 4), no designed chaos route or chaos bonus, and the dome, telescope and gallery are never used. Success moments are a toast and a bell. 'DOME OPEN' doesn't open the dome, and the final light-up of the dome stars happens off-screen while the win camera cuts Pip in half. The best physical move (throwing the cart far) is punished twice: it loses the Elegant star through the moving-target tier, and it adds prop dollars to a 12-credit cost limit. A clean scripted solve takes 20 s of game time. The time limit (360 s) is generous, so time is never felt.

> *observatory-teach:* Rolling the cart away and hearing the buzz drop is a nice physical beat. Sweeping a knob while the corner line glides across the spectrum and the Morse comes clean is a satisfying toy. The rest is sitting at a desk clicking. There is no chaos route or physical consequence: the latch failing slams nothing, the dome never opens, and the win camera misses the dome light-up. The cable, the game's star, is unused in the one room whose lesson is cable routing. Building the shutter and the room receiver cable would turn the two best ideas (DC must reach the latch; keep the line away from the motor) into physical comedy.

#### Playability

> *observatory-models:* Pip can walk through the dome shell and then vanishes completely behind it from the back orbit (shots 66b, 72), the main playability issue from this dimension. The cart carry lifts the cart to head height, and it lands tilted on furniture. The tall bookshelf tips over when Pip brushes it (shot 30), which is fine as chaos. Draw calls are 1084 (60 fps on the host GPU). The browser closed with no console or page errors on every script (g.close() returned []).

> *observatory-play:* The clean route has no soft-lock. Walks are short (spawn to cart 7 m, cart to bench 6.5 m), so there is no dead walking. Bench-first, wrong parts and failed logs are all recoverable, and a skipped cart step still lets the job finish (forgiving). The key-map hazards are serious:
> - R moves the cable at the bench but reloads the room outside it, and that wipes progress (reproduced).
> - F at the bench silently stands Pip up.
> - Tab at the bench toggles survey invisibly.
> - Esc twice pauses.
> The knob drag is twitchy (about 10 px per step). The whips are 5–8 px click targets, and their caption plates aren't clickable. LOG, SCOPE and SPEAKER have no hover prompt.
> On a 390×844 phone, the bench is cropped: the capacitor and the whip rack are off-screen, and there are no touch buttons for turn/LOG/S/H. The survey crops the room, and the station panel covers Pip.
> Other issues: the rack and dome shell don't fade, and they hide Pip at back orbits. Draw calls are about 1,100, and the survey drops to 34 fps. A sprint rampage can shove a heavy desk against the bench front so a straight-line approach stalls (a human can walk around it). The audit reports zero start overlaps, and zero console or page errors in all runs.

> *observatory-teach:* Every scripted path ran with zero console errors across four scripts. Cart pickup, carry and drop work. The bench acts, knob drag/arrows, and Esc to stand up work. The job advances correctly, the gust flips the whip, and logging tiers work. There were no soft-locks: a failed LOG just costs a mistake and you keep tinkering. Minor issues: the route lever overlaps the '1.5 m' rack tag, and the step toast goes stale after a part swap.

#### Teaching

> *observatory-models:* From the model side, the rack, the motor and the bench cable need to be one visible physical system (rack jack → floor lead → bench RECEIVER) for the EMI and rerouting lesson to land. The motor needs motor cues (fins, shaft, terminal box, visible noise arcs) rather than a reel silhouette. The exhibits should physically depict what they label: a dish with a feed horn, and a prism splitting a white beam.

> *observatory-play:* (Dimension secondary here.) The simulation is honest and the bench now uses real E6 values with a corner-frequency tag and a sweeping scope line, which fixes R4A's 'values can't be reasoned about'. Failure toasts explain the physical cause (a series C passes no DC, a resistor divides the 12 V). But failures don't happen in the world: the latch drop is a grey lamp, and the gust is invisible. Job 3 is free brute force over 4 rods × 2 orientations, which rewards trial over c = fλ, though the RADIO gallery panel (λ ≈ 3 m, 100 MHz) is a nice hidden hint the player never sees from the bench. The 'Elegant' tier depends on how far the cart was thrown.

> *observatory-teach:* The model underneath is honest and better than any other station I have read. It is a true complex transfer function with a 50 Ω source and a 600 Ω load (logic.ts:76-82). The coils have winding resistance. A series C really blocks DC (latch 0 V). A shunt L really shorts it (0.39 V). A series R really divides the 12 V (470 Ω leaves 6.4 V), and the toast names that number. The quarter-wave arithmetic is right (100 MHz → 0.75 m), and so is the ~20 dB cross-polarisation penalty. The E6 knob values are real. The live before/after spectrum with the |H(f)| curve, the corner lines sweeping as the knob turns, and the Morse audio are the best 'concept is the mechanic' feedback in the game. Carrying the noisy cart away and hearing the scope clean up is a genuine physical lesson. The real problems are in gating and wording, not in the physics. (1) Tier 1 'Decodes' advances every job, so the room can be finished without a filter in job 1 and with one capacitor in job 2. The LC idea and the DC-latch idea are then never met, and that run still grades A/A/A. (2) The per-part corner tags mislead in the LC pair (the coil reads '11 kHz' while the filter acts at 1.6 kHz). (3) Some captions are false: 'ringing' when the circuit is over-damped, and 'steady DC to the latch' with a shunt coil. The 'resonance makes it louder' moment described in PROGRESS and the spec never happens on the intended path. (4) The antenna failure prints 0.75 m. (5) Cable routing, the room's spatial idea, is a bench lever with no room cable. Truthfulness at the level taught is mostly good. The things that would mislead are the filter label (series C + shunt C called 'high-pass', which is a band-pass), the reroute working regardless of where the motor is, and the rainbow false colour on the spectrum gallery.

#### Clarity

> *observatory-models:* Job-yellow (#ffc94d/#ffd66b) sits on a beanbag, a chair and a dozen crates, while the motor cart (the first job item) is teal. At the start the most eye-catching yellow shapes are therefore decoration. The objective marker is a flat, semi-transparent yellow cone with no outline. From a high orbit it reads as a yellow leaf on the rug (shots 13-o90, 63b), and at the start it covers the ROOF RECEIVER plaque. The receiver line isn't drawn from the rack to the bench, so 'away from the receiver' and 'past the motor' have no visible anchor in the room. The safety sentence on the back wall is hidden behind the plinths and a clutter desk. Gallery panel names read at zoom 9, but the λ/f lines are about 8–10 px and unreadable at the game camera (fine as decoration, not as teaching).

> *observatory-play:* The start view is readable: the yellow marker sits over the motor cart, there is no prompt at spawn (R3A N1 fixed), and the full room fits the 16:10 survey. But two goals are on screen from t=0: the card says 'Roll the cart' and the station panel says 'Clean up the garbled message'. Several things contradict each other:
> - If the cart step is skipped, the card shows 'Roll the noisy motor cart' through all three transmissions.
> - Prompts point at the wrong thing: 'Turn the knob' at the start of job 2 (no shunt-C value can pass) and throughout job 3 (the antenna job), and 'Grab the cart' or 'Grab the chair' after the cart is down.
> - Most damaging: the scope shows a green S/N and a perfect decode while the tone is at 7%, and the log then fails.
> The bench has about 100 words of text plus duplicate values (S/N twice, corner frequency three times). The can tags' corner frequency, the key link between value and frequency, is about 4–5 px. Numbers like '−180.0 dB' read as a bug. The latch lamp and the decoded line are good on-device state cues. The scope's step view with the 'latch needs 9 V' line is clear.

> *observatory-teach:* The bench is legible at a glance: board topology (RECEIVER → SERIES → node with SHUNT to GROUND → DECODER/LATCH), clear can icons, a big scope, and the S/N coloured by threshold. Clarity breaks in five places. (1) Text load: about 70 words, with S/N duplicated on the scope and panel, and step captions both on the screen and in a toast. (2) The value tags' corner line is about 6 px, unreadable. (3) The decoder readout shows heavy junk while the toast says 'Decodes'; the win shot can end on '%TAR% ?LE?R'. (4) Absurd numbers (−180 dB) and a TONE ● lit with 0 % tone. (5) The latch job refers to a 'shutter' and a 'dome motor' that have no model in the world. The in-room flow is clear: the marker sits on the cart, the card and prompt agree on the target (only the verb differs), and the bench marker follows.

#### Models

> *observatory-models:* The observatory has a real identity: a night-sky dome with constellation lines over a brass-and-cream telescope, a navy receiver rack with a mast, a seven-panel spectrum gallery with lit hoods, and a warm wood work zone around a well-made signal bench. Up close the bench is the best model in the room. The green filter board has copper traces and jacks, the slot pads are clear, the tilted scope cabinet has a live canvas screen, and the candy-style resistor/coil/capacitor cans, rod rack, antenna ground-plane disc, lever and round LOG button all read at bench view and give far more than 6 cues. Outlines and the toon ramp are consistent, and every lit surface is toon() (366 toon, 119 basic, no Standard/Phong). The weak models are the room fixtures and clutter. The dome is a walk-through, un-faded half-shell with a blank 20 m² exterior and a telescope poking through it. The rack is a plain navy box with a floating one-sided plaque and no cable to the bench. The motor looks like a cable reel and is carried overhead, with an offset bug. Two exhibits (dish, prism) read as a bowl and a flag. The gallery light rail floats when the back wall cuts away. The clutter repeats: 13 blob-hued beanbags, 10 identical unlit lamps, purple shelves of saturated block books, and job-yellow crates.

> *observatory-play:* (Dimension secondary here.) The bench is rich: a filter PCB with copper traces, cans with real component tops (resistor bands, coil windings, capacitor can), a brass jack, a whip rack, and a scope cabinet with a live screen. The room props are consistent toon. Issues: the motor cart is carried tilted and lands on its end or on clutter; the marker is unoutlined; the gust dust puff floats mid-air; and the win confetti pieces are fist-sized over the scope screen.

> *observatory-teach:* (Not my dimension; noted in passing.) The bench reads as a proper toy workstation. The filter cans have distinct component tops (banded resistor, copper coil, capacitor can). The receiver rack has a plaque and mast. The dome has no shutter or motor. There is no cable linking the rack to the bench; the bench lead starts in mid-air at the desk edge. The gust dust reads as white balls.

### Spectrum (`spectrum`)

Reviewers: `spectrum-models`, `spectrum-play`, `spectrum-teach`.

#### Fun

> *spectrum-models:* The room has charm: a rainbow research hall, a smoking toaster, a mesh Faraday cage and a mirror relay. The win moment fires confetti and a cheering Pip, but the push-in crops Pip at the bottom-left and the result card covers the tower. Model-level fun opportunities are untaken. The tower gives no visual reward (its rings are buried), the toaster smoke is a veil rather than a gag, and the pod never visibly changes state on the device except the head swap. A pod status ring and puffs that rise from the toaster would make the cause and effect of each delivery more physical.

> *spectrum-play:* What works: the room shows its problem before you touch anything. A green beam leaves the tower and dies on the storeroom's brick wall with a red stop disc (shots 01, 08). Radio shows as pink broadcast rings and a dashed line that stops at the lab shutter (shot 17). The quiet room's copper mesh, the smoke and the yellow HATCH frame read as physical obstacles. Delivery 2 is a real, satisfying puzzle: stand the board on A, drag the tower onto it, turn the board through the hatch. A 2° nudge (arrow key) knocks the beam onto the shutter, so aiming matters (shots 33–35). Coworkers react to thrown props (alarmed=2 within 0.2 s, shot 65).
> What doesn't work:
> - Two of the three deliveries are a single band key-press after long walks. The live LINK meter shows the answer before SEND, so there is no tension.
> - About 43 of 46 s of a clean bot run is walking, carrying the pod between corners of a thin, empty hall.
> - The success moments are invisible: the beam, the pulse and the pad bursts are hidden at the desk, and the desk flips to the next job instantly. The win shot shows no beam.
> - There is no cable, slingshot, chaos route or chaos bonus. The only slapstick available (throwing the pod) costs damage 1 and cost 30 against a 5-credit cost limit.
> - Grading is toothless: 540 s time limit, best of three, so every run is A.

> *spectrum-teach:* Carrying the pod and standing mirror boards on the floor marks gives the room a physical, Good Job-style shape. The hand-aimed hall map with the live ray bouncing off the board (shots 13-15) is the best toy in the room: the beam flips back off an idle mirror, then swings through the hatch. The deliveries are short (about 50 s for a clean run), and the three obstacles are distinct.
> 
> What's missing:
> - Success happens off-screen: the beam and the pulse are hidden while Pip sits at the desk, and the win shot frames the tower, not the pod.
> - No chaos or alternate physical route exists: no blinds to pull, no cage door to prop open, no detector heads to swap, no coworkers walking through the beam.
> 
> Each of those would be a funny physical act that also teaches.

#### Playability

> *spectrum-models:* Not my primary dimension, but noted while capturing. The survey (Tab) shows the whole room at 1440×900. Orbiting to the back or east leaves the far shell walls as 0.9 m lips (DR-75). The storeroom wall didn't fade when it hid Pip's body from a high camera (shot 14), while the same wall did fade in shot 33. The faded wall leaves its cap, piers and STOREROOM sign opaque. Draw calls are 1133 at the start view (60 fps on the host GPU), far over the ~250 budget. The level has 5 point lights. All capture scripts closed their browsers with zero console or page errors.

> *spectrum-play:* No console or page errors in any of 8 runs. The start audit is clean (overlaps []). The clean route walks without stalls, and drive.walkTo never got stuck.
> Forgiving snaps are consistent: the 'Set the pod on the pad' prompt appears exactly where a drop will snap (2.2 m), and the same holds for mirror marks (2.1 m). A dropped, thrown or flat-lying mirror can be picked up again, and parked items unpark cleanly, so I found no soft-lock on desktop.
> Problems:
> - **Phone (P0):** at 390×844 the bench crops off SEND and the RADIO/MICRO keys, with no touch fallback.
> - **Camera:** Pip, the pod and the pads disappear behind the 2.1 m brick and the 2.05 m shutter at the default zoom, because the single occlusion ray clears the wall top.
> - **Map aiming:** a click on a mirror turns it instead of aiming the tower at it.
> - **Prompts:** 'E Carry the pod' actually drops it, and 'E Pick up the pod/mirror' undoes the step just finished.
> - **Draw calls:** about 1125.
> - **Timing (bot, sprinting):** job 1 ≈ 8 s walking, job 2 ≈ 20 s, job 3 ≈ 15 s. The longest single carry is about 7–9 s.

> *spectrum-teach:* The full clean route completed with zero console errors in run1 and run3. Failed sends are explained and recoverable at once with another band or another aim (DR-20 passes). The prompts track the desk state, but they steer toward brute force: 'P Power' whenever the margin is short, and 'Another band' whenever the path is blocked. A missed aim reads 'TOO WEAK' on the big link screen, so the wrong fix (more power) looks plausible. Walking the pod between rooms three times is the main time cost. It is fine at about 15 s per leg.

#### Teaching

> *spectrum-models:* The room's lesson is that obstacles act differently per band, and the models support it well for brick, metal, mesh and glass. Two visuals undercut it. The near-IR beam is drawn passing straight through a solid bookshelf placed by clutter in the lab beam corridor (P1), and invisible bands are rendered as vivid pink and orange lasers with no 'false colour' note (DR-35). The exhibits case (UV lamp, X-ray tube, gamma pig) is a good idea, but its objects are too small and generic to read at the game camera, so the warning sentence on the wall does the teaching instead of the models.

> *spectrum-play:* Not my dimension, but it shapes the fun. The physical ideas are good and truthful at the level taught: brick passes radio, a 30 cm hatch passes light but not a 3 m wave, mesh reflects long waves, smoke scatters short ones. The R4B corrections are in: 20 log d everywhere, near-IR also loses to sunlight, the thermal example is now 'heat cameras', and mirrors are aimed by hand. The live dB preview lets the player pass by reading a gauge instead of predicting. Band hues are still false colour (radio red, near-IR pink) without a caption; that's for the teaching reviewer (DR-35).

> *spectrum-teach:* Electronics truth, strengths: the physics in logic.ts is mostly sound and well commented. The ideas checked out: c = f·λ for all bands; one 20·log d spreading law for every band (the R4B 10·log d bug is fixed); brick passing radio but stopping light; window glass opaque to 10 µm thermal IR (confirmed: thermal cameras can't see through windows); smoke scattering short wavelengths hardest, with LWIR passing (confirmed: scattering is negligible at 8–14 µm, which is why firefighters use thermal cameras); metal reflecting everything; a mesh passing light but not RF; and a hole much smaller than λ/2 blocking a wave.
> 
> Where teaching falls short: the room doesn't make the concept the mechanic. The wavelength-versus-material decision is a 5-key list. The result (CLEAR LINK, margin in dB, Path clear or blocked) shows live before committing, so trying each band in turn solves every job at no cost. Prompts ('another band', 'P Power') and messages ('long-wave thermal IR slips through', 'Light passes between the wires') print the answers. The wall chart is the full answer key. The reason behind the mesh and the hatch, the ratio of wavelength to gap size, is never something the player sees or uses:
> - the hatch verdict can't be reached;
> - the toast says 30 cm while the hatch is 60 cm;
> - the mesh drawn on screen has holes at λ/2 of Wi-Fi.
> 
> Several simplifications would mislead a careful learner: the 'Faraday cage' has an open doorway and only two mesh sides; the lab blocks radio 'by the shutter' although its side wall is brick and its door is open, which contradicts job 1. Broadcast bands are drawn as rings but scored as one straight ray. Sunlight, the key to job 2, is invisible. Invisible bands are drawn in vivid false colours with no label.
> 
> The moment where the player really applies an idea is aiming mirrors (angle in = angle out) through the hatch, and that part works.

#### Clarity

> *spectrum-models:* The brick, glass, metal, mesh and smoke obstacles are each distinct in material at the game camera, and the floor mirror marks (dashed lilac rings with letters) and pad rings read well. Clarity loses on colour hierarchy. Job yellow is spent on a chair and crates, while the pod and mirrors are cream, grey and lilac and blend into a hall whose floor is luma 209–233, so Pip, the held pod and the target aren't the highest-contrast shapes. Signs are single-sided floating planes: TEA hovers in air, POD DOCK stands on edge with no foot, and the QUIET ROOM sign faces into its own room, so it is invisible from the approach. The wall carries a 13-word sentence ('…exhibits only. Not safe to stand beside.'), against DR-49. In the bench view, band, path and margin are each shown on both the monitor and the side card, and the monitor captions are microtext.

> *spectrum-play:* The scene does most of the explaining: pad rings with floor tags, lettered dashed mirror marks, the HATCH sign, the 'WHAT GETS THROUGH?' wall chart, and the RX pod visibly swapping detector heads. The bouncing marker floats over the pod and then the pads, and stays visible even when the pad is hidden.
> Problems:
> - **Too much text:** about 62 HUD words at the desk, with band, λ and f printed three times (toast, monitor, panel) and path and margin twice.
> - **Wrong status:** the LINK screen says 'TOO WEAK' for a missed beam.
> - **Method on the card:** step 4 names the method (mirror).
> - **Hatch:** it is never prompted and is drawn as plain metal on the map when shut.
> - **Prompt vs card:** the pill contradicts the card twice per run.
> - **Small labels:** bench labels are about 10 px and meter captions about 6 px.
> - **Lookalike crates:** white clutter crates beside the storeroom pad look like the pod.
> - **Marker shape:** the marker is a yellow cone in a room with three orange traffic cones, so its shape is a little ambiguous.

> *spectrum-teach:* Bench layout:
> - Band keys on the left with the wave ribbon; the live hall map in the centre; power, hatch and SEND on the right.
> - The two screens show λ, f and the link meter. The panel repeats band, power, path and margin.
> - That puts the same value in two places (DR-41): band and λ on the wave screen and the panel; margin on the link screen and the panel.
> 
> Text problems:
> - The disclosure lines ('ribbon not to scale', 'works'/'reliable') are about 5 px tall.
> - The link screen's status ignores a missed beam.
> - 'Path: clear' is shown even through 25 dB of smoke.
> - The job card names the method ('stand a mirror on a floor mark').
> - The floor marks and pads read well at the game camera. The HATCH and GLASS LAB signs are mounted, and the hatch frame is clearly yellow.

#### Models

> *spectrum-models:* Every distinct fixture was captured at the game camera and at zoom 9 (shots 10–44, 92–98, A6–A8, B0–B3). Works well: the brick storeroom with its wooden plank door, lintel and pier caps; the slatted lab shutter with its roller box, yellow hatch frame and sliding hatch door; the copper-mesh quiet room with real posts and rails (the see-through mesh reads instantly as a cage); the mirror boards (gradient silvered pane, both faces, lilac rail, proper stand feet); and the dispatch bench, the best model in the room (band keys with ink bezels, a wave ribbon strung between posts, a tilted map lectern, two housed screens, power keys, a lever and a send button, well past 6 cues). The coworkers (cap keeper, lab scientist, headphone reader, alarmed tea blob) read as blobs and stay on model. Weak: the transmitter tower, the room's hero object (its five band rings have a smaller radius than the mast and render inside it; it reads as a glove on a stick on a black hole); the pod (an arcade-joystick silhouette, and the lid handle runs into the mast plate); the shelf stock (bread loaves); the counters (big blank slabs); and the toaster (too small, hidden by smoke). g.audit(.02) and g.audit(.04) both report 0 overlaps at start, and the decor fixtures have solid() colliders, so the audit can see them. The overlaps that remain are logical ones the audit can't see: clutter inside beam corridors (bookshelf in the NIR beam), clutter in front of the ladder, stripes under the rug, and the handle in the pod plate.

> *spectrum-play:* Out of scope for this pass. Noted in passing: the mirror boards read as glass whiteboards rather than mirrors. The pod's mast and detector head read well when it's carried at zoom 9 (shot 07).

> *spectrum-teach:* Not this reviewer's dimension. Noted only where a model carries the lesson: the copper mesh texture's 6.25 cm cells contradict 'holes far smaller than the wavelength', and the 0.6 m hatch frame contradicts the 30 cm toast. The lab has no visible sunlight. The pod's detector heads are modelled distinctly (dipole, patch, horn, domes) but swap automatically, so their shapes teach nothing.
