### R5-029

**R5-029 | P1 | garage | teaching | Garage kickback arc whites out the switch, node and ACROSS SWITCH socket for over 1 s (40% of the board at quality 2), and draws an air arc across a MOSFET**

Found by: `gap2-quality2-retake#3` (P1 teaching), `garage-models#6` (P1 visual-bug), `garage-teach#4` (P1 teaching). Batch: B4 (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*gap2-quality2-retake* — **Garage kickback arc at quality 2 whites out 40% of the bench board and 100% of the switch, against 17% at quality 0 (the 'over 1 s' duration is about 0.6 s).** garage-models and garage-teach report that the arc whites out the switch for over 1 s. I swept the bench view every 0.1 s after PULSE in job 1, at q2 and q0 on the same simulated frame (04-arcsweep.mjs, 44 crops). The arc is visible from +0.8 s to +1.3 s, six frames or about 0.6 s, at both qualities. That shortens the claimed 'over 1 s', but it still breaks DR-79, which limits flashes near a taught part to 120 ms. The extent is much worse at quality 2. Board-crop pixels above 245 luma reach 29–40% at q2 and 11–17% at q0. Over the switch and the ACROSS SWITCH socket they reach 100% at q2 in all six frames, against 55–81% at q0. At q2 the white field spreads across the MOTOR, NODE, SWITCH and CONTROLLER sockets, the scope trace and its 'RESET at shutdown!' caption, the PULSE button and the ACROSS MOTOR / AT CONTROLLER labels. At q0 it is a blob over the switch. The cause is a hot(×3) arc core, a 0.7 m glow sprite at 0.5–1.0 opacity (DR-66 caps it at 0.5), and a point light of 6–16 intensity that flickers on the same board, all fed through bloom. The arc is the failure the job teaches (the kickback spike at the switch), so hiding the switch and the scope at that moment hides the lesson. Verdict: the claim holds on 'whites out the switch', the duration shrinks to about 0.6 s, and it gets worse at quality 2.

*garage-models* — **Kickback arc still whites out the switch, the node and the ACROSS SWITCH socket for over 1 s (still open from research F4).** The research pass (research-external F4) flagged this. It is unchanged. When PULSE lands with no path, the arc uses:
- a core of hot('#e8f8ff',3) (station.ts:186);
- an additive glow sprite of size .7 at opacity .8 (station.ts:188), above the DR-66 0.5 cap;
- a PointLight on the board (station.ts:189);
- arcT=.6 s, plus spark bursts.

The crops at +0.0 s and +0.4 s after the switch opens (garage-models-70-arc-0.0, -72-arc-0.4) show the switch's black body, the NODE test point and the dashed ACROSS SWITCH socket bleached into one pale blob. The whole left half of the PCB is tinted white. The full frame at +1.25 s (-57) still shows the bloom. This is the exact moment and part being taught (no path, so the current arcs across the switch), and the effect hides the switch. It also exceeds DR-79's 120 ms flash limit near a taught part.

*garage-teach* — **The shutdown failure shows an air arc jumping across a MOSFET, and the white bloom hides the switch being taught.** With no protection, the switch node rises until the MOSFET avalanches at 75 V (logic.ts:126). The game shows this as a jagged white arc chain, a glow sprite and a flickering point light across the SWITCH (station.ts:186-189 and :407-411, triggered at :390).

A real MOSFET doesn't spark through air. In unclamped inductive switching, the coil's ½LI² is dumped into the die as heat. Repeated, it burns the silicon: round burn marks, cracked die ([Nexperia AN10273](https://docs.ampnuts.ru/nexperia.com.datasheet/application-note/AN10273.pdf), [AN11243](https://docs.ampnuts.ru/nexperia.com.datasheet/application-note/AN11243.pdf)). Visible arcing belongs to mechanical contacts: relays, knife switches. A learner takes away 'transistors spark when you switch a motor'.

It also fails DR-66. In `garage-teach-34/35/36-arc-*.png` the arc is a white bloom blob covering the ACROSS SWITCH socket and the SWITCH part for the whole 0.6 s. The jagged line itself is unreadable, and it sits over the empty socket where job 2's TVS fix goes.

The toast text ('the switch was forced into breakdown') is accurate; the picture contradicts it.

**Evidence.**

**Either way:**

### R5-030

**R5-030 | P1 | meeting, lunch | teaching | Meeting: the power strip is not the visible hub — cables plug into a ghost default socket box (also left under the Lunch lift), and the cyan ring stays after placing**

Found by: `meeting-models#3` (P1 teaching), `meeting-play#14` (P2 overlap), `lunch-models#9` (P2 visual-bug). Batch: R-meeting (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*meeting-models* — **The power strip is not the visible hub: the cable, the projector lead and both appliance cords plug into the generic black 'socket' box that covers the strip.** The concept taught here is a load budget: three loads (kettle 2.5 A, heater 2 A, projector 1 A) share one strip whose 5 A breaker trips (meeting-strip.ts:1-7). The world should show that topology: reel → strip, and strip → three plugs. In the model it doesn't. Every cable level gets a generic target socket, `new T.BoxGeometry(.48,.38,.3)` in #384454 at (t.x,.25,t.z) = (12.3,.25,-2.25), plus a cyan torus at y .15 (game.ts:87-88). In the meeting the strip snaps to (t.x,.08,t.z+.3) = (12.3,.08,-1.95) (game.ts:211). The strip is .26 deep, so it butts against the box and lies half under its shadow and the ring, and its four outlets are hidden (meeting-models-32, -35, -37). The reel cable visibly ends in the black box (-35, -36). The projector lead is a decor tube that ends at (12.3,.05,-2.4), inside the box (decor.ts:150). Both appliance cords are drawn to (t.x+.25,.08,t.z), also the box, not the strip (meeting-strip.ts:94). A player sees a cable go into a black crate, three cords go into the same crate, and an orange strip lying next to it doing nothing. When the breaker trips, the pulsing red reset cap appears on the side of the box at (t.x+.32,.22,t.z) (meeting-strip.ts:89), not on the strip's own red switch (prefabs.ts:138). That teaches "the box trips", not "the strip trips on the sum of its plugs". It breaks DR-26 (the mechanic is the concept: plugging into the strip), DR-47 (device state on the device) and DR-37 (invisible wiring should be drawn). The plain BoxGeometry also has no edge radius (DR-58).

*meeting-play* — **Placed power strip is buried under the Playground's black 'socket' box, and the cyan target ring stays after plug-in.** game.ts always builds a 0.48×0.38×0.3 dark socket box at level.target for every cable floor, and hides it only in stations and the lobby. In the meeting the strip snaps to (t.x, 0.08, t.z+0.3). The socket box at (t.x, 0.25, t.z) then sits on top of the strip, covering most of its sockets; only the red reset button and one corner of the orange strip show (shots 23, 75, 77). The player places a strip and then sees a black block where the strip should be. Once the cable is plugged in, the cyan torus target ring keeps pulsing around the strip, so the 'done' state looks like the 'go here' state. This breaks DR-70 (nothing interpenetrates at rest) and makes DR-47 (device state on the device) worse, because the strip's own sockets and the plugs in them are hidden.

*lunch-models* — **A stray default 'target socket' box sits under the lift car at (12, 0.25, −6), with no purpose and no collider.** Game always builds the generic target ring and a 0.48 × 0.38 × 0.3 dark socket box at level.target. Lunch's target is {x:12, z:−6}. LunchRuntime hides game.target (the ring) but not the socket box. A dark featureless cube therefore sits on the lift-room floor right in front of the lift, between the hazard stripe and the car. It looks like a job object (a socket or a battery), Pip walks straight through it (lunch-models-97), and it is visible in every lift-room shot (lunch-models-53, -57, -94). This is a false affordance (DR-17) at the most important station of the room.

**Fix.**

*From meeting-models:* **Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** The fix also has to move the rope's connected end. The `this.plugPosition.set(level.target.x,.28,level.target.z)` in the snap branch (game.ts ~203) must become the strip inlet (stripAt().x-.45,.1,stripAt().z) for the meeting, or the cable will still end in mid-air where the box was. Also note that the strip outlets run along x at -.3+k*.19 in the prop's local frame, and the strip is snapped with an identity rotation, so the world offsets given are valid only while that rotation is kept.

Reviewer's fix: In the meeting, hide the generic socket box and ring once the strip is placed, or never create them for this level: in game.ts:88 skip `socket` when level.id==='meeting' and keep only the ring as the drop marker until stripPlaced(). Then make the strip the endpoint of every connection. The rope plug end should seat at the strip's inlet (stripAt().x-.5, .1, stripAt().z). The projector lead in decor.ts:150 should end at outlet 1 (x -.3 on the strip: 12.0,.16,-1.95). The kettle and heater cords (meeting-strip.ts:94) should end at outlets 3 and 4, with b = strip position + (-.3+k*.19, .16, 0). Add a small plug head, `rbox(.1,.08,.12,.03)` INK, at each plugged outlet. When an appliance is unplugged, move that plug head to the floor beside the strip, so the player sees an empty outlet. Move resetCap to the strip's own switch position (strip x + w/2-.06, y .16).

*From meeting-play:* In the Game constructor, set socket.visible=false when level.id==='meeting' (the strip is the socket there). In render(), hide this.target once this.connected, or scale it to 0 over 0.3 s on plug-in. Draw the plugged plug on the strip's first socket: plugPosition = strip top socket (t.x-0.3, 0.17, t.z+0.3).

*From lunch-models:* In src/game.ts:88, keep a reference (this.targetSocket=socket). In the LunchRuntime constructor (lunch-runtime.ts:42), add game.targetSocket.visible=false. Station and hub levels already skip it. Alternatively, skip building the socket when level.id==='lunch'.

*Merged entry:* apply one fix for the shared root cause and check it against every room and reviewer listed above; where reviewers proposed different fixes, prefer the verifier-corrected one, then the lead (first) reviewer's.

### R5-031

**R5-031 | P1 | playground | teaching | Playground: the lamp has no switch — "Switch the lamp on" is E at a bare pole, with no lever and no visible on/off state**

Found by: `playground-teach#0` (P1 teaching), `playground-models#1` (P1 teaching), `playground-play#1` (P1 teaching). Batch: R-playground (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*playground-teach* — **The switch that 'closes the loop' does not exist as an object: no lever, no on/off state, nothing to look at.** The Playground's only electrical lesson (per docs and R4B: 'a switch closes the loop') is taught by a text prompt, not by a thing. No switch mesh exists anywhere in the room. decor.ts playground() builds a lamp post, a bulb sphere and a socket box, but no switch (grep 'switch' in src/levels/decor.ts, dressing.ts, src/render, src/props finds nothing). The 'switch' is an invisible 1.9 m radius around switchAt (7.55,-6.35), which is just the lamp post's base (game.ts:244 nearSwitch; level switchAt in playground.ts:6). Pressing E flips the boolean `switchedOn` and spawns 6 sparks (game.ts:217). The only way to know the switch state is to read the prompt pill. Shot 14 shows 'E Switch on (needs power first)'. Shot 15, after pressing E, shows the identical scene, with only the pill changed to 'E Switch it off'. In shot 24 (HUD hidden, plugged in, switch off) a first-time viewer cannot tell why the lamp is dark, or that a switch is involved at all. This breaks DR-26 (the concept must be a physical act on an object, not a prompt) and DR-47 (device state shown on the device). It also breaks DR-37: the open switch is a hidden rule, because the player plugs in, sees nothing happen, and has to read the card to learn that a switch exists. A learner leaves without having seen a switch open or close a gap, which is the one idea the room claims to teach.

*playground-models* — **The lamp has no switch: 'Switch the lamp on' targets the bare base of the post.** Step 3 of the tutorial is 'Switch the lamp on', and the room is supposed to teach that a switch closes the loop. But there is no switch model anywhere. level.switchAt is (7.55,-6.35), which is exactly the centre of the lamp post (decor.ts:89 places the lamp group at target+(0.55,-0.35)). The player presses E anywhere within 1.9 m of the post and the lamp lights. Nothing in the world flips, clicks over or changes state apart from the bulb. The objective marker for this step is drawn at the same point, so the post skewers the bouncing cone. The only rule this room teaches about electricity, 'the circuit is open until the switch closes it', is never shown by an object, and players get no idea what a switch looks like before the Meeting projector switch. It also leaves 'plugged in but off' invisible: before E the lamp looks exactly like the unpowered lamp.

*playground-play* — **There is no switch: 'Switch the lamp on' is E at a bare lamp pole, and the switch state is invisible.** The playground's third step (src/ui/objectives.ts:26) and the concept it teaches ('a switch closes the loop', per research-docs) have no switch model. switchAt (7.55,-6.35) in src/levels/playground.ts:6 is exactly the lamp pole's position (src/levels/decor.ts:89, group at t.x+.55, t.z-.35), and decor builds no switch mesh (grep 'switch' in decor.ts finds nothing). The player presses E at a grey pole; the only feedback is 6 sparks and a click (src/game.ts:217). The marker points at mid-pole (shots 14, 39). The state is also invisible. Before power, E toggles switchedOn with the prompt 'Switch on (needs power first)', and the next E silently toggles it back off (g-misc log: sw true → false → true, with nothing visible changing). A player who presses E at the lamp while exploring can leave it ON and then win the moment they plug in, or leave it OFF and not know why the lamp stays dark. A switch that can't be seen can't teach 'open vs closed'.

**Evidence.**

*From playground-teach:* In decor.ts playground(), add a chunky wall-box-style rocker or toggle switch on the lamp post at about (t.x+.55, 1.05, t.z-.35+.12), facing the approach (towards −x/+z):
- A housing rbox(.22,.32,.12,.03) in INK-outline neutral (#f0ece2), with a lever box(.07,.16,.06) in job yellow #ffc629.
- The lever rotates +0.45 rad (ON) / −0.45 rad (OFF).
- A small 'I/O' decal, or a red OFF / green ON pip (MeshBasicMaterial, unlit).

Return the lever from Decor (e.g. `decor.switchLever`). In game.ts, set `lever.rotation.x = switchedOn ? .45 : -.45` whenever switchedOn changes (game.ts:217), with a 60 ms snap tween and the existing click sound.

Optionally draw the lamp's own cord as a TubeGeometry from the socket box (t.x,.2,t.z) up into the post base, with the switch visibly on that line, so the 'loop' runs socket → switch → bulb. Move switchAt to the lever, so the E radius centres on a visible object.

*From playground-models:* In decor.ts playground() add a wall-box switch on the camera-facing side of the post at y 1.1: a housing rbox(.18,.26,.09,.03) in '#f0ece2' at (t.x+.55, 1.1, t.z-.35+.12), an INK rocker or toggle box(.05,.11,.05) pivoting about x, and a pilot dot sphere(.025) in INK (off) or lit('#57e38f') (on). Return the toggle and pilot meshes through Decor (for example decor.switch). Add a short conduit tube from the socket up the post to the switch so the loop is visible: socket → switch → bulb. In game.ts:217, rotate the toggle to ±0.45 rad and swap the pilot material when switchedOn changes. Move level.switchAt to the switch's front (7.55,-6.0) so the marker sits over the switch rather than the post. Optional: when connected but off, give the bulb a faint 'ready' tint so 'powered but open' reads.

*From playground-play:* **Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** Also refuse the toggle before power, or keep the lever visibly ON so pre-switching is readable. For example, in Game.interact only allow switchedOn=true when connected, and otherwise play a dead click and leave it off. Return it in Decor (e.g. decor.switch), and in Game.interact rotate the lever ±35° when switchedOn changes. Add a small indicator lamp on the box, dark when the loop is open and green only when connected && switchedOn. Point the step-3 marker at the box (switchAt y≈1.0). Optionally draw a short visible lead from the socket box up the pole to the switch, then to the bulb, so the series path reads.

*Merged entry:* apply one fix for the shared root cause and check it against every room and reviewer listed above; where reviewers proposed different fixes, prefer the verifier-corrected one, then the lead (first) reviewer's.

### R5-032

**R5-032 | P1 | playground, meeting | teaching | The idle route hint streams cyan current-like dots on an open circuit, from Pip, straight through crates, and leads to the door even before the strip is fetched**

Found by: `playground-teach#7` (P1 teaching), `playground-play#2` (P2 teaching), `meeting-play#18` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-playground (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*playground-teach* — **The idle route hint uses flowing cyan dots on an open circuit and draws them straight through a crate stack (DR-29 known, confirmed).** After 35 s without connecting (game.ts:446-448), 40 glowing dots in #9ff3ea ×1.4 (game.ts:100-101) stream from Pip's feet to the socket. The current pulses are cyan #6fe9ff (actors.ts:81): nearly the same colour, the same 'flowing beads' motion, the same meaning to a learner.

They appear while the circuit is open and the plug is lying by the reel (shots 12, 13). So the one picture the game uses for 'current flowing' is shown when no current can flow. That is the exact misconception DR-29 forbids (electricity 'flows to the device' before the loop is closed).

The path comes from detour() over level.obstacles only (the two pillars), so it ignores props. In shot 12 the dotted line runs over the crate stack at about (1,1) and across chairs. It also starts at Pip rather than at the plug, which the player hasn't picked up, so it isn't even the cable's route.

*playground-play* — **The cyan 'route hint' dots flow on an open circuit, start from Pip rather than the plug, and run straight through crates and shelves.** After 35 s without a connection, 40 glowing cyan dots stream from Pip toward the socket (src/game.ts:100, :446). Three problems. (a) Moving glowing dots are the game's language for current (the pulses on a live gold cable). Showing them on an open circuit, before the plug is in, teaches the 'electricity flows out to the device' misconception (DR-29, EXT M2). (b) They start at Pip's feet even during step 1, when Pip has not picked up the plug. In shot 33 Pip stands at spawn and the dots lead away from the reel, contradicting the card ('Pick up the reel's plug'). (c) The path is `detour(Pip, target, this.obstacles)`, and this.obstacles holds only the two pillars. So the dots cut straight through the crate stack (shot 33), the bookshelves and clutter (shot 37), a route the cable or Pip cannot actually take.

*meeting-play* — **The idle route hint (after 35 s) leads to the door even when the strip hasn't been fetched, and it uses glowing current-like beads.** After 35 s without connecting, 40 cyan glowing beads flow from Pip to level.target along a detour path (shots 43, 44, 67). During step 1 (the strip not fetched, card saying 'Fetch the power strip by the printer'), the beads still lead to the boardroom door, away from the strip that is 1 m behind Pip. So the hint contradicts the card. They also look exactly like current pulses moving along an open circuit, the 'electricity flows to the device' misconception (DR-29, a known issue confirmed here).

**Evidence.**

- `src/game.ts:100-101` (40 cyan dots)
- `src/game.ts:446-448` (shown after 35 s while !connected; detour from Pip over pillars only)
- `src/render/actors.ts:81` (pulse colour #6fe9ff)

**Fix.**

The target ring (game.ts:87, #64ddd4) and the ring bursts are static cyan MeshBasicMaterials, so 'no cyan MeshBasicMaterial except Pulses' would fail for the wrong reason. Check instead that no moving bead effect is visible while loads[0].state!=='on'.

Reviewer's fix: Replace the dots with a non-electrical cue in the route-tape language:
- Yellow #ffc629 floor chevrons (flat boxes .3×.012×.1, rotated along the path), stepping one by one, spaced 0.8 m, with no glow and no motion along the path (or a slow hop), so they can't read as current.
- Start the path at the plug while it isn't held (g.plugPosition), and at Pip only when he holds it.

*From playground-play:* In src/game.ts:446, replace the flowing dots with a static or slowly blinking dashed floor line, or footprints, in a non-electric colour such as warm white #fff3d6 at opacity 0.6, so moving beads stay reserved for live current. Start it at the plug while !holdingPlug, and at Pip or the plug end once carrying. Route it with the same obstacle list the rope uses (pillars plus props of mass ≥3 near the path, as in simulateCable), or around the lane polyline the level declares (playground.ts:6 lanes[0]).

*From meeting-play:* Route the hint to the current step's at(g) (export a helper from objectives.ts, or have ObjectivesHUD set g.hintTarget). Replace the glowing spheres with flat, non-emissive floor chevrons or footprints in job yellow (#ffd84a), spaced 0.8 m and fading in sequence, so the hint never resembles current.

*Merged entry:* apply one fix for the shared root cause and check it against every room and reviewer listed above; where reviewers proposed different fixes, prefer the verifier-corrected one, then the lead (first) reviewer's.

- *playground-play:* Advance 36 s idle and retake playground-play-33: the line starts at the plug, does not cross a crate or shelf, and nothing moves along it. Grep for flowing-bead effects confirms pulses only render when circuit.loads[0].state==='on'.
- *meeting-play:* Rerun s4.mjs: shot 43 must show chevrons from Pip to the strip (step 1), not to the door, with no emissive beads. grep game.ts for the bead material and expect no MeshBasic glow.

**Rules:** DR-29

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — game.ts:100-101 builds 40 MeshBasicMaterial dots, #9ff3ea ×1.4. game.ts:446-448 shows them after 35 s while !connected, along detour(Pip→target, this.obstacles). this.obstacles is only level.obstacles, the two pillars (game.ts:73), whereas the rope also adds furniture (game.ts:280). This is DR-29's own 'Known' item, and it still reproduces. verify-12/13 at t 37 show cyan beads streaming on an open circuit. (3/3 merged findings CONFIRMED.)

### R5-033

**R5-033 | P1 | arcade, arcade-rush | teaching | Arcade cabinets repeat answers: story cabinets 3–5 share 470+470 Ω and Rush cycles about nine answers with no escalation**

Found by: `arcade-play#7` (P1 teaching), `arcade-rush-play#7` (P1 fun). Batch: B5 (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*arcade-play* — **Cabinets 3, 4 and 5 all have the same answer (470 + 470 Ω): two of five puzzles are repeats.** `best()` for the Claw (12 V green, ★ 10–13.3 mA), the Handheld (9 V red, ★ 5–8.3 mA) and the Coin hopper (5 V base, ★ 4–6 mA) is the same chain: 470 + 470 = 940 Ω.
- Claw: 10.5 mA. Handheld: 7.44 mA. Hopper: 4.57 mA. All tier 3 in s2 and s3.
- The spec says so itself: "the same chain keeps it in the ★ zone" (tests/station-arcade.spec.ts:47-52).

After the Claw, a player who found 940 Ω just rebuilds it twice. The battery-life idea and the base-resistor idea are explained in text but never change what the player has to do. The last 40 % of the room is rote, and DR-27 (each job adds an idea the player must act on) fails for jobs 4 and 5.

*arcade-rush-play* — **No escalation: Rush is the same number-match loop 30 times with about nine answers.** `rushJob()` only makes single-LED cabinets.
- **Variety:** 4 colours, supplies of 3.3/5/9/12 V, 3 current bands, and 5 one-shot faults.
- **No other kinds:** there are no battery-life cabinets, no transistor-base cabinets, and no combined faults. Every cabinet uses the same pink bench cabinet model.
- **Few answers:** in the 32-cabinet run, the elegant fixes collapse to about nine chains: 470; 220; 470+470; 220+470; 47+220; 100+220; 220‖470; 47+47; 100. Many repeat back to back (white 9 V → 470 three times).
- **'backwards' gives the answer away:** the job starts with the correct chain already in place, and the story says it is backwards, so the whole job is pressing F.
- **Flat loop:** each cabinet takes about 5 s (2 s to read, 1–7 keypresses, 2 s soak). Difficulty, pace and stakes never change across the 180 s, and the world never changes: no queue of kids, no cabinets crowding the bench, no rising tension.

After about 5 cabinets a player is matching a lookup table, not reasoning about I = (V − Vf) ÷ R. R4B's redesign ideas for the arcade (kid queue, blocks popping across the room, a battery time-lapse, A6) were NOT BUILT. For a mode whose whole point is replay, this is the main fun problem.

**Evidence.**

### R5-034

**R5-034 | P1 | arcade-rush, arcade | teaching | Arcade: a popped LED toast says it "runs hot and dies early" — the wrong cause for an LED that just died outright**

Found by: `arcade-rush-teach#2` (P1 teaching), `arcade-teach#13` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-arcade (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*arcade-rush-teach* — **An LED that pops says it 'runs hot and dies early'.** When the LED is driven past 2.5 × its rating it pops after 0.5 s. There is a flash and a puff, the power cuts, and a spare goes in. The toast for this event is `judge(...).problems[0]`, which for any over-rating LED reads '62.5 mA is over the LED's 20 mA rating: it runs hot and dies early. (I = (V − Vf) ÷ R)'. The game has just shown instant death, and the sentence describes slow wear. The two failure modes the arcade carefully separates (over-rating shortens life; a gross overload kills at once, logic.ts:14) get the same words exactly when the difference is visible. A learner concludes either that 'dies early' means 'pops now' or that the text is decoration. In rush this happens on every 5 V red or green 'hot' cabinet (job 4 with this seed).

*arcade-teach* — **Popped-LED toast says 'it runs hot and dies early', the wrong cause for an LED that just died outright.** popLed() shows judge().problems[0] (station.ts:307-309), which for any over-rating LED is '… over the LED's 20 mA rating: it runs hot and dies early. (I = (V − Vf) ÷ R)' (logic.ts:158). The 47 Ω pinball LED at 62.5 mA (3.1×) vanishes in a flash and smoke (arcade-teach-31), but the toast describes slow wear. The fallback 'The LED ran far past its rating and popped.' (station.ts:309) is never reached because problems[0] always exists. The single cause sentence (DR-28) contradicts the event on screen, and the player cannot tell the gross-overload rule (ledPop 2.5×) from the 'runs hot' rule, the distinction review4 asked for.

### R5-036

**R5-036 | P1 | arcade-rush, arcade | teaching | Arcade: an overdriven LED looks paler/whiter ("white-hot", incandescent imagery) than a correctly driven one, and the LED HEAT bar barely moves before it pops**

Found by: `arcade-rush-teach#7` (P1 teaching), `arcade-teach#14` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-arcade (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*arcade-rush-teach* — **An overdriven LED looks paler and weaker than a correctly driven one, and the LED HEAT bar barely moves before it pops.** The core intuition is that more current means a brighter, hotter LED. At 7.1 mA (well under the band) the red LED dome is saturated red with a clear halo. At 62.5 mA (3×) the dome is lerped toward white, up to 70 %, and reads pale pink-white, with a broad orange wash from the point light over the whole board. The over-driven LED reads as washed out, not glaring. Separately, the pop is triggered by current (`r.level > ledPop` for 0.5 s), but the LED HEAT bar follows a 2 s thermal time constant. At 0.3 s it showed 33 °C, and the LED popped at 0.65 s with the heat bar still low. The meter the player is told to watch never shows the cause before the failure.

*arcade-teach* — **An overdriven LED flashes white and the story calls it 'white-hot': incandescent imagery that teaches the wrong overload cue.** animate() lerps the LED dome colour up to 70 % toward #ffffff once heat.led > 0.9 (station.ts:407). The red and green LEDs in arcade-teach-13/-16/-30 read as white domes with coloured halos. The claw story says 'The claw light glows white-hot' (logic.ts:73). An LED's colour comes from its semiconductor bandgap, not from temperature, so an overdriven red LED is a brighter red (slightly red-shifted as it heats). It never turns white. White-hot is a filament or resistor-wire image. Players who later see a white LED may read it as 'overloaded'. Separately, an unlit red LED is drawn 55 % toward white (station.ts:501, tint()), so the pinball's red LED looks white at rest (arcade-teach-03), which blurs the colour lesson (the different Vf per colour) further.

Removing the lerp alone won't fix the pop case, because the lerp isn't active there. Express overdrive through halo size and bloom, and cap ledLight intensity at about 2 with distance 0.8. The LED-heat or pop-trigger change is as proposed.

Reviewer's fix: In animate(): keep the LED's hue (no lerp to white). Express overdrive as glare: halo scale `.4+min(3,level)*.6`, a bloom-only core, a slight size pulse and the flicker, and cap the board wash (ledLight distance 0.8, intensity ≤ 2). Give the LED its own fast thermal constant (`HOUSE.ledTau=.25`) and trigger the pop from `heat.led > HOUSE.ledPop`. Rescale the LED HEAT bar to 0–3× with a red 'burn-out' zone above 2.5×, so the bar visibly races into the red before the pop.

### R5-037

**R5-037 | P1 | garage | teaching | Garage: every part has exactly one legal socket, the socket glows and the prompt names the key, so "where protection goes" is never a decision and tray-order brute force gets an A in 22 s**

Found by: `garage-teach#0` (P1 teaching), `garage-play#6` (P1 teaching), `garage-teach#2` (P1 teaching). Batch: R-garage (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*garage-teach* — **Where a part goes is never a decision: each part fits one socket, the socket glows, and the prompt names the key.** The room's core idea is: when the switch opens, the coil's current needs a path, and where you give it that path decides the clamp voltage and how fast the coil empties. But the player never chooses the place.

- Every part has exactly one legal socket (`slots:['fly']`, `['switch']` or `['ctrl']`).
- `act('slot')` refuses any other socket with a 'hm' (station.ts:204).
- The moment a part is picked up, its one socket turns yellow (station.ts:270).
- The prompt then reads 'S Fit it' or 'A Fit it' (station.ts:462). In `garage-teach-33-held-tvs-prompt.jpg`, with the TVS held, only ACROSS SWITCH glows and the prompt says 'S Fit it'.
- Hovering a wrong socket says 'It does not fit here' (station.ts:445).

So the topology question (across the motor or across the switch?) is answered by the UI before the player can think about it. The only real decisions left are which of 5 parts, a flip, and a ground lever.

This also hides a true and teachable result. A TVS across the motor is a valid fast clamp; a plain diode across the switch does nothing useful. The game forbids both instead of letting the player find out. That breaks DR-26 (the concept should be the mechanic) and DR-38 (tiers should reward understanding, not following prompts).

*garage-play* — **Every part has exactly one legal socket, so 'where does protection go' is never a decision; brute-forcing five parts solves every job.** PARTS gives each part a single slot: diode→fly, clamp→fly, tvs→switch, snubber→switch, cap→ctrl (src/stations/garage/logic.ts:37-41). When a part is held, the only socket that fits glows (station.ts:270) and the prompt names its key ('A Fit it', station.ts:462; shot 17). Hovering any other socket says 'It does not fit here' (shot 46). The topology idea the sockets are named after (ACROSS MOTOR vs ACROSS SWITCH vs AT CONTROLLER) is therefore never chosen by the player. The only decisions are which of five parts, flip, and the ground lever. With PULSE free of mistakes (only TEST failures, shorts and a reversed cap count), a player can cycle 1-5 and P until the scope turns green, without understanding why. The ART/AGENTS goal 'play by doing, the mechanic is the concept' is weakened: the room shows the concept beautifully (beads circling the motor and diode loop, the arc at the switch) but the act is a menu pick. This breaks DR-26 (the concept is taught by a physical act, not by picking from a list) and DR-38 (trial and error reaches 'elegant').

*garage-teach* — **Brute force solves every job in tray order: 1 → A → P → Enter, then 2, then G. A-grade in 22 s with no understanding.** PULSE is free and unlimited, and it costs neither credits nor mistakes, except for a short or a reversed cap. The solution order matches the tray and key order:
- Job 1: part 1 (DIODE).
- Job 2: part 2 (CLAMP) or part 3 (TVS).
- Job 3: the only remaining control, G, because the clamp from job 2 is still fitted and already meets the stop spec.

`garage-teach/run3.mjs` plays exactly this 'press the next key' strategy. The result card (`garage-teach-48-result-card.jpg`) shows **A / A / A in 0:22**, with Reliable and Elegant stars.

Because every job's fewest-parts answer is 1 (`logic.test.ts` expects `n===1`), 'Elegant' only means 'don't add extras'. It never means 'chose the right clamp level'. Job 3 in particular reduces the whole star-ground lesson to 'try the lever'.

No moment requires *applying* the idea to a new situation. Every job's fix is the next untried control. This breaks DR-38 and DR-26.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/garage/logic.ts:36-42`
- `src/stations/garage/station.ts:204`
- `src/stations/garage/station.ts:270`
- `src/stations/garage/station.ts:445`
- `src/stations/garage/station.ts:462`

**Fix.**

*From garage-teach:* **Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** Keep the free-placement plan, but correct the TVS truth and the tests. A unidirectional TVS across the motor acts as a plain diode (band to +12 V: fault 'slow' on the stop line) or a short (flipped: fault 'short'). Verify cases: TVS in fly unflipped → stopline fault 'slow'; flipped → 'short'; diode in switch → 'stop'; flipped diode in switch → 'stuck'; clamp flipped in switch → passes job 1 with spike ≈ 25 V. To offer a fast clamp across the motor, keep the CLAMP 24 V (diode + zener in series) as the only part that does it, or add a bidirectional TVS. Also keep the yellow socket glow as a 'can sit here' cue on every legal socket (station.ts:270), not just the correct one.

Reviewer's fix: - **logic.ts:** make placement free. Set `diode`, `clamp` and `tvs` to `slots:['fly','switch']`, the snubber to `['fly','switch']`, and keep the cap at `['ctrl']` (or also allow `'fly'`, as a 'cap across the motor' that only filters).
- **logic.ts `shutdown()`:** for a diode-like part in `switch`, apply `diodeI(x, fwd, rev)` across node→ground. A diode across the switch (band to node) then never conducts at shutdown, so the result is no path and a reset, which is truthful. A TVS in `fly` clamps at V+33 across the motor. Add the matching cases to `flyChain` and `shorted()`: a flipped diode across the switch conducts forwards, so the motor never stops.
- **station.ts:270:** glow every socket the held part *can* sit in, not just the right one.
- **station.ts:462:** change the prompt to 'A/S/D Fit it'.
- **station.ts:445:** remove 'It does not fit here' for protection sockets.
- Re-run `fewestParts`/`cheapest` (`allSetups` grows to roughly 6×6×3×2).
- **Messages:** e.g. 'The diode across the switch never conducts when the node rises: the coil still has no path.'

*From garage-play:* Let the diode-like parts fit both protection sockets. In logic.ts, set slots ['fly','switch'] for diode, clamp and tvs, and ['switch','fly'] for the snubber. The shutdown() solver already handles any thresholds in either place (flyChain for fly, the tvs branch for switch). It needs a generic diode-across-switch branch, using diodeI(x, fwd, rev) with the part's vf/vbr, in place of the TVS-only one.
Then a diode across the switch gives the coil no path, and a TVS across the motor clamps at about 45 V. Both are truthful and teach WHERE.
In prompt(), drop the socket letter from 'Fit it' and say 'A/S/D Fit it'. Keep the glow for every legal socket.
Charge a small credit per PULSE beyond the third in a job, so brute force shows on the cost axis (DR-38).

*From garage-teach:* **Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** Keep the shuffle, the board clear, job 4 and the cost limit. Make the 'charge for PULSE' item consistent with finding 15: charge only for PULSEs that swap parts after the first per job, and keep a polarity flip with an immediate re-PULSE free, so curiosity about polarity isn't taxed twice. Make the job-3 tier-0 prompt neutral ('Change the setup', with no key list naming only the parts). The verify step should use a real cycling player (try parts 1→5 with PULSE, then G), not run3.mjs.

Reviewer's fix: - **Shuffle the tray** per run (seeded `PART_IDS` order in station.ts:166 and the key map at :330), so the key number doesn't encode the answer.
- **Clear the board between jobs** (`this.slots={};this.star=false` after `jobIndex++`, station.ts:229), so job 3 must be rebuilt: fast clamp *and* star ground.
- **Add a final 'road test' job 4** that applies everything from an empty board: stop spec 1 ms, shared 0.15 Ω, and a tighter spike limit (e.g. `spikeReliable 40`), so only clamp + star, or TVS + star, is reliable.
- **Charge for PULSE:** make each PULSE after the first per job cost a small 'bench time' (+0.1 credit to `spent`). Exploration stays possible but cycling all parts shows up in the cost grade.
- **Tighten the cost limit:** with `limits.cost` at `cheapest × 1.25`, brute force lands at C or B.

*Merged entry:* apply one fix for the shared root cause and check it against every room and reviewer listed above; where reviewers proposed different fixes, prefer the verifier-corrected one, then the lead (first) reviewer's.

Retake `garage-teach-33`: with a part held, all compatible sockets glow and the prompt doesn't name one key. 3. `tests/station-garage.spec.ts` still passes with the spec's sequences.
- *garage-play:* Unit test in logic.test.ts: judge(kickback, {switch:{part:'diode'}}) gives fault 'stop' (no path), and {fly:{part:'tvs'}} gives a clamp at about 45 V. Run the spec unchanged (the clean route still works). Retake garage-play-17: both protection sockets glow.
- *garage-teach:* 1. Re-run `run3.mjs` (key-order player): it must fail at least one job and finish below A on cost. 2. `tests/station-garage.spec.ts` clean route updated for the board clear and job 4; the clean run still reaches A.

So the topology choice is made for the player (DR-26, DR-38). (3/3 merged findings CONFIRMED.)

### R5-038

**R5-038 | P1 | lunch | teaching | Lunch: the card skips the conveyor and the second surge (conveyor start on the running lift) has no cue; the card order is wrong**

Found by: `lunch-teach#6` (P1 teaching), `lunch-play#15` (P2 clarity). Batch: R-lunch (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*lunch-teach* — **Second surge lesson (conveyor start on top of the running lift) has no cue at all, and the card's step order walks players into it.** The room requires the conveyor to start before the lift. The conveyor's 3-bar kick plus the running lift's 3 is 6, over cart A's 5 (docs/LEVEL_02_LUNCH_RUSH.md:38). The card orders step 6 'Start the lift winch without tripping a breaker' before step 7 'Send the tray up on the lift', whose marker then moves to the conveyor (src/ui/objectives.ts:49-50). In the trap run (s5-solve trap) I docked the cap, started the lift, and step 6 ticked done (liftRan latches, :49). Then I switched the conveyor on: cart A tripped at once.
What the player sees (shot T-37): only the HUD dial A turns pink. Nothing happens at the conveyor or the lift. No badge appears, because capHint fires only when the lift kicks with no cap (src/lunch-runtime.ts:269). The card reads 'Send the tray up on the lift' and still claims the breaker-free start was achieved.
After the reset, both motors restart together and the cart trips again. The plausible conclusion is 'the capacitor is broken or empty', which is the wrong lesson. Staggered motor starting is a real and valuable idea (vendor guidance for battery stations says to start one high-draw device at a time, because simultaneous surges overload the inverter), but here it is a hidden rule that can only be learned by failing blind, against DR-37.

*lunch-play* — **The card skips the conveyor, so the HUD chain says 'conveyor' while the card says 'lift' and the start order is never shown.** After the tray is placed, the card jumps to 'Start the lift winch without tripping a breaker' (src/ui/objectives.ts:49). Its marker points at the winch. At the same time, the top HUD chain highlights the conveyor icon as the current stage (lunch-play-c11 to c17).

The conveyor needs its own cable and switch (thin-2 → (5,-5), E). Its start-up kick is also why the design wants 'conveyor before lift' (LEVEL_02 step 6). Neither appears on the card or in the world, so the two only UI elements disagree about what comes next.

The 'Send the tray up' step's marker does fall back to the conveyor (:50), but only after the lift has run.

**Evidence.**

- `src/lunch-runtime.ts:269`
- `src/sim/electrical.ts:36-46`
- `docs/LEVEL_02_LUNCH_RUSH.md:38`

**Fix.**

*From lunch-teach:* (1) Apply the kick-visibility fix (the telltale needle plus a jerk at the motor) to the conveyor too. The belt lurches and groans at the conveyor when its start-up trips the cart.
(2) Generalise capHint into a per-motor 'surge' badge: when a trip happens within 1.5 s of any load's start, float that motor's spike glyph over it (conveyor or lift), with no text.
(3) Make step 6 done only when the lift runs AND no trip happened in the next 3 s, or merge steps 6 and 7 into 'Send the tray up on the lift (without tripping a cart)'.
(4) Option: show the cart's pip strip as running load plus the hollow ghost pips of the next start, so the 1.5 + 3 versus 3 + 3 comparison can be read before switching.

*From lunch-play:* Insert a card step after 'Carry the tray': {text:'Get the conveyor moving', done:g=>g.lunch.powered('conveyor')||job.transport>0, at:()=>({x:5,z:-5})}. Then 'Start the lift winch…' and 'Send the tray up'. This also makes the dots match the 3-stage HUD chain.

*Merged entry:* apply one fix for the shared root cause and check it against every room and reviewer listed above; where reviewers proposed different fixes, prefer the verifier-corrected one, then the lead (first) reviewer's.

- *lunch-play:* Retake c14: the card and the HUD chain both point at the conveyor, and the marker sits over the blue motor box.

**Rules:** DR-27, DR-28, DR-37, DR-39, DR-42

Shot T-37 shows 6 green dots, 'Send the tray up on the lift', only the HUD dial A pink, and no cue at the conveyor or lift. (2/2 merged findings CONFIRMED.)

### R5-039

**R5-039 | P1 | meeting | teaching | Meeting: the breaker trip never shows its cause at the faulty part or names it; "E Reset the strip" invites an endless re-trip loop**

Found by: `meeting-play#1` (P1 teaching), `meeting-teach#5` (P1 teaching). Batch: R-meeting (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*meeting-play* — **Breaker trip never says why or points at the cause; 'E Reset the strip' invites an endless re-trip loop.** The load-budget beat is the room's only electricity lesson, and at the moment it fires the game does not show its cause. Pip presses E at the projector switch. The breaker trips (a spark burst at floor level and a short shake), the kettle glow and heater grille go dark, and the projector stays off. Then:
(1) The job card keeps saying 'Switch the projector on in the boardroom', and the bouncing marker stays over the projector, not over the strip or the appliances (shots 22, 23, 39).
(2) The only prompt is 'E Reset the strip', because Pip stands within 1.6 m of the strip at the switch. Pressing E resets the breaker, the 5.5 A load trips it again in the same frame, and the prompt reappears. In the s3 run I pressed E four times in a row: trips went 1→4 with no escalation, no hint and no change in the card.
(3) Nothing in the world connects the trip to 'too many things on one strip'. The kettle and heater just look switched off. The wall gauge is tiny and floats in the doorway (see the gauge finding). The only way to learn the fix is to wander within 1.3 m of the kettle and read 'E Unplug the kettle', which is the text naming the method.
A new player will either loop on reset or think the projector is broken. This breaks DR-28 (failure shows its cause in the world, then one sentence naming the physical cause), DR-42 (card and marker point at the current step's object, not the projector) and DR-37 (hidden rule). It also weakens DR-26, because the lesson ends up taught by a prompt rather than by the scene.

*meeting-teach* — **The trip has no in-world cause cue at the faulty part and no sentence naming the cause.** The trip effects (meeting-strip.ts:82) are:
- 14 small yellow sparks at y 0.3, 4 dust puffs and a 0.12 shake at the strip;
- the kettle and heater glows go out.

At the default camera, Pip stands between the camera and the strip (Pip at z -3.2, strip at z -1.95, camera behind Pip). The sparks are almost fully hidden (shot 07, +0.15 s), and by +1 s the frame shows no failure at all (shot 08).

No toast or sentence ever names the cause, which DR-28 requires: a world cue at the faulty part, then one sentence naming the physical cause. The appliances going dark is a good cue, but it reads as 'the power went', not 'too much on one strip'.

Resetting while overloaded (trip 2) gets identical feedback, so the player learns nothing new from the second failure.

**Evidence.**

- `src/meeting-strip.ts:73-75` (prompt order)

**Fix.**

*From meeting-play:* **Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** Keep (a) to (c). Replace (d): do not light anything on the unpowered kettle or heater. Show that they are still plugged in, but unpowered, through things that need no power. Their cords stay drawn into the strip (they already are), the strip's mechanical reset button pops up (resetCap already does this), and the gauge needle drops to 0 and shows a tripped flag. Also shrink the reset radius, or prefer the switch when Pip is closer to it, so that E at the projector switch does not silently reset and re-trip the strip.

Reviewer's fix: (a) In src/ui/objectives.ts meeting step 3, make the text and marker state-aware: while g.strip?.tripped, show 'The power strip tripped: too much on it' (cause, not method) and set at() to the strip position. On the second trip, move the marker to the appliance drawing most (the kettle).
(b) In src/meeting-strip.ts render(), while tripped, float a small icon over each load still plugged into the strip (kettle, heater, projector). The icon is a stacked bar of its draw (2.5 / 2 / 1) next to a red limit line at 5, using the same Gauge zone colours. The sum then reads visually as 5.5 > 5.
(c) Make the reset refuse with a visible reason when it would instantly re-trip. If the load after reset exceeds STRIP_LIMIT, still trip (truthful), but on trips≥2 play a double-buzz, flash the overloaded zone on the gauge, and jiggle the kettle and heater cords.
(d) Have the kettle and heater keep a dim 'standby' LED (red dot) while tripped, so they read as 'plugged in, no power' rather than 'off'.

*From meeting-teach:* **Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** Drop step 1 (auto-turning game.yaw toward the strip at the trip). The hard rule requires a player-controlled orbit camera, and the win push-in at game.ts:373 is an end-of-level exception, not a mid-play one. Make the cue visible from the player's own camera instead: emit the burst and a smoke column at y 0.8-1.4 so it clears Pip's silhouette, pop up a tall red breaker flag on the strip, and dim the boardroom pendants. Keep the one-sentence cause toast (under 25 words, fading after 4 s per DR-40) and the second-trip variant.

2. Add a puff of smoke from the strip and a 'thunk' of the boardroom lights dimming (pendant glow off for 0.3 s).

4. On a repeat trip after a reset with no load removed: 'Still too much on the strip.'
5. Reuse the station toast element (shared.ts), and fade it after 4 s (DR-40).

### R5-040

**R5-040 | P1 | meeting | teaching | Meeting: the star cable shows no current pulses while it feeds the kettle and heater (4.5 A) and pulses do not match the circuit**

Found by: `meeting-play#3` (P1 teaching), `meeting-teach#6` (P1 teaching). Batch: R-meeting (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*meeting-play* — **The star cable shows no current pulses while it feeds the kettle and heater (4.5 A), and stays 'live gold' while the breaker is tripped.** Once the server cable is plugged into the strip, the kettle steams and the heater grille glows: the cable is carrying 4.5 A (snapshot draw 4.5). The cable turns gold but shows no moving pulses (shots 18, 19), because Pulses.update is gated on loads[0], the projector, alone. Pulses appear only after the win, when the projector runs.
After a trip, nothing flows (draw 0), yet the cable stays the same 'connected' gold (shots 22, 39). The tint is keyed to `connected`, not to current.
In the one room that teaches 'loads on a strip add up', the cable says the opposite: it shows the kettle and heater taking no current, and shows a tripped circuit as still live. This breaks DR-29 (moving dots mean current flows and only then), DR-46 ('a live cable carries pulses') and DR-47 (state shown on the device). It also weakens AGENTS 10 (truthful at the level taught).

*meeting-teach* — **Current pulses don't match the circuit: none on the reel while it feeds the kettle and heater; idle hint dots flow on an open circuit.** Pulses are drawn only when loads[0] (the projector) is on: game.ts:305 calls pulses.update(..., this.circuit.loads[0].state==='on').

- After plug-in the reel carries 4.5 A to the kettle and heater (snapshot draw 4.5), yet it is plain gold with no pulses (shots 03, 24).
- The kettle and heater cords (meeting-strip.ts:94-96) never show flow.
- So the room teaches that current flows only when the 'target' device is on. It also hides the point that the reel is already carrying most of the strip's budget.

Separately, re-checking known DR-29: the 40-dot cyan idle hint (game.ts:101, :446-447) still flows from Pip toward the door at 40 s, with nothing plugged in (shot 20). That contradicts 'dots mean current' on the same floor.

**Evidence.**

- `src/game.ts:305` (pulses on only when circuit.loads[0].state==='on', i.e. the projector)

**Fix.**

*From meeting-play:* In src/game.ts drawCable(), compute live = (this.circuit.draw.get('supply')??0) > 0 && !this.circuit.sources[0].tripped. Pass live to pulses.update instead of loads[0].state==='on'. Keep pulse speed constant (DR-30) and scale pulse density or brightness with draw/STRIP_LIMIT, so 4.5 A looks busier than 1 A. Tint the hose GOLD only while live; when connected but tripped, use a desaturated grey-gold (#b9ad86) and stop the pulses.

*From meeting-teach:* 1. Drive reel pulses from the strip draw: (this.circuit.draw.get('reel')??0)>0, with density or speed scaled to draw/limit.
2. Draw pulses on each appliance cord while its load is on. Reuse Pulses with the cord's TubeGeometry curve.
3. Replace the idle hint dots with static, non-glowing chevrons painted along the route, or footprints. That keeps moving dots reserved for current.

### R5-041

**R5-041 | P1 | meeting, lunch | teaching | Breakers trip on the same frame the load goes over (Meeting at 1.1×, Lunch carts at 1.2–1.8× for 1 s), which real breakers never do**

Found by: `meeting-teach#0` (P1 teaching), `lunch-teach#3` (P1 teaching). Batch: R-meeting (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*meeting-teach* — **The breaker trips on the same frame the load goes over: the cause is never seen, and an instant trip at 1.1x is false.** The load-budget beat is the only electricity in Big Meeting, and its key moment can't be read.

What happens:
- The gauge needle is set to draw/limit*0.9, or to 1 while tripped (src/meeting-strip.ts:84).
- Circuit.tick trips the source in the same tick the total passes the limit (src/sim/electrical.ts:46).
- So the needle's last live reading is 4.5 A / 5 A = 0.81, in the yellow (shot 25).
- Pressing E at the projector then jumps the needle straight to pinned red (shots 07, 23).

The player never sees 5.5 A sitting past the limit (the cause) before the CLACK (the effect). The switch press is the only visible cause, so 'loads add up until they pass the limit' becomes 'the projector switch breaks the strip'.

It is also false at the level taught. 5.5 A on 5 A is a 1.1x overload. Real thermal-magnetic breakers follow an inverse-time curve. Miniature UL 489 breakers must not trip at about 105% of rating, and must trip at 135% within about an hour:
- Schneider UL 489 calibration FAQ: https://www.se.com/us/en/faqs/FA98008
- Altech UL 489 datasheet: https://wolfautomation.com/content/altech-1pole-489-ctrip-datasheet.pdf

The game teaches that a strip trips the instant it is 0.01 A over. This confirms research leads M-2 and E-1.

*lunch-teach* — **The carts' 'breakers' trip instantly at 1.2–1.8× for one second, which real breakers never do. Reframe the carts truthfully as battery power stations with a surge rating.** src/sim/electrical.ts:46 trips a source on any draw above `limit+1e-6`, on the first tick. The kick trips are 9 on 5 (1.8×) for 1 s, and 6 on 5 (1.2×) for the conveyor after the lift. Under IEC 60898-1, a B-curve MCB must not trip within an hour at 1.13× In, must trip within an hour at 1.45× In, and trips instantly (<0.1 s) only at 3–5× In. So at 1.2–1.8× for one second a real breaker would not trip at all. The room therefore teaches two false rules of thumb: 'a breaker trips the moment you go a hair over', and 'motor inrush always trips breakers'. It also inverts the real relationship, because here the cable (src/sim/electrical.ts:49) is the slow, time-integrating element and the breaker is the instant one.
The prompt and HUD wording both say 'breaker' (src/lunch-runtime.ts:189, the bonus 'Never trip a breaker' at src/ui/objectives.ts:52). The room also never says AC or DC, and the capacitor-supplies-the-kick idea (L-1) is only true on a DC bus. On AC mains, a 'motor start capacitor' works by phase shift, not stored energy.
There is a truthful real-world device that behaves exactly as the game does: a portable battery power station. It has a continuous rating and a short surge rating, its electronic overload protection cuts out at once when a motor's start-up draw exceeds the surge limit, and buffering peaks with supercapacitors on a DC bus is real practice.

**Fix.**

*From meeting-teach:* **Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** Do NOT add the accumulator to every Source in src/sim/electrical.ts. Lunch uses the same Circuit, two 5 A sources: lunch-runtime.ts:43-47 gives the lift a 9 A kick for 1 s and the conveyor a 3 A kick, and electrical.test.ts:8 and :10 ('lift kick trips unless…', 'reverse order trips') depend on brief overloads tripping straight away. A global I²t dwell of acc>=0.5 would stop the short, small overload in the reverse-order case from tripping and break the capacitor lesson. Make it opt-in instead: add an optional Source field (e.g. thermal?:{acc:number;trip:number;instant:number}) that only MeetingStrip sets (meeting-strip.ts:29). Keep instant tripping for sources without it, and keep the DR-36 comment next to it. Unit tests: 5.5 A on the thermal source has not tripped at 1 s and has tripped by 3 s; the existing Lunch tests still pass unchanged. routes.spec.ts:16 wait goes from .3 to about 3 s.

Reviewer's fix: Give the strip a short, visible overload dwell before it trips:
1. Add an accumulator to Source (or keep it local to MeetingStrip): acc += max(0,(I/limit)^2 - 1)*dt.
2. Trip at acc >= 0.5, which is about 2.4 s at 1.1x. Also trip instantly when I > 3*limit.
3. During the dwell:
   - map the needle to min(1.15, I/limit)*0.87 so it visibly sits past the red line;
   - play a rising hum (audio.tone 90-140 Hz);
   - jitter the strip mesh and flicker the kettle and heater glows.
4. Then CLACK.
5. Add a DR-36 comment: 'real breakers trip in minutes at 1.1x; compressed to about 2 s as game tuning'.
6. Update src/sim/electrical.test.ts and tests/routes.spec.ts switchProjector (src/routes.spec lines 15-19), which waits 0.3 s: wait 3 s instead.

*From lunch-teach:* Option A (recommended, keeps every puzzle number):
- Make the carts 'battery power carts': a 48 V DC decal plus a battery-cell glyph on prefabs.ts:166.
- Rename the protection in player copy to 'overload cut-out': lunch-runtime.ts:189 becomes 'Reset cart B's overload cut-out', objectives.ts:52 becomes 'Never overload a cart'.
- Call the capcart a 'supercap cart' in NAMES (objectives.ts:59) and in the prompts at lunch-runtime.ts:175 and :182.
- Add a comment at electrical.ts:46: '// electronic overload cut-out (like a battery power station's inverter), trips at once; tuning values'.
- Leave thermal-magnetic breaker curves for a later room that teaches them.
Option B: keep 'breaker', give Source an I²t accumulator (`acc+=max(0,(I/limit)^2-1)*dt`, trip at acc≥4) plus an instant trip at I>3·limit, and raise the lift kick to ≥16 so the lesson survives. That is more code and more tuning.
Either way, update the docs (docs/LEVEL_02_LUNCH_RUSH.md:9, GAME_DESIGN.md:23).

*Merged entry:* apply one fix for the shared root cause and check it against every room and reviewer listed above; where reviewers proposed different fixes, prefer the verifier-corrected one, then the lead (first) reviewer's.

- *lunch-teach:* Grep player strings for 'breaker' in src/lunch-runtime.ts and src/ui/objectives.ts. With option B, a unit test: 1.5× for 0.5 s does not trip, 1.5× for 6 s does, 3.2× trips in the same tick. The tests/lunch-rules.spec.ts kick test still passes.

### R5-042

**R5-042 | P1 | meeting, lunch | teaching | While tripped, the gauges read full scale with zero current flowing, so unplugging shows no effect and the start-up kick is invisible**

Found by: `meeting-teach#1` (P1 teaching), `lunch-teach#2` (P1 teaching). Batch: R-meeting (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*meeting-teach* — **While tripped, the gauge reads full-scale with zero current flowing, so unplugging shows no effect.** meeting-strip.ts:84 sets gauge.set(tripped ? 1 : draw/limit*.9). Once the breaker trips, the circuit draw is 0 A, but the needle is pinned at maximum (shots 13 and 23). A needle is a meter, so this teaches 'a tripped strip has the most current'.

It also kills the one moment where the player could watch cause and effect. In shot 13, unplugging the kettle while tripped leaves the needle exactly where it was. The player gets no evidence that removing a load lowered the total, until reset happens to work. Real load meters read zero when the breaker is open.

*lunch-teach* — **A start-up kick is invisible: the trip happens in one tick, the needle jumps to full scale on zero current, and nothing happens at the motor.** The lift's 9-bar kick and the conveyor's 3-bar kick trip the cart on the first simulation tick (src/sim/electrical.ts:46). The player sees the HUD dial turn pink, and the needle is driven to full scale because the source is tripped: src/ui/lunch-hud.ts:49 (`g.tripped?180`) and the in-world gauge `gauge.set(source.tripped?1:…)` (src/lunch-runtime.ts:308). That is untruthful twice over. A tripped breaker carries zero current, so a needle at full scale tells the learner that a lot of current is flowing right now. And the actual peak, 9 bars, is beyond the dial's scale and is never shown.
At the motor itself nothing happens. Shots 21 and 22 at the winch show Pip, a slack cable and an unchanged winch. The spark and dust burst are 25 m away at cart A (src/lunch-runtime.ts:264), off screen. Nothing tells the player that the lift runs on 3 and only needs 9 for a moment, which is the entire reason a capacitor helps. A reasonable player who has seen the needle slam will conclude that the lift needs more than a cart can give. They will try the thick cable, which cannot help because the breaker is still 5, and get no new information. DR-28 requires the failure to show its cause at the faulty part. DR-47 requires each device to show its own state.

2. Add a faint ghost needle (a second line in Gauge.set at 35% alpha) for the demand the strip would carry if reset: the sum of the steady draws of the plugged and enabled loads, computed in MeetingStrip.render.
3. Unplugging the kettle while tripped then visibly drops the ghost needle from 5.5 to 3 A, below the red line. That is the cause-and-effect image the lesson needs.

It records the highest draw in the last 3 s, pinned past the red end with a '9' pip if it is over scale. The live needle drops to 0 on a trip. ### R5-043

**R5-043 | P1 | observatory | teaching | Observatory: "Elegant" is a moving target that depends on where the cart landed, and job 1 introduces four new ideas at once**

Found by: `observatory-play#6` (P1 teaching), `observatory-teach#11` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-observatory (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*observatory-play* — **'Elegant' is a moving target that depends on where the cart landed, so the intended filter loses the star.** The elegant tier compares the player's parts cost with cheapest(job,{cartDistance:max(cartDistance,4)}). That uses the cart's actual distance. In the clean spec the cart lands about 7.9 m away, and a 1.5 µF shunt capacitor plus the reroute is the cheapest fix, so it rates Elegant. If the player throws the cart further (the fun move, which landed it 9.7–11.6 m away), the reroute alone passes. The same 1.5 µF fix then logs 'Reliable. Cheaper parts can do it too (cost 0 vs 1)' and the Elegant bonus star is gone. The player did 'more' in the room and gets a worse grade, with a message saying the filter, the lesson of the job, wasn't needed. Nothing on screen says the tier depends on cart distance. This rewards a luck variable, not understanding, and makes job 1's filter optional for anyone who throws hard. Breaks DR-38 (tiers reward understanding, not luck) and DR-02 (chaos never punished).

*observatory-teach* — **Job 1 introduces four new ideas at once, and the elegant tier changes with where the cart was dropped (with a wrong 'Cheaper parts' note).** (1) Job 1 asks the player to meet, all at once: noise falls with distance (the cart), coupling depends on routing (the lever), series vs shunt topology, and a shunt C setting a low-pass corner frequency. That is four new ideas in the first job (DR-27 allows at most two).
(2) The 'cheapest' target is recomputed from the cart's distance at log time (logic.ts:177-179). If Pip carries the cart 10 m or more away (the room allows up to about 17 m), 'no cans + reroute' becomes the elegant answer (n2/numbers output: d=10 gives 12.7 dB with no filter). The taught 1 µF shunt then drops to tier 2 with the note 'Reliable. Cheaper parts can do it too (cost 0 vs 1)'. 'Cheaper parts' when the answer is no parts is wrong wording, and the bonus 'Elegant: the leanest filter each time' is lost for doing the lesson well.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/observatory/logic.ts:177-179` (best = cheapest(job,{cartDistance:max(s.cartDistance,CART_SAFE)}))
- `src/stations/observatory/logic.ts:133` (coupling 1.2/distance)
- `tools/observatory-play/08-chaos-grade2.mjs` log 'log1 … tier 2 … Cheaper parts can do it too (cost 0 vs 1)' with cartD 9.66

**Fix.**

*From observatory-play:* Make the elegant reference fixed per job. Compute `best` with a fixed design distance, cheapest(job,{cartDistance:CART_SAFE}), as station.ts:82 already does for the cost limit, and treat any setup at or below that cost as tier 3. Also cap cartCoupling's benefit: `Math.min(1,1.2/Math.max(.3,Math.min(distance,6)))`. Moving the cart then helps up to 6 m, and the filter stays required for a reliable decode (check that job 1's no-cans reroute at 6 m stays below 12 dB). Add a logic.test.ts case: tier(1.5 µF shunt, rerouted, cartDistance 12) === 3.

*From observatory-teach:* Split job 1 into two beats. Beat 1a: move the cart; the scope alone shows the noise falling, with no filter needed to log (tier 2 when ≥ 12 dB, rerouting optional). Beat 1b: a second noise source the player cannot move (the dome motor, see the shutter finding) needs the shunt-C filter.
In judge(), cap the distance used for `best` at CART_SAFE (use CART_SAFE, not max(distance, CART_SAFE)), so the elegant target is stable. When best.cost===0, write 'A cleaner setup needs no cans at all here'.

*Merged entry:* apply one fix for the shared root cause and check it against every room and reviewer listed above; where reviewers proposed different fixes, prefer the verifier-corrected one, then the lead (first) reviewer's.

### R5-044

**R5-044 | P1 | observatory | teaching | Observatory: the job 2 latch failure and job 3 gust have no world event — the shutter latch and dome motor do not exist in the room**

Found by: `observatory-play#8` (P1 teaching), `observatory-teach#2` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-observatory (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*observatory-play* — **Job 2 latch failure and job 3 gust have no world event: failures and twists are sentences or invisible.** Job 2's lesson is that a series capacitor blocks the 12 V DC, so the dome-shutter latch drops out. When it fails, nothing happens to the dome. The only cues are a small lamp on the bench going grey and a 2-line toast ('The latch dropped out: a series capacitor passes changes but no steady DC…'). Standing up and surveying the room shows no change at all. The success messages 'DOME OPEN' and 'STARS CLEAR' also have no world consequence until the very end. In job 3, the 'gust over the roof' that lays the whip flat is the twist that should teach polarisation. In practice the fitted whip is the 3.1 cm stub, so going 'flat' is a 1–2 px change. The dust puff is a small cream disc hanging in mid-air in front of the clutter, and the player is never shown that anything happened. Job 3 is then solved by clicking each of four rods and toggling orientation (8 free tries), with no cost and no physical act beyond clicking. R4A asked for the shutter to slam shut and for whips carried up the mast. Breaks DR-28 (failure shows its cause in the world first), DR-37 (hidden rules shown by the world) and DR-26 (concept taught by a physical act).

*observatory-teach* — **The 'shutter latch' and the 'dome motor' don't exist in the world: job 2's noise source and its failure consequence are invisible.** Job 2 reads 'Keep the shutter latch powered … The dome motor whines at 4 kHz' (logic.ts:124-125). Job 3's message is 'DOME OPEN'. But room.ts:67-79 builds the dome as a static half-shell with a telescope. There is no shutter, no dome motor and no slit that opens (shots 43, 01). The noise in jobs 2 and 3 therefore has no physical source the player can see, hear in the room or move (logic.ts:141: 'reaches the receiver through its own mount').
When the latch drops out (series C or series R logged), the only consequence in the world is a 4 cm lamp on the board turning from green to dark (station.ts:125, :239; shot 25), plus the sentence in the toast. Nothing slams, nothing closes, the telescope doesn't move. DR-28 asks that failure show its cause in the world first; DR-47 asks that devices show their state; DR-37 says hidden rules must be shown.
The success payoff is just as invisible. 'DOME OPEN' and the final 'STARS CLEAR' only appear as text. The lightUp() glow (room.ts:109) is behind the win push-in camera (shots 36 and 17 frame the bench and gallery, not the dome). The player never sees the circuit do anything physical.

### R5-045

**R5-045 | P1 | observatory | teaching | Observatory: cable routing, the room's spatial idea, is a lever on the bench; no physical cable runs from the roof receiver to the bench**

Found by: `observatory-teach#3` (P1 teaching), `observatory-models#2` (P1 model-detail). Batch: R-observatory (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*observatory-teach* — **Cable routing, the room's spatial idea, is a lever on the bench; the receiver cable doesn't exist in the room, and 'past the motor' is physically inconsistent (REGRESSION check: still open since R4A).** The coupling model measures the motor's distance from the rack at RX (-3.25,-2.45) (room.ts:16, station.ts:314). But the 'route' that halves the noise is a lever on the bench, which swaps between two short red tubes lying on the desktop (station.ts:129-133, :187-188, :233).
In the room there is no cable from the ROOF RECEIVER rack to the bench at all. The bench's red lead starts in mid-air at the desk's left edge (shots 40, 42, 07). So once Pip has carried the motor 7 m away (shot 05), the bench still says 'ROUTE: PAST MOTOR', and flipping a lever 7 m from the motor still gains exactly 6 dB (logic.ts:133). That teaches the wrong causal story: noise pickup depends on where the cable runs relative to the source. Here it depends on a lever, wherever the motor is.
It also leaves AGENTS rule 4 ('the cable is the star') unused in the room where routing a cable away from a noise source is literally the lesson. R4A ('the big miss: cable routing is a bench lever') and NEXT_STEPS.md:26 already raised this; it is still not done.
The noise source itself barely reads: the motor's only cue is a 3-particle spark burst every 0.5–1.1 s (station.ts:316), not visible in any of my room shots (40, 42), and nothing links the cart to the receiver line. The noise is visible only on the bench scope.

*observatory-models* — **No physical cable from the roof receiver rack to the bench: the receiver line ends in mid-air at the bench edge.** The whole first transmission is about the receiver's cable picking up motor noise: 'roll the motor away, reroute the cable'. RX at (-3.25,-2.45) is 'where the receiver's cable leaves the rack'. Yet nothing in the room joins the rack, at (RX.x-.3, RX.z-.2) = (-3.55,-2.65) with its right face at x≈-3.1, to the bench, whose left end is at x≈-2.15. The two red TubeGeometry routes on the bench start at local x=-2.2, y=.02, at the bench's edge, and stop there (station.ts:127-130). In the room shots there is a visible 1 m gap of bare floor between the rack and the bench (shots 63, 63b, 60). In the bench view the red cable runs off the left edge of the bench into nothing (shot 43, crop 43c). The player can't see that the bench line is the rack's line, so moving the motor away 'from the receiver' and rerouting 'past the motor' have no physical anchor. In a game whose star is the cable (AGENTS 4), the only cable in the room is a short bench decal.

### R5-046

**R5-046 | P1 | playground | teaching | Playground: the cable reel is shown as the power source — it is not plugged into anything, so the loop the room teaches is not truthful**

Found by: `playground-teach#2` (P1 teaching), `playground-play#3` (P1 teaching). Batch: R-playground (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*playground-teach* — **The cable reel is shown as the power source: it isn't plugged into anything, the poster says so, and the glowing wall socket next to it is inert.** The reel at (-8,4) stands free in the middle of the floor. No lead runs from it to any wall outlet (game.ts:90-91 builds the drum, axle, foot and spool; decor adds nothing that connects it). The circuit's source `supply` (game.ts:102) is never drawn. The wordless how-to poster on the side wall (decor.ts:98-101; shots 01, 03, 13) reads: yellow reel → orange cable → black plug → teal socket → sun lamp. The reel is the start of the chain.

Meanwhile the back wall has a 'practice wall' of five sockets, one with a green 'live' glow (decor.ts:96-97). It is exactly what a real player would plug a reel into, and the game does nothing with it: carrying the plug there gives 'F Drop the plug' (shot 23).

So the first lesson in an electronics game teaches that a reel (an extension lead) makes electricity. That is the extension-lead version of the well-documented 'battery as current source' / 'source gives out current that gets used' misconception. The reviews cited here (Harvard Project Zero SimpleCircuits, https://pz.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/SimpleCircuits.pdf; Wainwright, https://fg.ed.pacificu.edu/wainwright/Publications/MisconceptionsArticle.06.pdf) report it persisting past school. It breaks AGENTS rule 10 and DR-37 (invisible wiring must be drawn). It also sets up the Meeting, where the reel comes from a 'server closet' with 'the one live outlet', so the two rooms disagree about where power comes from.

*playground-play* — **The reel has no visible source, so the 'loop' the room teaches is not truthful or readable.** The anchor reel at (-8,4) is a free-standing spool on an ink base plate (src/game.ts:89-91), 2 m from the side wall, with nothing connecting it to a wall outlet or supply. The practice wall of five sockets is on the back wall, far away and unconnected (src/levels/decor.ts:96-97). The level is meant to teach that a switch closes the loop (research-docs 1.2), but the scene shows electricity appearing from an unplugged reel and ending at a lamp, with no source and no return. That breaks AGENTS 10 (electricity truthful at the level taught). It is also a missed play-by-doing beat: the first room could show 'source → cable → switch → lamp' as physical objects. The how-to poster (decor.ts:98-104) shows reel → plug → socket → lamp and also omits the source and the switch.

**Evidence.**

- `src/game.ts:90-91` (reel anchor, free-standing)
- `src/game.ts:102` (Circuit source 'supply', never drawn)
- `src/levels/decor.ts:96-101` (practice wall with green glow socket; poster starting at the reel)

That would feed the reel from its own output end, which is electrically meaningless and muddier than the problem it solves. Just remove the green glow from the practice wall, and put the live pilot on the new outlet that the reel's fixed lead runs into.

Reviewer's fix: Make the supply visible and put it first.

1. In decor.ts playground():
   - Mount a wall outlet plate on the side wall right by the reel, at about (-9.85, .45, 4.0): rbox(.38,.38,.1) with two dark holes.
   - Move the green glow from practice-wall socket k===2 to this outlet, as its 'live' pilot.
   - Draw a short fixed lead (TubeGeometry, radius .05, hose white) from the reel drum (-8,.35,4) to that outlet, ending in a plug seated in it.
2. Change the poster glyph to begin with an outlet icon: outlet → reel → plug → lamp.
3. Either remove the green glow from the practice wall, or let the reel's free plug actually plug into practice-wall sockets (with nothing happening, which is truthful, since a wall socket isn't a load).
4. Optionally put a small flashing breaker on the outlet plate, so the Meeting's breaker isn't the player's first sight of one.

*From playground-play:* **Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** Drop the 'no return' argument. A lead from the reel to a wall outlet is enough at this level.

Give the outlet a small green 'live' pip. Update the howto glyph to show outlet → reel → plug → socket → switch → lamp. ### R5-047

**R5-047 | P1 | playground, lunch | teaching | Current pulses run one way at one speed and density whatever the current, and at hose radius they are nearly invisible**

Found by: `playground-teach#3` (P1 teaching), `lunch-teach#9` (P1 teaching). Batch: R-playground (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*playground-teach* — **Current pulses run one way on a single hose, and at radius = hose radius they are nearly invisible.** The room's only picture of current is Pulses (src/render/actors.ts:80-86): 4 capsules travelling from the reel to the lamp along the one hose, and only while the load is on (game.ts:304-305).

**What it teaches.** electrical.ts:1-2 says each lead models both conductors and that a missing return is explicit 'rather than teaching a one-wire circuit'. The rendering undoes that. One tube, with slugs moving one way, source to lamp, and none coming back, is the textbook 'current flows to the device and is used up' picture. Licht & Thijs found 61% of 13–14-year-olds hold that view (reported in the misconception reviews: https://fg.ed.pacificu.edu/wainwright/Publications/MisconceptionsArticle.06.pdf). DR-29 and DR-30 require the opposite.

**How it reads.** The capsules have radius .1 (actors.ts:82 default) and the hose has radius .1 (game.ts:304). They are coincident with the hose surface, so they show only as faint white-cyan stripes on the gold cable. In the win shots (10, 29) a single pale slug can be found near the plug. At the game camera the 'current now flows' signal effectively isn't there. With only 4 slugs on an 18 m cable, they are about 4.6 m apart, which makes it worse.

*lunch-teach* — **Current pulses run at the same speed and density whatever the current, so the cable never shows that more load means more current.** Pulses.update (src/render/actors.ts:85) moves a fixed 3 slugs at `time*3/length`, the same for a 0.5-bar lamp, the 2-bar fridge and the 4-bar kitchen feed. LunchRuntime only switches them on or off (src/lunch-runtime.ts:320). In shot S-30b the thick cable's pulses are faint pale stripes that blend into its black and yellow bands, and the thin fridge feed shows none that I can read at the game camera.
The cable is the star (AGENTS 4) and the room's quantity is current through each cable against its rating. Making pulse rate proportional to current is the PhET-style way to make that visible, and it makes overload predictable: a thin cable visibly crowded with pulses is about to cook. Today heat is the only signal, and it arrives only once the damage has started.

**Evidence.**

- `src/render/actors.ts:80-86` (Pulses: 4 slugs, radius .1, one direction)
- `src/game.ts:304-305` (hose radius .1, pulses on when loads[0] on)
- `src/sim/electrical.ts:1-2` (lead = both conductors)

- [playground-teach-26b-winpush-pip-crop.jpg](shots/playground-teach-26b-winpush-pip-crop.jpg)
- [verify-playground-teach-11-win-pushin-nohud.jpg](shots/verify-playground-teach-11-win-pushin-nohud.jpg)
- `src/render/actors.ts:82` (CapsuleGeometry(radius=.1,.4))
- `src/render/actors.ts:80-86`

- [lunch-teach-S-30b-crop-pulses.jpg](shots/lunch-teach-S-30b-crop-pulses.jpg)
