### R5-184

**R5-184 | P2 | arcade, arcade-rush, garage | teaching | Arcade and Garage: the "PTC fuse" re-arms every 2.5 s while powered into the fault, like a bimetal breaker; real polymer PTCs latch until power is removed**

Found by: `arcade-teach#2` (P2 teaching), `arcade-rush-teach#6` (P2 teaching), `garage-teach#14` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-arcade (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*arcade-teach* — **The 'PTC fuse' behaves like a bimetal auto-reset breaker: it re-conducts every 2.5 s while powered into the fault, clicks and glows red.** Code: the fuse cools while still powered (station.ts:373-374, comment 'cools whether or not the bench is on'), then trips again 0.15 s later (station.ts:376). In fail.mjs I left the pinball's as-found fault powered for 8 s and sampled every 0.25 s. The trace was TTTTTTTTTT.TTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTTT., so the fuse cycles about every 2.65 s with a click tone, sparks and the TILT marquee each time. The disc itself goes orange-red with a red halo (arcade-teach-04-pinball-trip.jpg, station.ts:422-425), and the story says 'The fuse keeps clicking' (logic.ts:65). A real polymer PTC (PPTC) does not behave like this. After tripping, a small leakage current keeps it hot and high-resistance for as long as the fault and the voltage remain: it latches. It resets only once the power is removed and it has cooled. Littelfuse says the device stays latched until the fault is cleared and power is removed, and that it needs the low joule-heating leakage current to stay tripped. A PPTC trips at about 125 °C, so it does not glow red, and it makes no sound. The game describes the part as a 'PTC' (logic.ts:13, :28) but gives it a bimetal thermal breaker's behaviour, so a learner gets a false model of a common protection part. Review4 asked for the RESET button to go; this fix went too far the other way.

*arcade-rush-teach* — **The 'PTC fuse' re-arms while powered and keeps re-tripping; real polymer PTCs latch until power is removed.** Still open from the research lead (A-1); the rush story leans on it ('The fuse keeps clicking'). The fuse cools whether or not the bench is on and conducts again after 2.5 s. With the fault still in place it trips again: in my run cabinet 0 was still or again tripped 3.2 s after power-on with the bench left on. That is a bimetal auto-reset breaker. A polymer PTC stays latched (high resistance, held hot by a small leakage current) until the fault is cleared AND power is removed (Littelfuse technical paper; Wikipedia 'Resettable fuse'). It also adds dead time: after fixing the chain the player must wait out 'FUSE COOLING 1.4 s' even though the circuit is now fine. That is a locked wait inside a 3-minute shift, repeated on every tripping cabinet. The red-hot halo is also untruthful: a PPTC trips at about 125 °C and doesn't glow.

*garage-teach* — **The PTC fuse glows red like a filament and clicks back on.** On trip, the fuse disc lerps from yellow to `#ff3b2a` at up to 2× emissive (station.ts:350), with sparks (`garage-teach-37-crop-short-fuse.jpg`). A polymer PTC trips at roughly 125 °C: it gets warm, it doesn't glow red.

In this circuit the auto-reset is truthful, because the short only exists while the MOSFET is on, and the test stops driving it. But the red-hot glow repeats the arcade's A-1 lead (a PTC shown as a glowing bimetal). The comment 'Tripped, it glows red' (station.ts:131) codifies it.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/arcade/station.ts:376`
- `src/stations/arcade/station.ts:8`
- `src/stations/arcade/station.ts:422-425`
- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:13`
- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:28-29`
- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:65`

**Fix.**

Change the prompt at station.ts:483 to {key:'P',text:'Power off to reset'}. Replace the red lerp at station.ts:424 with a warm amber tint (#ffb14d, no halo, or halo opacity ≤ 0.25). Story logic.ts:65 becomes 'The fuse keeps tripping.' Update the header comments (logic.ts:13, station.ts:8) to say 'stays tripped while power is on; resets once switched off and cool'. Update tests/station-arcade.spec.ts:31-32: after removing the across block, POWER off, wait 2.6 s, then POWER on.

*From arcade-rush-teach:* **Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** Either option is truthful. (a) The reviewer's latching PTC: cool only while !powered, prompt 'P Power off to reset'. Or (b) the cheaper fix: keep the cycling and treat it as a bimetal auto-reset breaker, change the disc model to a small metal-can breaker, and fix the comments. Either way, drop the red-hot glow and let a fixed chain clear the trip on the next power-cycle without waiting out the full fuseCool.

Reviewer's fix: Take option (b) from the lead: in update(), count `cooling` down only while `!this.powered`. Keep `tripped` latched while powered, and show the prompt 'P Power off to reset the fuse'. Shorten fuseCool to 1.0 s in rush (power-off is now the cost, which teaches 'remove power before rework'). Replace the red halo with a warm amber tint (#ffb347, halo opacity ≤ 0.3). Rename the rush story to 'The fuse keeps cutting out.'

*Merged entry:* apply one fix for the shared root cause and check it against every room and reviewer listed above; where reviewers proposed different fixes, prefer the verifier-corrected one, then the lead (first) reviewer's.

### R5-185

**R5-185 | P2 | meeting, playground | teaching | The playground plug is the Meeting coupler model and the player pushes a live male plug into the load: power flows the wrong way through the connectors**

Found by: `meeting-teach#7` (P2 teaching), `playground-teach#13` (P2 teaching). Batch: B7 (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*meeting-teach* — **Power flows the wrong way through the connectors: Pip pushes the live male plug from the closet into the strip's sockets (a 'suicide cord').** The reel is anchored at the closet outlet (meeting.ts:33, anchor -11.4,-7.8), and Pip carries its free end.

- That end is modelled as a male plug: the plug and coupler prefab is a body plus two brass pins (src/props/prefabs.ts:101-102); game.ts:86 uses it as this.plug. The action-bar icon is a pronged plug, and the prompts say 'Pick up the plug' and 'Plug in' (shots 01, 30).
- The free end of a cable that is live from the wall would then have energised, exposed pins. That is the male-to-male 'suicide cord' the CPSC warns against: https://abc7news.com/post/federal-safety-agency-warns-not-use-male-double-pronged-extension-cords-due-risk-electrocution-fire/18907805/ and https://acworks.com/blogs/ac-works-connector/the-dangers-of-double-male-ended-cords.
- The strip is a distributor (it feeds the kettle and heater), yet it is fed through one of its own outlets (strip sockets, prefabs.ts:138). That is backwards: a strip is fed by its own plug.

At the level taught (source to cable to strip to loads), the connector genders show the direction of supply, and this teaches it reversed. It applies to the Playground lamp socket too.

*playground-teach* — **The playground plug is rendered with the Meeting 'coupler' model, and it is a live male plug going into the load.** The cable's end is makeProp('coupler','#ffcc52') (game.ts:86). The coupler and plug kinds share one mesh (prefabs.ts:101). In the Meeting, a teal 'coupler' is a different job item that joins two reels (objectives.ts NAMES 'coupler'), so the same object means two things (DR-50). It is also a male plug with prongs (shot 29 shows the prongs), and it comes from the energised side. Pip carries a plug that is live as soon as the reel is fed, into a 'lamp's socket' (objectives.ts:25).

In real wiring, the energised side always carries the female connector, so live pins can't be touched. A male-to-male or live-plug arrangement is the notorious 'suicide cord' (https://www.slashgear.com/1859724/suicide-extension-cord-explained-what-happens-plug-in-danger-risks ; the CPSC warning summarised at https://hackaday.com/2022/09/17/the-cpsc-says-plug-to-socket-not-plug-to-plug-please). Lamps have plugs; supplies have sockets. At the game's level the loop still works, but the parts are assigned backwards. That is cheap to fix now and would mislead later, once players see real plugs.

**Fix.**

*From meeting-teach:* **Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** Fix the evidence: the receptacle is the dark socket box at game.ts:88, not the strip's sockets at prefabs.ts:138. The lighter fix is to make the carried end a female connector (no pins, slotted face) and turn the game.ts:88 box into the strip's own short plug lead. Moving the reel drum to the boardroom would change the cable-length and strain design of every cable floor, so treat it as out of scope.

Reviewer's fix: Make the hand-held end a socket.
1. Add a 'connector' render of the free end in prefabs.ts: an orange box with a slotted face and no pins.
2. Give the strip a short stub lead ending in a plug (prefabs.ts:138).
3. On snap (game.ts:205), seat the strip's plug into the connector with the existing plugFlash.
4. Keep the verbs, but word the prompts truthfully: 'Pick up the cable end', 'Connect the strip'.
5. Alternative with the same geometry: move the reel drum, with its sockets, to the boardroom side, and have Pip walk the plug back to the closet outlet. That matches how real reels are used.
6. Do the same in the Playground: put a plug on the lamp's lead.

*From playground-teach:* Swap the gender without changing the mechanic:
1. The reel's free end is a trailing socket: a chunky yellow block with two dark holes, no prongs, and its own prefab kind 'outlet-head'.
2. The lamp gets a short cord from its base ending in a plug that lies on a little stand where the socket box is now.
3. Pressing F at the lamp still 'joins' them, so the snap logic is unchanged.
4. Copy: 'Pick up the cable end', 'Take the cable to the lamp and plug the lamp in'.

If that's too much churn, at minimum give the playground end its own plug mesh distinct from the Meeting coupler, and call the target an 'inlet'.

*Merged entry:* apply one fix for the shared root cause and check it against every room and reviewer listed above; where reviewers proposed different fixes, prefer the verifier-corrected one, then the lead (first) reviewer's.

**Verify.**

The reel is anchored at the closet outlet (meeting.ts:33), so the free end carries live pins, which is reversed from real reel use. One detail is wrong: the strip is not fed through one of its own outlets. (2/2 merged findings CONFIRMED.)

### R5-186

**R5-186 | P2 | qfn | teaching | QFN: board 3's chip glows red-hot at 135 °C the moment the board loads, before anything is wired or powered**

Found by: `qfn-teach#2` (P2 teaching), `qfn-play#17` (P2 clarity). Batch: R-qfn (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*qfn-teach* — **The board-3 chip glows red-hot at 135 °C the moment the board loads, before anything powers it.** Board 3 drops in with U1 tinted orange-red, a pulsing red glow sprite and the panel row 'Chip 135 °C · ≤ 70', before a single track exists (qfn-teach-13-b3-start-chip-hot-unpowered). The run log at that moment reads thermal {vias:0,temp:135}, with VIN at 1/4 pads and GND at 1/6. chipTemp() (logic.ts:233) depends only on the via count. update() (station.ts:393-396) tints and pulses the body from it whether or not the chip has VIN and GND. The tint stays in every later shot, including while GND is still open (qfn-teach-15). The cause and effect is backwards: a chip heats because current flows through it once it is powered. Showing a disconnected chip at 135 °C teaches that heat belongs to the part, or to the vias, rather than to the power it dissipates. It also gives the answer away (the red chip says 'put vias here') before the player has wired anything. That cuts against DR-37 (the world shows the rule) and DR-28 (failure shown as a consequence of the player's design).

*qfn-play* — **Board 3's chip glows 135 °C hot before anything is wired or powered, washing out its pin labels.** update() tints the QFN body and pulses its heat sprite from live.thermal whenever the board has a thermal pad (station.ts:394-396). The temperature model is chipTemp(vias) only (logic.ts:233, :276-278). The moment board 3 loads, with no VIN track and nothing plugged into J1, the chip glows red-orange 'over limit' (qfn-play-30) and the panel reads 'Chip 135 °C'. That teaches the wrong cause (heat with no power) and makes the first thing the player sees an unexplained alarm. The glow also covers the chip's VIN and ISET pin tags.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:233`
- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:276-278`
- `src/stations/qfn/station.ts:137`
- `src/stations/qfn/station.ts:393-396`
- [qfn-teach-13-b3-start-chip-hot-unpowered.jpg](shots/qfn-teach-13-b3-start-chip-hot-unpowered.jpg)
- [qfn-teach-15-b3-no-thermal-check.jpg](shots/qfn-teach-15-b3-no-thermal-check.jpg)
- v1.mjs output f2: {vias:0,temp:135,limit:70} on a blank board 3
- [qfn-play-30-b3-placed.jpg](shots/qfn-play-30-b3-placed.jpg)
- `src/stations/qfn/station.ts:394-396`
- [verify-qfn-play-17-crop-chip.jpg](shots/verify-qfn-play-17-crop-chip.jpg)
- [verify-qfn-play-16-b3-start.jpg](shots/verify-qfn-play-16-b3-start.jpg)

**Fix.**

*From qfn-teach:* **Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** Gate on U1.1 (VIN), U1.2 (GND) and J1's pins being on one piece of copper, not on the whole VIN/GND nets being done. Otherwise the chip stays cold until J2 and R1 are wired, which is too late to foreshadow the heat.

Reviewer's fix: In check(), compute `powered` = nets VIN and GND both done (or at least U1.1, U1.2 and U1.EP joined to J1). While unpowered, set thermal = {vias:n,temp:HEAT.ambient,limit,powered:false}. Don't push the thermal note or mark the board unreliable for heat; the board is tier 0 anyway because nets are open. In station.ts:393-396, ramp the tint and glow only when thermal.powered. Lerp it over about 1.5 s so the player sees the chip *warm up* the moment the last supply track lands, which is the payoff beat. Panel row (station.ts:417): show 'Chip — (no power)' until powered.

*From qfn-play:* Show heat only once the chip is powered in the model: VIN and GND nets joined, or after a CHECK (the 'power-on test'). Before that, show the chip neutral with a small thermometer icon reading '?'. Keep glow opacity ≤0.35 and raise the sprite to y 0.3 so the pin tags stay readable.

*Merged entry:* apply one fix for the shared root cause and check it against every room and reviewer listed above; where reviewers proposed different fixes, prefer the verifier-corrected one, then the lead (first) reviewer's.

**Verify.**

- *qfn-teach:* Retake qfn-teach-13: the chip body is its normal ink colour and the panel shows 'Chip — (no power)'. Then lay the layer-1 VIN/GND tracks and capture at +0.2 s and +1.5 s: the chip warms to orange. Unit test: blank(driver) gives thermal.temp === 25.
- *qfn-play:* Board 3 start shot: no glow. After VIN and GND are routed with no vias, the glow appears. After 5 vias it's cool.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-28, DR-37, DR-47

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — Confirmed. check(blank(driver)) returns thermal {vias:0,temp:135,limit:70}, because chipTemp depends only on the via count (logic.ts:233, 277). station.ts:393-396 tints and pulses the body with no power check. qfn-teach-13 shows a red-hot U1 with VIN 1/4 and GND 1/6. (2/2 merged findings CONFIRMED.)

### R5-187

**R5-187 | P2 | arcade-rush | teaching | P = I²R never decides a rush cabinet: block heat and parallel heat-sharing are untested**

Found by: `arcade-rush-teach#12` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-arcade (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

The Arcade teaches series, parallel, P = I²R against a ¼ W rating with a 60 % house margin, battery life and base drive. Rush generates only LED cabinets whose elegant fix runs its hottest block at no more than about 32 % of rating (fixHeat 0.03–0.32 across the sampled jobs). The ¼ W rating and the 60 % rule never bind, and a side-by-side pair is only ever needed to hit a resistance value, never to share heat. Rush also has no battery cabinets and no transistor base. The 3-minute drill exercises only one formula and one trap, with no escalation over the shift. The heat half of the lesson gets no moment of application.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:204-221` (rushJob: LED only; supplies 3.3–12 V)
- jobs.mjs output: fixHeat ≤ 0.32 for all 16 jobs
- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:168` (margin rule)
- `mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-rush-teach/stats.mjs:` fixHeatMax 0.403, marginBindJobs 57/300
- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:168` (margin note → tier 1)

**Fix.**

**Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** Correct the premise: the margin does bind on about 19% of jobs for near-top-of-band chains. It never forces a parallel pair. The escalation idea is fine as a P2 enhancement.

Reviewer's fix: Escalate within the shift. Cabinets 1–4 use the current generator. From cabinet 5, mix in 'hot rail' LED cabinets (24 V supply or a 30–40 mA band with imax raised for a high-power LED), where any single block that meets the band runs above 60 % of ¼ W, so only a parallel pair or a series split passes reliably. From cabinet 8, add battery cabinets with a life target (≥ 30 h) and occasional base-drive cabinets (reusing JOBS[4]'s Base load). Keep the `best()` solvability check. Reflect the new idea in the story ('Bright one: its block keeps scorching').

**Verify.**

- Unit test: for rushJob n ≥ 4, at least 25 % of jobs have a single-block solution that fails the margin (tier ≤ 1) and a pair solution that is tier 3. Rerun jobs.mjs and check fixHeat.

**Rules:** DR-26, DR-27

**Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE — Rush is LED-only (logic.ts:204-221), with no battery or base cabinets and no escalation. That is confirmed. The claim that the ¼ W rating and the 60% rule 'never bind' is overstated. Over 2000 jobs the elegant fix runs its hottest block at up to 40% (not 32%), and in 57/300 jobs (19%) some in-band chain fails the 60% margin (e.g. a single 470 near the top of the band on 12 V).

The 'dim' fault is three 470 Ω blocks. On 12 V that gives 7.1 mA, which the story calls 'Barely glowing. The player says it looks broken.' ### R5-189

**R5-189 | P2 | arcade-rush | teaching | 'Backwards' cabinets on 9 V and 12 V put the LED beyond a typical 5 V reverse rating, but the game says it simply 'stays dark'**

Found by: `arcade-rush-teach#14` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-arcade (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

The 'backwards' fault is generated on any supply (jobs 11, 12, 14 with this seed are 12 V and 9 V). The rule says a reversed LED just stays dark. Typical 5 mm LED datasheets give a maximum reverse voltage of 5 V. On 9 or 12 V a reversed LED is past its rating; the series resistor limits the breakdown current, but this is outside spec. 'Stays dark' is right in what is seen, but it teaches that reversing an LED is always harmless on any supply.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:8,` :153, :214
- jobs.mjs output jobs 11, 12, 14 (12 V / 9 V backwards)
- https://www.farnell.com/datasheets/1662254.pdf
- https://components101.com/diodes/5mm-round-led
- `mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-rush-teach/stats.mjs:` back 416, backHi 234

**Fix.**

Restrict the 'backwards' fault to supply ≤ 5 V in rushJob. Or, when reversed on a supply above 5 V, add a tier-0 note: 'Backwards on 12 V is past a typical LED's 5 V reverse rating; it may fail.'

**Verify.**

- Unit test: no rush job with start.reversed has supply > 5, or its judge note mentions the reverse rating.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-34

**Verdict:** PLAUSIBLE — Confirmed that 234/416 (56%) of 'backwards' rush jobs are on 9 or 12 V, so the reversed LED sees the full supply (read() vLoad=V, logic.ts:127). Typical 5 mm LED datasheets list VR = 5 V max. In practice the series resistor limits any breakdown current and many LEDs survive, so 'stays dark' is the truthful observed result. The teaching harm is small: it is an omitted caveat, not a false statement.

### R5-190

**R5-190 | P2 | arcade | teaching | Rhythm pad (blue LED on 3.3 V) teaches false precision: with 0.3 V of headroom, real Vf and supply spread swing the current from 0 to 27 mA**

Found by: `arcade-teach#11` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-arcade (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

The Rhythm pad is the only cabinet that really needs reasoning (one elegant answer, 47‖47 = 23.5 Ω; analyse.mjs), so it is the room's 'apply the idea' moment. It rests on Vf being exactly 3.0 V on an exact 3.3 V rail (logic.ts:59, :67-70). Sweeping blue Vf from 2.8 to 3.2 V and the rail ±5 % (3.135–3.465 V) with the intended 47‖47 gives anywhere from 0.0 to 27.1 mA (analyse.mjs). Real blue LEDs span roughly 2.8–3.6 V, and practitioners say a series resistor cannot regulate a blue LED on 3.3 V: use 5 V or a constant-current driver. The game grades this as 'Elegant ★' and teaches that a 0.3 V headroom design is ideal, which is the opposite of the real lesson. The story line 'Only 0.3 V is left over' (logic.ts:69) states the key fact but frames it as a puzzle detail, not a warning. The bumper's design (3 V of headroom) is barely affected by the same Vf spread (14.5/13.6/12.7 mA), which is the contrast worth teaching.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:59`
- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:67-70`
- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:171`
- `mockups/review5/tools/arcade-teach/analyse.mjs` output (Vf2.8/V3.465: 27.1mA … Vf3.2/V3.135: 0.0mA)
- [arcade-teach-11-rhythm-parallel.jpg](shots/arcade-teach-11-rhythm-parallel.jpg)
- https://zbotic.in/led-forward-voltage-and-current-limiting-resistor-guide/
- https://forum.arduino.cc/t/blue-led-resistor/355433
- `mockups/review5/tools/arcade-teach/analyse.mjs` output (Vf/V sweep line)
- `mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-teach/v1.mjs` log 'rhythm pair' iL 12.24 tier 3

**Fix.**

Keep the parallel puzzle and make it honest.
- In judge() (logic.ts:170-172), cap the tier at 2 when V − Vf < 0.8 V, with the note 'Works, but with only 0.3 V spare, a slightly different LED or a sagging supply swings the current a lot. Real designs leave more headroom or use a current driver.'
- Or move the Rhythm pad to 5 V with a white LED (Vf 3.0) and band 12–20 mA. Then 47‖47 + 47 + 47 = 117.5 Ω gives 16.9 mA, and parallel is still needed. Re-check with best().
- Optionally add a 'TOLERANCE' toggle on the meter that ghosts the LIGHT bar at Vf ± 0.2 V, so headroom becomes visible.
- Update logic.test.ts:172-176 and tests/station-arcade.spec.ts:36-40.

**Verify.**

- logic.test: the rhythm 47‖47 verdict carries the headroom note (or the new 5 V job's best() needs a side-by-side pair). Retake arcade-teach-11.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-38

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — The arithmetic checks out. 47‖47 + 1 Ω wire = 24.5 Ω. At the nominal 3.0 V / 3.3 V that is 12.2 mA (my run: 12.24 mA, tier 3). analyse.mjs gives 27.1 mA at Vf 2.8 / 3.465 V and 0 mA at Vf 3.2 / 3.135 V. Grading a 0.3 V-headroom design as Elegant ★ does miss the real lesson. I lowered it to P2.

### R5-191

**R5-191 | P2 | arcade | teaching | No visible consequence when the logic pin is overloaded: motor FULL, lamp lit, only a sentence and a formula**

Found by: `arcade-teach#12` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-arcade (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

Hopper with a single 47 Ω block gives 89.6 mA from a pin rated 20 mA. judge() fails it with '89.6 mA is over the logic pin's 20 mA rating. (I = (5 V − 0.7 V) ÷ R)' (logic.ts:159). In the world (arcade-teach-34), the MOTOR bar reads FULL in mint, the coin wheel spins, the cabinet lamp lights (drive ≥ 1, station.ts:410-411), and only the BASE bar passes its red line. The 'LOGIC PIN' supply is a plain brass post (station.ts:150), with no chip to warm, smoke or brown out. The visible cue praises the fault, and the cause exists only as text plus a formula, which is method, not cause (DR-28; review4 A8). The empty-chain case says the junction 'draws amps' (logic.ts:151). A 5 V logic pin cannot source amps: its output resistance (tens of ohms) limits it to roughly 60–150 mA, above an ATmega328P's 40 mA absolute maximum.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:151`
- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:159`
- `src/stations/arcade/station.ts:150`
- `src/stations/arcade/station.ts:410-411`
- [arcade-teach-34-hopper-47-overpin.jpg](shots/arcade-teach-34-hopper-47-overpin.jpg)
- [arcade-teach-19-hopper-empty-trip.jpg](shots/arcade-teach-19-hopper-empty-trip.jpg)
- https://www.arduino.cc/playground/Main/ArduinoPinCurrentLimitations/
- [verify-arcade-teach-13-hopper-47.jpg](shots/verify-arcade-teach-13-hopper-47.jpg) (MOTOR FULL, block 110 °C)
- `mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-teach/v2.mjs` log 'hopper 47 2.6s': toast 'The 47 Ω block turned 377 mW into heat ... it popped.'

**Fix.**

**Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** Also cover the misattributed pop. Either keep a base-job block from popping while the pin is the limiting fault: check `r.iLoad>j.load.imax` before popBlock for base loads. Or make the pin/chip brown out first (drive→0), so the pin, not the block, is the visible failure. With HOUSE.pinR 40 Ω, recheck best(hopper) and the rush generator, because read() changes.

Reviewer's fix: Replace the SUPPLY post for base jobs with a small black 'logic chip' rbox(.18,.04,.12) with 8 legs.
- Add a heat value: hotBody-style lerp to orange and a smoke wisp when iLoad > imax.
- Above 2× imax, the pin 'browns out': drive drops to 0, the motor stops, and the chip's status dot goes red.
- Model the pin with a 40 Ω output resistance (HOUSE.pinR) in read() for base jobs, so the empty chain gives (5 − 0.7) / 41 ≈ 105 mA. That still trips the 100 mA fuse, or remove the fuse from the base channel.
- logic.ts:151 base text: 'Nothing in the chain limits the current: the pin tries to push about 100 mA, five times its 20 mA rating.'
- Drop the formula from logic.ts:158-159 and show it live as the meter's ACROSS CHAIN tile instead (see the trial-and-error finding).

**Verify.**

- Retake arcade-teach-34 with the HUD hidden. The chip glows orange and smokes, the motor stalls, and a first-time viewer names 'the chip is overloaded' without the toast.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-28, DR-34, DR-47

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — Partly corrected. Hopper with a single 47 Ω block: MOTOR FULL in mint, and only the BASE bar passes its red line (verify-arcade-teach-13-hopper-47.jpg). The LOGIC PIN is a plain brass post (station.ts:150). The overloaded pin has no device-level consequence. The claim 'no visible consequence' is wrong, though.

### R5-192

**R5-192 | P2 | arcade | teaching | Rhythm pad introduces three new ideas at once (polarity, parallel, low headroom); the ladder has no reuse step**

Found by: `arcade-teach#17` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-arcade (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

Job order (logic.ts:62-83):
1. Series limiting plus the across trap.
2. Polarity (flip), parallel (side by side, the only way to reach the band) and the 0.3 V headroom idea.
3. Power rating (P = I²R) plus series chaining.
4. Battery life.
5. A transistor base.

Cabinet 2 piles on polarity, parallel and headroom, and the next cabinet never asks for parallel again (best() for claw, handheld and hopper is 470+470 in series). So 'side by side' is used once and dropped. Polarity is never revisited either. DR-27 asks for one new idea per job, reusing the previous one.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:62-83`
- `mockups/review5/tools/arcade-teach/analyse.mjs` output (best per job)
- `tests/station-arcade.spec.ts:36-55`
- `mockups/review5/tools/arcade-teach/analyse.mjs` output: best bumper [220], rhythm [47‖47], claw/handheld/hopper [470,470]

**Fix.**

Split the ideas over the jobs:
- 2 Rhythm: reversed only, with a working single-block chain. That is polarity alone.
- 3 Claw: 220 Ω start, power rating, needs about 1 kΩ in series.
- 4 Handheld: battery, the lowest current that is still visible.
- 5 Hopper.
- Add a 6th or replace one: 'Light gun' with a white LED on 5 V, where the bins lack a small enough single value, so a side-by-side pair is required and must reuse polarity (it starts reversed).
Check each with best() and judge(start) < 2 in logic.test.ts:204.

**Verify.**

- A table of new and reused ideas per job in logic.test.ts comments. best() for the parallel job contains a two-block position. Retake bench shots per job.

### R5-193

**R5-193 | P2 | arcade | teaching | A ¼ W block 'pops' within 1.7 s at 1.77× its rating; real resistors are qualified to survive about 6× for 5 s**

Found by: `arcade-teach#3` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-arcade (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

A block pops as soon as its smoothed heat passes 1.0× its rating (station.ts:383-384, `b.h>1`). With tau 2 s, failTime(1.77) is 1.66 s, and even 1.2× pops in 3.6 s (analyse.mjs). On the claw as found, 220 Ω at 44.8 mA is 441 mW (1.77×). In the capture it glowed at 0.8 s and had popped off the board in a puff of debris by about 2.4 s (arcade-teach-13, -14). The toast reads 'It is a ¼ W part: it popped.' In reality, power ratings are long-term continuous ratings. IEC 60115-1's short-time overload test applies 2.5× rated voltage (6.25× rated power) for 5 s and requires no flashover, burning or breakdown. A ¼ W film resistor at 0.44 W runs very hot (around 200 °C or more), discolours, smells and drifts, and fails over minutes or hours. The game teaches 'over the rating means instant explosion', which conflicts with the gentler, correct LED rule it already uses ('runs hot and dies early', ledPop 2.5×). The Hopper 47 Ω case (1.51×, arcade-teach-34) is about to pop for the same reason.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/arcade/station.ts:383-385`
- `src/stations/arcade/station.ts:301`
- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:161-162`
- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:194-196`
- `src/stations/arcade/logic.test.ts:207-209` ('a part at 150 % of its rating fails after a couple of seconds')
- [arcade-teach-12-claw-hot-0_8s.jpg](shots/arcade-teach-12-claw-hot-0_8s.jpg)
- [arcade-teach-13-claw-hot-1_4s.jpg](shots/arcade-teach-13-claw-hot-1_4s.jpg)
- [arcade-teach-14-claw-popped.jpg](shots/arcade-teach-14-claw-popped.jpg)
- https://html.alldatasheet.com/html-pdf/911492/VISHAY/TNPW-E3/2214/10/TNPW-E3.html
- https://www.vde-verlag.de/iec-normen/preview-pdf/info_iec60115-1{ed5.0}b.pdf
- [verify-arcade-teach-08-claw-1_4s.jpg](shots/verify-arcade-teach-08-claw-1_4s.jpg)
- [verify-arcade-teach-09-claw-1_8s.jpg](shots/verify-arcade-teach-09-claw-1_8s.jpg) (block gone, toast 'it popped')
- `mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-teach/v2.mjs` log 'hopper 47 2.6s': 47 Ω block popped, mis +1

**Fix.**

**Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** The alternative 'start the claw at 100 Ω to keep a pop' does not work. At 98 mA the LED passes ledPop and pops at 0.5 s, before the block (0.6 s), so the claw's pop moment becomes the LED's, not the block's. With blockPop 2.5×, no single-block claw start gives a block pop without the LED popping or the fuse tripping first (47 Ω trips at 206 mA). Adopt the 'keep 220 Ω and let it scorch' option: brown plus smoke, with judge's existing 'it scorches' wording. Optionally add a slow failure (pop after about 8 s above 1×) so the consequence still lands in the world.

Reviewer's fix: Add HOUSE.blockPop=2.5 in logic.ts, labelled a house value ('a gross overload; real parts survive brief overloads, but run scorching above their rating').
- station.ts:383: pop only when h>HOUSE.blockPop.
- Between 1× and 2.5×: the block browns, using hotBody's existing lerp toward '#8a4b2a' plus a smoke wisp. judge() already returns tier 0 ('it scorches'); keep that, and change the toast at logic.ts:162 to '…but it is a ¼ W part: it is scorching and will fail.'
- The claw start (220 Ω, 1.77×) then scorches without popping. To keep the claw's 'pop' moment, start it at 100 Ω (3.84×), which pops in about 0.6 s. Note that the LED pops first at 4.9×. Alternatively keep 220 Ω and let it scorch, which is the more truthful lesson.
- Update logic.test.ts:207-209 and the claw part of tests/station-arcade.spec.ts:41-44.

**Verify.**

- Unit test: a block at 1.5× for 10 s is still on the board (heat ≥ 1, no pop) and the verdict is tier 0 'scorching'. At 3× it pops. Retake arcade-teach-13/14: at 2.4 s the 220 block is browned and smoking, not popped.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-28, DR-36

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — Code and run agree. A block pops at heat >1 (station.ts:383). The claw's 220 Ω block at 1.77× popped by 1.8 s in my run, with heat 0.89 at 1.4 s (verify-arcade-teach-08/-09), and analyse.mjs gives failTime 1.66 s. The hopper's 47 Ω at 1.51× also popped (v2 log 'hopper 47 2.6s'). Real ¼ W parts survive short overloads well beyond this, so 'pops off in 2 s at 1.8×' is exaggerated. I lowered it to P2.

### R5-194

**R5-194 | P2 | arcade | teaching | An LED at 21 mA is a FAIL: the 20 mA test current is treated as an absolute maximum**

Found by: `arcade-teach#4` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-arcade (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

led() sets imax 0.02 (logic.ts:60), and judge() makes anything above it tier 0, 'over the LED's 20 mA rating: it runs hot and dies early' (logic.ts:158). The claw with a single 470 Ω block gives 21.0 mA (5 % over) and Fails, with the play test blocked (analyse.mjs: claw single 470 '21.0mA t0'). The meter draws the LED's red limit line at exactly 20 mA (station.ts:569). Typical 5 mm LED datasheets characterise at IF = 20 mA but rate the continuous forward current at 30 mA (for example Waitrony W05310YUC: continuous 30 mA, measured at 20 mA), and Cree recommends 10–30 mA. The game teaches '20 mA is a cliff', the most widespread LED misconception, and the 'dies early' wording does not match a 5 % margin. It also makes the claw's 470 Ω answer fail for a reason a real tech would call fine-but-warm.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:60`
- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:158`
- `src/stations/arcade/station.ts:569`
- `mockups/review5/tools/arcade-teach/analyse.mjs` output (claw 470: 21.0mA t0)
- https://www.elemon.com.ar/images/productos/hojas-de-datos/hojas-de-datos-no-linkeadas-a-nada/waitrony/w05310yuc.pdf
- https://www.alldatasheet.net/html-pdf/330263/CREE/C503B-RAS/202/2/C503B-RAS.html
- `mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-teach/v1.mjs` log 'claw single 470': iL 21.02, mis 7, soak 0, toast '...dies early'
- `mockups/review5/tools/arcade-teach/analyse.mjs` output: claw 470 '21.0mA t0'

**Fix.**

Give Led two numbers in logic.ts: `inom:.02` ('rated, the datasheet test current') and `imax:.03` ('absolute maximum').
- judge(): tier 0 only above imax (30 mA).
- 20–30 mA becomes tier 1 with the note '24 mA is above the LED's 20 mA rated current: it runs warm and wears out sooner.'
- Keep the band top at 20 mA so reliable or elegant still means at or below rated.
- ledPop becomes 2.5× of inom (50 mA). Unchanged.
- Meter: draw a dashed amber line at inom and a solid red line at imax on the LIGHT bar (station.ts:569).
- Update logic.test.ts:182 (the claw 100 Ω case is still tier 0 at 98 mA).

**Verify.**

- logic.test: claw 470 alone is tier 1 with a 'rated current' note, and bumper 100 Ω (29.7 mA) is tier 1. Retake arcade-teach-24-crop-meter-playtest.jpg and confirm the two limit lines.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-34

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — Reproduced. The claw with a single 470 Ω block reads 21.02 mA, tier 0, toast '21.0 mA is over the LED's 20 mA rating: it runs hot and dies early'. It counts a mistake (mis 6→7) and the soak never starts (v1 log 'claw single 470'). imax .02 (logic.ts:60) is used as the hard fail line (logic.ts:158).

### R5-195

**R5-195 | P2 | arcade | teaching | LED HEAT shows °C values that teach a wrong number: the 'limit' line sits at 45 °C and LEDs pop at about 43 °C**

Found by: `arcade-teach#5` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-arcade (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

The LED HEAT bar plots m.led (a current ratio) against a red line at 1 and labels it in °C as 25 + m.led·500·imax·vf (station.ts:570). For a red LED the line falls at 45 °C. In arcade-teach-30 the 47 Ω pinball LED shows 43 °C and then pops at 0.7 s (arcade-teach-31). The pop is driven by the instantaneous r.level > 2.5 (station.ts:386), not by the heat the bar shows, so the bar has not crossed its own line when the LED dies. The failure therefore does not show its cause on the instrument meant to show it (DR-28). The number is also misleading in itself: 5 mm LEDs are specified to operate up to 65–95 °C ambient, with junction limits around 100–125 °C, and 45 °C is a warm, perfectly healthy LED. A learner reading the bench leaves believing LEDs fail at 45 °C. The handheld at 31.7 mA ('runs hot') shows only 46 °C (arcade-teach-16).

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/arcade/station.ts:570`
- `src/stations/arcade/station.ts:386`
- `src/stations/arcade/logic.ts:36-37`
- [arcade-teach-30-led-47-whitehot-0_4s.jpg](shots/arcade-teach-30-led-47-whitehot-0_4s.jpg)
- [arcade-teach-31-led-popped.jpg](shots/arcade-teach-31-led-popped.jpg)
- [arcade-teach-16-handheld-overdriven.jpg](shots/arcade-teach-16-handheld-overdriven.jpg)
- https://www.alldatasheet.net/html-pdf/330263/CREE/C503B-RAS/202/2/C503B-RAS.html
- [verify-arcade-teach-16-led47-cold-0_5s.jpg](shots/verify-arcade-teach-16-led47-cold-0_5s.jpg) (LED HEAT 39 °C below the line; LIGHT bar past it)
- `mockups/review5/tools/verify-arcade-teach/v2.mjs` log '47 cold 0.5' hled 0.69, '47 cold .65' popped (mis 1)

**Fix.**

Either:
(a) Drop °C from LED HEAT. Label the bar 'LED LOAD' with right-hand text like '1.6× rated'. Draw the pop threshold (2.5×) as a skull tick and the rated (1×) as a dashed line, using the instantaneous r.level for the bar, so a pop is always visible as the bar sitting past the skull tick.
Or:
(b) Keep °C with honest values. Junction = 25 + θ·I·Vf with θ = 500, and mark the abs-max junction at 100 °C. Pop when the smoothed junction temperature exceeds 125 °C, which with θ 500 is about 100 mA for red. That needs ledPop re-derived from temperature, so `popLed` triggers from heat.led and the bar always crosses its line first.
Option (a) is simpler. Change station.ts:570 and drawMeter's bar() call, and gate popLed on the same value the bar shows.

**Verify.**

- Retake arcade-teach-30 (47 Ω pinball, 0.4 s). The LED bar sits beyond its pop tick before the pop frame (arcade-teach-31), and no °C under 100 is labelled as a limit.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-28, DR-31

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — Reproduced from cold with 47 Ω on the pinball. heat.led was 0.69 at 0.5 s (≈39 °C on the bar, below its red line at 45 °C) when the LED popped at about 0.55 s (v2 log; verify-arcade-teach-16 shows 'LED HEAT 39 °C' under the line one frame before the pop). The pop is driven by instantaneous r.level>2.5 for 0.5 s (station.ts:386), not by the bar (station.ts:570).

### R5-197

**R5-197 | P2 | garage | teaching | Motor spin-up of 4 ms and 'the surge lasts milliseconds' understate a real motor start by 1–2 orders of magnitude**

Found by: `garage-teach#13` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-garage (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

The start surge uses `MOTOR.spinUp:4e-3` (logic.ts:52), and the scope's START view spans 0–20 ms (station.ts:314). The capacitor message says 'the surge lasts milliseconds' (logic.ts:188).

A delivery-robot drive motor with gearbox and cargo has a mechanical time constant of tens to hundreds of ms, so stall current flows far longer. The electrical L/R of 2.5 ms here is almost as long as the 'mechanical' spin-up, which is physically odd.

The conclusion ('a bulk cap can't ride through a start surge, fix the ground') is right, and would be even stronger with a realistic spin-up: 1000 µF through 1 Ω (τ = 1 ms) does almost nothing against a 150 ms surge. As it stands, though, the learner calibrates 'motor starts take 4 ms'.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/garage/logic.ts:52`
- `src/stations/garage/logic.ts:186-189`
- `src/stations/garage/station.ts:310-316`
- [garage-teach-23-j3-scope-start.jpg](shots/garage-teach-23-j3-scope-start.jpg)
- [garage-teach-25-j3-cap-partial.jpg](shots/garage-teach-25-j3-cap-partial.jpg)
- `src/stations/garage/logic.ts:149-155` (startDip: the cap's k depends on tm/tc)

**Fix.**

- **logic.ts:52:** set `spinUp` to about 80e-3.
- **station.ts:157 `startTrace`:** set `span` to 300e-3; relabel the axis '0 → 300 ms'.
- **startDip:** recompute (the cap's effect shrinks; job 3 stays solvable only by star ground, which is the point).
- **logic.test.ts:** update `cap < bare` (still true, smaller margin).
- **logic.ts:188:** reword to 'the surge lasts as long as the motor takes to spin up, far longer than this capacitor can hold up'.

**Verify.**

- `logic.test.ts` start-surge cases pass with the new constants. Retake `garage-teach-25`: the scope shows a long sag the cap barely dents.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-32

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — MOTOR.spinUp is 4e-3 (logic.ts:52), the START view spans 20 ms (logic.ts:157, station.ts:314), and the cap message says 'the surge lasts milliseconds' (logic.ts:188). A loaded drive motor's mechanical time constant is tens to hundreds of ms, so 4 ms is unrealistically short. I checked the proposed change: with tm = 80 ms and tc = 1 ms, the cap's filter factor k ≈ 0.95.

### R5-199

**R5-199 | P2 | lunch | teaching | Heat on a cable uses the same white→orange→red ramp as strain, and it cooks 33% over in 6 s on a linear (not I²) rule**

Found by: `lunch-teach#10` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-lunch (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

A cable lying on the floor over its rating turns orange (heat>.4) and then red (>1.2) (src/lunch-runtime.ts:318). That is the same palette the game teaches for strain on a held cable (AGENTS 4; the Playground). In shot 12 the slack thin cable glows orange-red exactly the way an over-stretched cable does, so a Playground graduate reads it as 'stretched too far'.
The heat rule (src/sim/electrical.ts:49) is linear in overload, `(amps/rating−1)·dt`, and kills a cable at heat 2. So 4 on 3 (133%) is dead in 6 s (log: dead between +4.5 and +6.3 s). Joule heating goes as I²R, and a cable 33% over warms over minutes. The 6 s is acceptable as tuning, but it is not labelled as tuning (DR-36), and it teaches 'a little over = instant smoke'.

**Evidence.**

- `src/lunch-runtime.ts:318`
- `src/sim/electrical.ts:49`
- [lunch-teach-11-thin-kitchen-warm.jpg](shots/lunch-teach-11-thin-kitchen-warm.jpg)
- [lunch-teach-12-thin-kitchen-hot.jpg](shots/lunch-teach-12-thin-kitchen-hot.jpg)
- [lunch-teach-13-thin-kitchen-scorched.jpg](shots/lunch-teach-13-thin-kitchen-scorched.jpg)
- `src/sim/cable.ts:83` strainColor palette
- `mockups/review5/tools/verify-lunch-teach/circuit-check.mjs:` '4 on 3 cable dead at 6.02 s (proposed I^2 rule rate 0.778 /s -> 2.57 s)'

**Fix.**

**Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** The proposed formula is wrong. ((amps/rating)**2-1)*dt gives 0.778/s at 1.33×, so the cable dies in about 2.6 s, not 'still about 6 s'. The finding's own verify line (0.78/s) contradicts its fix line. To keep about 6 s, scale it: edge.heat += ((amps/rating)**2-1)*dt*0.43. Or keep the unscaled I² rate and raise the death threshold from heat>=2 to heat>=4.7 (and the tint thresholds .4/1.2 to match). The unit test should then assert about 0.33/s at 1.33×.

Reviewer's fix: Show heat with a different language: an emissive pulsing core plus heat-shimmer sprites and smoke wisps rising from the cable (reuse this.puff along the cable when heat>.4), with the hose tint going toward a dull brown-red 'cooked' rather than the bright strain orange.
Change electrical.ts:49 to `((amps/rating)**2-1)*dt`, which is still about 6 s at 1.33×. Add a comment: '// I²R heating; time scale is tuning, real cables take minutes'.

**Verify.**

- Retake shot 12: the heated cable is clearly different from a strained one (compare with a held-cable strain crop). Unit test: heat rate at 1.33× equals 0.78/s.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, AGENTS 4, DR-36, DR-46

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — The heat tints WARM #ffa04a and HOT #ff5a3a (lunch-runtime.ts:10,318) nearly match the strain ramp's #ff922f and #f34e56 (src/sim/cable.ts:83). Shot 12 shows the slack thin cable in bright strain-like orange-red. Harness: 4 bars on a 3-bar cable dies at 6.02 s under the linear rule (electrical.ts:49), and there is no tuning comment.

### R5-202

**R5-202 | P2 | meeting | teaching | A kettle 'left on' draws power forever, and its 'on' state is a big white fog ball**

Found by: `meeting-teach#11` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-meeting (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

The room claims the kettle is 'left on, as office kettles are' (meeting-strip.ts:2-3), and it draws 2.5 A steadily. Real kettles switch themselves off when the water boils, using a steam-triggered bimetal: Ingenia, https://www.ingenia.org.uk/articles/how-do-kettles-know-when-to-switch-off. A permanently drawing kettle is a wrong mental model, and it makes the 'unplug the kettle' answer arbitrary.

The kettle's 'on' cue is a white glow sprite, scale 0.6, at 1.25 m (meeting-strip.ts:47). It renders as a large translucent white sphere beside the gauge (shots 04, 25), which reads as fog, not a working appliance.

**Evidence.**

- `src/meeting-strip.ts:2-3`
- `src/meeting-strip.ts:47`
- `src/meeting-strip.ts:91-92`
- [meeting-teach-25-crop-gauge-loaded.jpg](shots/meeting-teach-25-crop-gauge-loaded.jpg)
- [meeting-teach-04-plugged-close.jpg](shots/meeting-teach-04-plugged-close.jpg)
- [verify-meeting-teach-02-plugged-close.jpg](shots/verify-meeting-teach-02-plugged-close.jpg)
- [meeting-teach-05-plugged-close-orbit.jpg](shots/meeting-teach-05-plugged-close-orbit.jpg)

**Fix.**

Swap the kettle for a hot-water urn, which sits on its thermostat all day (reuse the cyl body, taller, with a tap). Or keep the kettle and make it re-boil in a cycle: kick 2.5 A for 8 s, then 0 for 6 s, a nice 'it only trips when the kettle comes on' beat.

Replace the white halo with:
- the existing steam puffs (already at :92);
- a small red lit lamp on the appliance's switch.

Keep the heater's orange grille.

**Verify.**

- A close-up shows no white halo sphere, and the urn's or kettle's lit lamp reads at zoom 9. Update the comment at meeting-strip.ts:2-3.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-47, DR-66

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — The kettle is a constant 2.5 A steady load with no cycling (meeting-strip.ts:19, 32), and the header claims office kettles are left on (lines 1-2). Real kettles cut out at the boil. The 'on' cue is a white glow sprite, scale 0.6, at y 1.25 (meeting-strip.ts:47) at opacity 0.35-0.45, and it renders as a large translucent white disc over the doorway (verify-02 upper right, meeting-teach-05 left, meeting-teach-25).

### R5-203

**R5-203 | P2 | meeting | teaching | The tidy route is a daisy chain (wall, reel, coupler, reel, strip), which real safety guidance forbids, and the room never frames it**

Found by: `meeting-teach#13` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-meeting (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

The intended clean solution (tests/routes.spec.ts:38-45, LEVEL_01 'Clean') joins two extension reels with a coupler, then feeds a power strip from them.

Office safety guidance from ESFI and OSHA says strips plug directly into the wall and cords are not chained. Chaining violates 29 CFR 1910.303(b)(2) as typically applied: https://ehs.okstate.edu/site-files/documents/daisy_chaining_factsheet.pdf and https://www.ocwr.gov/wp-content/uploads/2016/09/fastfacts_power_strips.pdf.

A game that teaches electricity truthfully shouldn't present the forbidden setup as the 'tidy' answer without comment. The coupler is also the same model as the plug (prefabs.ts:101), so it doesn't read as a rated joiner.

**Evidence.**

- `tests/routes.spec.ts:38-45`
- `docs/LEVEL_01_BIG_MEETING.md:19-20`
- `src/props/prefabs.ts:101`
- [meeting-teach-31-mailcart-coupler-reel-close.jpg](shots/meeting-teach-31-mailcart-coupler-reel-close.jpg)
- `docs/LEVEL_01_BIG_MEETING.md:20`

**Fix.**

Reframe the parts so the clean route is a legitimate setup:
- Make the second reel a single long heavy-duty site cable.
- Make the 'coupler' a rated inline connector with a visible rating plate.
- Make the strip a rated 'distribution box' (a real thing on sites), so the setup reads as wall, heavy lead, distribution box, appliances.

At minimum, add a DR-36 comment in meeting.ts. Never put the Lunch thin-cable lesson on chained leads.

**Verify.**

- Close-up of the coupler and distribution box showing a rating plate. Code check: the comment exists.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-36

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — routes.spec.ts:38-45 and LEVEL_01:20 make the clean route reel + coupler + second reel, then the strip. The coupler and the plug share one model (prefabs.ts:101 'case coupler: case plug'). meeting.ts has no DR-36 comment framing it. Daisy-chaining extension leads and strips does go against common office safety guidance. I did not open the external URLs; that claim is consistent with general knowledge.

### R5-207

**R5-207 | P2 | observatory | teaching | The filter name in the panel is wrong for series C + shunt C: it is called 'high-pass', but it is a band-pass**

Found by: `observatory-teach#9` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-observatory (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

describe() returns 'high-pass (series C)' whenever the series part is a capacitor, ignoring the shunt part (logic.ts:150-155). With series 1 µF and shunt 1.5 µF, the panel reads 'Filter: high-pass (series C)' while the tags show '↑245 Hz' and '↓2.3 kHz' (shot 25). That circuit is a band-pass: high-pass at 245 Hz, low-pass at 2.3 kHz. Its curve on the scope (shot 25) is a hump, which contradicts the label. Similarly, series L + shunt L shows the generic 'filter', and series R + shunt L shows 'high-pass (shunt L)', which is acceptable.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/observatory/logic.ts:150-155`
- [observatory-teach-25-job2-series-C-fail.jpg](shots/observatory-teach-25-job2-series-C-fail.jpg)
- `mockups/review5/tools/verify-observatory-teach/num.mjs:` 'name CC high-pass (series C) LL high-pass (shunt L)'

**Fix.**

In describe(), add: s C + p C → 'band-pass (series C + shunt C)'; s L + p L → 'band-pass (series L + shunt L)'; s C + p L → 'high-pass (2-part)'; s R + p L → 'high-pass (RL)'. Add a unit test per pair.

**Verify.**

- Unit test: filterName({series:C1u,shunt:C1u5}) matches /band-pass/. Retake shot 25.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-34

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — describe() returns 'high-pass (series C)' for any series C (logic.ts:153); filterName({series:C1µ, shunt:C1.5µ}) gives 'high-pass (series C)' (num.mjs), and shot 25 shows the hump-shaped curve. One sub-claim is wrong: series L + shunt L returns 'high-pass (shunt L)', not the generic 'filter' (num.mjs: 'LL high-pass (shunt L)').

### R5-209

**R5-209 | P2 | qfn | teaching | Thermal vias cool the chip to 70 °C even when nothing is on layer 2 for them to carry heat into; in the reference route 3 of the 4 thermal vias end in bare laminate**

Found by: `qfn-teach#1` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-qfn (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

Board 3's heat lesson is 'thermal vias carry the chip's heat into the other copper' (logic.ts:94, note at :278: 'every via is one more path into layer 2'). The check doesn't model the other copper at all. logic.ts:276-277 counts every via whose cell lies in the EP and puts it into T = 25 + P/(1/110 + n/300), whatever is on layer 2. In my run (qfn-teach-21-win, qfn-teach-19-b3-vias-4) the only layer-2 track had failed, so layer 2 held a single 2-cell GND stub far from the chip. Four EP vias still took the chip from 135 to 70 °C, green, 'reliable' on heat. Even the hand-made REFERENCE.driver (logic.ts:316-317) has EP vias at [6,3], [6,4] and [6,5] that touch no layer-2 copper: the layer-2 GND track starts at [7,4]. So three of the four 'heat paths' end in nothing. A via moves heat only to the copper it lands on, and the copper area on the far side sets the limit. With too little receiving copper, more vias add little (https://www.lcsc.com/blog/qfn-pcb-layout-guide/, ROHM https://fscdn.rohm.com/en/products/databook/applinote/ic/common/heat_dissipation_effect_of_thermal_via_in_exposed_pad_type_package_an-e.pdf, Pericom https://www.pericom.com/assets/App-Note-Files/TQFN-Package-thermal-via-design-guide.pdf). As built, the game teaches 'more holes under the chip = cooler', which is the rule of thumb a beginner gets wrong in a real layout. The concept isn't the mechanic: the player only counts to 4.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:232-235`
- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:276-278`
- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:316-317`
- [qfn-teach-21-win.jpg](shots/qfn-teach-21-win.jpg)
- [qfn-teach-19-b3-vias-4.jpg](shots/qfn-teach-19-b3-vias-4.jpg)
- [qfn-teach-32-b3-layer2-view.jpg](shots/qfn-teach-32-b3-layer2-view.jpg)
- `mockups/review5/tools/verify-qfn-teach/v1.mjs` output: f1 thermal {vias:4,temp:70} with no layer-2 traces; f1l2 shows [6,4],[6,3],[6,5] with l2:false
- [qfn-teach-21-win.jpg](shots/qfn-teach-21-win.jpg) is actually a send-back toast (misnamed)
- `mockups/review5/tools/qfn-teach/run1.mjs` isEP filter puts [7,4] in the EP group, so the layer-2 GND trace from [7,4] failed

**Fix.**

**Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** The auto layer-2 pour under the EP is a sound way to keep it playable. If you add it, the reference's stray EP vias become valid automatically. Retune θ so that viasNeeded() stays 4 only when the pour is joined to the layer-2 GND track, and update logic.test.ts:73 and :79.

Reviewer's fix: In check() (logic.ts:276-278), count a thermal via only if its layer-2 node sits in a layer-2 GND copper component of at least K cells, and let that component's size set the spreading term. Example: T = ambient + P / (1/θ_board + 1/(θ_via/n + θ_spread)), with θ_spread = 900/cellsL2, where cellsL2 is the number of layer-2 GND cells (tracks, vias, through-hole pads) in the components the EP vias reach. To keep the lesson playable without a new tool, put an automatic layer-2 GND pour under the EP footprint (the 9 EP cells) as soon as the first EP via goes in. Draw it on layer 2 in station.ts redraw (a soft GND-blue square under the chip, visible when LAYER L2 is on). The player then makes it bigger by running layer-2 GND copper out from it. Retune P/θ so the reference still needs exactly 4 vias, and update REFERENCE.driver so every EP via joins the pour. Note text: 'Vias carry heat to copper on layer 2. With little copper there, they have nowhere to put it.' Update logic.test.ts:70-80, which expects {vias:3,temp:77}.

**Verify.**

- New unit test: driver REFERENCE with every layer-2 trace removed has thermal.temp > limit even with 4 EP vias. With the reference layer-2 copper restored it is ≤ limit. Retake qfn-teach-32 with LAYER L2: the pour under the EP is visible and joined to the GND track.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-26, DR-34

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — Confirmed in code and by a logic run. logic.ts:276-277 counts every via inside the EP cells and ignores layer-2 copper. I ran check() on REFERENCE.driver with all layer-2 traces removed: thermal={vias:4,temp:70,limit:70}, still green on heat. In the reference, only the via at [7,4] (and [10,2], outside the EP) touches a layer-2 trace; [6,4], [6,3] and [6,5] touch none. The claim is real.

### R5-210

**R5-210 | P2 | qfn | teaching | The exposed pad is 'not connected' on boards 1–2 and refuses copper; real QFN EPs are soldered down and usually tied to GND**

Found by: `qfn-teach#10` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-qfn (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

The temp sensor and the MCU are defined with EP 'NC' (logic.ts:81, :88), printed on the body as 'EP: not connected' (station.ts:153; visible in qfn-teach-05). Any track into the EP is refused: 'That is U1 pin EP (NC). Copper there would join it to …' (logic.ts:159). Real datasheets vary, but common guidance is to solder the EP down and tie it to ground. Some parts allow floating, and it must never go to another potential (NXP EB806 https://NXP.com/docs/en/engineering-bulletin/EB806.pdf; TI E2E https://e2e.ti.com/support/interface-group/interface/f/interface-forum/118754/tusb2046b---exposed-thermal-pad-on-qfn-package-soldered-to-gnd-or-left-floating). Two of three boards teach 'the big centre pad is unconnected and must be avoided', which is the less common case. Separately, the via rule 'No via inside a small pad: solder would wick down it' (logic.ts:181) silently doesn't apply to the EP, though EP vias also wick solder and cause voiding, which is why they're kept small or plugged (https://www.lcsc.com/blog/qfn-pcb-layout-guide/). Review 4 noted the QFN package itself (solder underneath, EP as heat path) is barely taught; that is still true apart from the poster (room.ts:58-59).

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:81`
- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:88`
- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:159`
- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:181`
- `src/stations/qfn/station.ts:153`
- [qfn-teach-05-b1-farcap-check-beads.jpg](shots/qfn-teach-05-b1-farcap-check-beads.jpg)
- mockups/review4/DESIGN_A.md:25 and :247 (same via-in-pad contradiction, still open)

**Fix.**

**Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** If the MCU EP becomes GND, the U1.2→EP→U1.7 shortcut under the body makes board 2's GND trivially short. Re-par 'mcu' (currently 35) and recheck that REFERENCE.mcu still costs exactly par (logic.test.ts reference test).

Reviewer's fix: Make the MCU's EP 'GND' (logic.ts:88), and add 'U1.EP' to the GND net there. The EP's solid pad then joins GND copper for free, which is also a nice routing shortcut that teaches 'the EP is a ground pad'. For the sensor, keep NC but label it 'EP: solder only (no net)'. In viaProblem's EP branch, add a soft note on the first EP via: 'Thermal vias are kept small (or plugged) so solder doesn't wick away from the pad.'

**Verify.**

- Unit tests: the mcu REFERENCE is still reliable at par (or re-par it), and routing GND through U1.EP is legal. Retake the board-2 bench shot: the chip reads 'EP: GND'.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-34

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — The code facts are as cited: EP 'NC' on the sensor and MCU (logic.ts:81, :88), the 'EP: not connected' print (station.ts:153), NC refusal (logic.ts:159), and the EP exempt from the small-pad wicking rule (logic.ts:181). An NC EP on a temp sensor is realistic, so that half is mild. An MCU EP is usually VSS/GND.

### R5-211

**R5-211 | P2 | qfn | teaching | 'L2 · bottom, thin tracks' suggests the bottom layer has thinner copper by nature**

Found by: `qfn-teach#11` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-qfn (section 5).

The panel row 'Drawing on: L2 · bottom, thin tracks' (station.ts:417; qfn-teach-32) and the narrower layer-2 render width (.052 vs .07, station.ts:197) present thinner tracks as a property of layer 2. ### R5-212

**R5-212 | P2 | qfn | teaching | Board 3 is an 'LED driver' with no LED, and every passive's purpose (ISET resistor, RST pull-up, series R) is invisible: the parts are just two-pad blocks**

Found by: `qfn-teach#12` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-qfn (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

Board 3's U1 is an 'LED driver' with VIN, GND and ISET (logic.ts:95), but it has no LED output pin, no LED part and no output connector. J2 is just 'power out' passing VIN/GND through. R1 (2 kΩ, ISET to GND) supposedly sets LED current that never flows. On board 2, R1 10 kΩ VDD→RST is a reset pull-up; on board 1, R1 100 Ω is a series output resistor. None of these purposes is ever shown or used: the values aren't drawn on the parts (twoPin tags show only the id, station.ts:174), and nothing depends on the value. The QFN bench is about layout, so this is acceptable scope. But a chip named 'LED driver' with nothing to drive invites the confusion 'what does this do?' and misses a cheap moment of meaning.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:81`
- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:88`
- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:95`
- `src/stations/qfn/station.ts:174`
- [qfn-teach-33-b3-three-vias-works.jpg](shots/qfn-teach-33-b3-three-vias-works.jpg)

**Fix.**

Make J2 'LED out' (pins LED+ and LED−/GND), with U1 pin 9 renamed OUT and ISET moved to pin 10, or keep the pass-through and rename U1 'regulator' with R1 as a feedback/enable resistor. Draw each passive's value on its body plate (label `${p.id} ${p.value}`). On the bring-up test (see the 'Works' finding), light a small LED strip on J2 when board 3 passes, so the board visibly does its job.

**Verify.**

- Retake the board-3 bench shot: the parts show values, and SHIP lights the LED on the output.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-26

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — U1 'LED driver' has VIN, GND and ISET only (logic.ts:95). J2 is 'power out' passing VIN/GND. There is no LED part or LED output. Passive tags show only the id (station.ts:174: label(p.id,…)); values never appear on the parts. This is acceptable scope for a layout bench, so P2.

### R5-213

**R5-213 | P2 | qfn | teaching | The chip limit of 70 °C teaches a wrong rule of thumb: a chip at 77 °C is marked unreliable, though 70 °C is a commercial *ambient* range and silicon junctions run to 125–150 °C**

Found by: `qfn-teach#7` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-qfn (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

HEAT = {power:1, ambient:25, board:110, via:300, limit:70} (logic.ts:232). The note says 'The chip runs at 77 °C (it must stay at or under 70 °C)' (qfn-teach-33/-34). A learner takes away '70 °C is too hot for a chip'. Datasheets pair a 0–70 °C *commercial ambient* range with a 125 °C junction limit, and silicon is often limited to 150 °C (Allegro AN295014, https://www.allegromicro.com/-/media/files/application-notes/an295014-computing-ic-temperature-rise.pdf; ICS datasheets via alldatasheet). Mixing up ambient and junction ratings is a classic beginner mistake, and the game teaches it. The per-via figure (300 °C/W) is in a plausible range: one vendor estimate is about 176 °C/W for a 0.3 mm via in 1.6 mm board (https://www.bestpcbs.com/blog/2026/07/thermal-vias/). Only the limit is off.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:232-235`
- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:278`
- [qfn-teach-33-b3-three-vias-works.jpg](shots/qfn-teach-33-b3-three-vias-works.jpg)
- [qfn-teach-19-b3-vias-2.jpg](shots/qfn-teach-19-b3-vias-2.jpg)
- v1.mjs output f7: [201,108.8,96.4]

**Fix.**

Use HEAT = {power:1.6, ambient:25, board:110, via:300, limit:100}, and label the row and note as the *chip* (junction), with a reason: 'must stay ≤ 100 °C for a long life (its absolute max is 125 °C)'. This keeps viasNeeded() = 4 and the reference unchanged: chipTemp(3) = 108.8 °C > 100 and chipTemp(4) = 96.4 °C ≤ 100, and 0 vias gives 201 °C, a dramatic start. Update logic.test.ts:73 ({vias:3,temp:109,limit:100}) and :79.

**Verify.**

- vitest src/stations/qfn/logic.test.ts passes with the new numbers. Retake qfn-teach-33: the panel shows 'Chip 109 °C · ≤ 100'.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-34, DR-36

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — HEAT.limit=70 (logic.ts:232). The note reads '…must stay at or under 70 °C' (logic.test.ts:73 expects 77 °C with 3 vias). I recomputed the proposed numbers: P=1.6 gives 201 °C at 0 vias, 108.8 °C at 3 and 96.4 °C at 4, so viasNeeded() stays 4 with limit 100. The fix is arithmetically right. P2 is right: the values are labelled tuning values (AGENTS 10), but the junction/ambient wording is a real misconception risk.

### R5-214

**R5-214 | P2 | qfn | teaching | 'Elegant to manufacture' and 'Shorter routes … are cheaper to make' name the wrong cost driver**

Found by: `qfn-teach#8` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-qfn (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

Tier 3 is named 'Elegant to manufacture' (station.ts:26). The tier-2 note says 'Track + vias cost N; par is P. Shorter routes and fewer vias are cheaper to make.' (logic.ts:282; shot qfn-teach-30). Copper track length is not a fabrication cost driver: fabs price on board area, layer count, hole count and size, and minimum feature sizes (https://www.protoexpress.com/kb/pcb-price-composition/, https://jlcpcb.com/blog/breaking-down-pcb-pricing-how-is-the-cost-determined). The via half is right: drill hits do cost. Tying par to 'cheaper' teaches that long tracks cost money, rather than the real reasons short tracks are better (less resistance, inductance and coupling; easier to inspect).

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/qfn/station.ts:26`
- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:19-20`
- `src/stations/qfn/logic.ts:282`
- [qfn-teach-30-b1-connector-right-edge-reliable.jpg](shots/qfn-teach-30-b1-connector-right-edge-reliable.jpg)
- [qfn-teach-30-b1-connector-right-edge-reliable.jpg](shots/qfn-teach-30-b1-connector-right-edge-reliable.jpg) (toast text)

**Fix.**

Rename tier 3 'Elegant' (TIERS[3]) and bonus text 'Elegant: every route at or under par' (keep it). Change the note to: 'Track + vias: N; par is P. Shorter tracks have less resistance and pick up less noise, and every via is another hole to drill.' Keep VIA_COST = 2 and its comment, which is truthful.

**Verify.**

- grep -n 'cheaper to make\|to manufacture' src/stations/qfn returns nothing. Retake the toast crop from qfn-teach-30.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-34

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — TIERS[3]='Elegant to manufacture' (station.ts:26). The tier-2 note at logic.ts:282 says 'Shorter routes and fewer vias are cheaper to make'; it appears in qfn-teach-30's toast. Track length is not a fab cost driver. The via half is fine (VIA_COST comment at logic.ts:19).

### R5-215

**R5-215 | P2 | spectrum | teaching | The 'Elegant' notes compare against a different band and so misattribute the waste ('more power than needed', 'more mirrors than it needs')**

Found by: `spectrum-teach#10` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-spectrum (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

judge() compares the player's setup with leanest(), the cheapest reliable setup over all bands (logic.ts:274-276, :292-295). Two misleading cases came up in play:
- (a) Storeroom with microwave at 10 mW: 10 mW is the minimum reliable power for microwave (1 mW gives 7 dB, sweep). The toast still says 'Reliable, but it uses more power than this delivery needs' (shot 41).
- (b) Quiet room with near IR routed around the smoke via mirror A at 1 mW, 11 dB: avoiding the scatter by going round it is a clever, truthful solution. It gets 'Reliable, but the beam bounces off more mirrors than it needs' (run3 log), because thermal needs 0 mirrors. For near IR that mirror is essential (without it 2 dB, sweep).

The player is told to cut power or mirrors, which would break their link. The real lesson, that a different band does better, stays hidden.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/spectrum/logic.ts:274-276`
- `src/stations/spectrum/logic.ts:292-295`
- [spectrum-teach-41-job1-micro-10mw-note.jpg](shots/spectrum-teach-41-job1-micro-10mw-note.jpg)
- `mockups/review5/tools/spectrum-teach/run3.mjs`
- `mockups/review5/tools/spectrum-teach/sweep.mjs`
- `mockups/review5/tools/verify-spectrum-teach/logic-check.ts` output: 'store micro 10 … uses more power', 'quiet nir via A … more mirrors than it needs', 'quiet nir 1 (no mirror) tier 1, 2 dB'

**Fix.**

In judge(), compute two references: `sameBand = solutions(job).filter(x=>x.setup.band===s.band)[0]` and `best = leanest(job)`.
- If sameBand uses less power or fewer mirrors: the current notes.
- Else if best uses less power or fewer mirrors: 'Reliable. Another band would get here with less.' This names no band, so it doesn't print the fix.

Add logic tests for both cases.

**Verify.**

- logic.test.ts: store, micro 10 mW → the note contains 'Another band'. Quiet, nir 1 mW + mirror A → the note does not contain 'mirrors than it needs'. Retake spectrum-teach-41.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-28, DR-38

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — My logic check reproduces both cases. Store, micro 10 mW gives 17 dB with 'Reliable, but it uses more power than this delivery needs', though micro at 1 mW is only 7 dB, so 10 mW is micro's minimum. Quiet, NIR 1 mW + mirror A gives 11 dB with 'Reliable, but the beam bounces off more mirrors than it needs', though NIR without the mirror is 2 dB.

**R5-216 | P2 | spectrum | teaching | Matching the detector to the band can never come up in play: the pod fits the matching head by itself**

**What is wrong.**

But the fix deleted the idea instead of making it physical. The R4B redesign ('Detector heads are props snapped onto the pod') was not built. That a dipole antenna, a thermopile and a photodiode are physically different sensors for different wavelengths is a strong, truthful idea, and it is now gone.

### R5-217

**R5-217 | P2 | spectrum | teaching | The cage mesh drawn on screen has about 6 cm holes, half of Wi‑Fi's 12.5 cm wave, so it would barely shield; the text says the holes are 'far smaller than the wavelength'**

Found by: `spectrum-teach#2` (P2 teaching). Batch: R-spectrum (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

meshTex (room.ts:26) draws 8 cells per 128 px tile, and each tile is repeated over 0.5 m (room.ts:99, `t.repeat.set(len/.5,mh/.5)`). Each hole is therefore 0.5/8 = 6.25 cm, which is clearly visible next to Pip (shots 30, 34). The failure message says 'its holes are far smaller than the microwave wavelength' (logic.ts:258). The bench shows λ 125 mm for microwave (shot 21). A curious player who compares the two sees holes at λ/2. The common rule is openings below λ/10, about 1.25 cm here. The usual estimate SE ≈ 20·log10(λ/2d) gives about 0 dB at d = λ/2, so a mesh this coarse is nearly transparent to 2.4 GHz. The picture and the sentence contradict each other, and the picture implies the wrong threshold.

**Evidence.**

- `src/stations/spectrum/room.ts:26`
- `src/stations/spectrum/room.ts:99`
- `src/stations/spectrum/logic.ts:258`
- [spectrum-teach-30-mesh-close.jpg](shots/spectrum-teach-30-mesh-close.jpg)
- [spectrum-teach-34-hatch-close.jpg](shots/spectrum-teach-34-hatch-close.jpg)
- https://hackaday.com/2018/09/26/building-a-hardware-store-faraday-cage
- https://www.physicsforums.com/threads/can-a-faraday-cage-effectively-shield-against-13-56-mhz-rf-interference.429914
- [spectrum-teach-30-mesh-close.jpg](shots/spectrum-teach-30-mesh-close.jpg) (viewed)
- [spectrum-teach-21-job3-micro-fail.jpg](shots/spectrum-teach-21-job3-micro-fail.jpg) (viewed: λ 125 mm next to the 'far smaller' toast)

**Fix.**

**Verifier correction (takes precedence over the reviewer's fix where they differ):** At 32 lines per 128 px, keep lineWidth 3 and the canvas is mostly copper. Drop lineWidth to about 1 and let mipmaps / anisotropy handle it, or use the 'coarse frame + fine overlay at low alpha' alternative. That avoids moiré at the 9 to 38 m camera distances.

Reviewer's fix: Change meshTex to a fine weave: 32 lines per 128 px over a 0.25 m repeat, which gives about 8 mm holes, below λ/10. Keep the copper posts and the top and bottom rails as the readable structure, so the fine mesh doesn't shimmer as moiré at the game camera. Alternatively keep the coarse texture at alpha 0.4 and lay a fine-weave overlay on top. Add a small mounted plaque on a copper post: 'mesh holes 8 mm · Wi‑Fi wave 125 mm'. That puts the size comparison in the world.

**Verify.**

- Zoom-9 crop of the cage (retake spectrum-teach-30). Count about 30 holes per 0.25 m, and confirm the hole size reads clearly smaller than the 12.5 cm λ ribbon when microwave is selected.

**Rules:** AGENTS 10, DR-34

**Verdict:** CONFIRMED — meshTex draws lines every 16 px on a 128 px canvas, so 8 cells (room.ts:26). meshWall repeats the tile every 0.5 m (room.ts:99, t.repeat.set(len/.5, mh/.5)), so holes are 6.25 cm. Shot spectrum-teach-30 shows large, clearly countable cells next to Pip. Shot 21 shows λ 125 mm and the 'holes are far smaller than the microwave wavelength' toast together. A hole of λ/2 is not 'far smaller'.

Visually (juice-audio-26), problem rings appear and a toast fades in. The board doesn't move, and nothing 'comes back from test'. The nearest coworkers stand at (±4.6,-5.6) and (6.6,5.6) (src/levels/qfn.ts:17-19), at least 5.7 m away, so snap().alarmed stayed 0 (s4 log 'ship scrambled 1 0'). ### R5-220

**R5-220 | P2 | arcade-rush | fun | Arcade Rush: the tray fetch and step-up eat ~6.5 s of the rush clock every run, before the player knows it started**

Found by: `arcade-rush-play#17` (P2 fun), `arcade-rush-teach#11` (P2 playability). Batch: B5 (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*arcade-rush-play* — **The tray fetch and 'step up' eat about 6.5 s of the rush clock every run, repeating the story level.** The rush clock is `game.time` from spawn, so the storeroom fetch, the carry and sitting down (about 6.5 s, or 11 s for a player who looks around first) all come off the 180 s shift. A player who has already finished the Arcade repeats the same chore every rush attempt before any scoring starts. It is short, but it is pure overhead on every retry, which matters most in a replay mode (DR-20: retries should be cheap). The objective card for these steps is also the long 'Carry the tray of resistor blocks from the storeroom to the service bench' sentence (DR-39 and DR-40).

*arcade-rush-teach* — **The rush clock runs during a repeated tray fetch, before the player knows it has started.** Rush uses game.time from spawn. The HUD reads 2:59 at the first frame, while the card still says 'Carry the tray of resistor blocks from the storeroom…'. The player must redo the Arcade's tray carry, which they have already done (rush is locked until the Arcade is finished). With my scripted ideal route Pip reached the bench at 171 s left; a human route costs 15–25 s. This is dead time with nothing to learn, eats about 10 % of the shift, and isn't signposted as part of the timed run.

**Fix.**

*From arcade-rush-play:* Either start the rush clock at the first `setActive(true)` (`rushStart=game.time`; use `game.time-rushStart` in `current()`, `complete()` and `rushStatus()`, and show 'READY?' on the HUD until then), or, in rush only, start with the tray already delivered (`trayReady=true`, bins visible) and Pip spawned at the bench stand. Shorten the step text to 'Bring the resistor tray to the bench'.

Alternatively, keep the walk but start the countdown on the first setActive(true): store `rushStart=this.game.time` and use `time−rushStart` in current(), complete() and rushStatus(). Show 'Sit at the bench to start the clock' until then.

### R5-221

**R5-221 | P2 | global, qfn | fun | Room lengths are very uneven: Playground solves in 5 s, the QFN bench takes ~40 inputs with a 720 s limit**

Found by: `progression#13` (P2 fun), `qfn-play#9` (P2 fun). Batch: B5 (section 5).

**What is wrong.**

*progression* — **Room lengths are very uneven: Playground is solved in 5 s, while the designer's limits range from 120 s (floors) to 720 s (stations).** Scripted clean solves measured in this review: Playground 5.1 s (playground-win.mjs: three walkTo legs and two keys), Meeting 21.4 s (meeting-time2.mjs), Arcade 31.6 s, Garage 26.2 s. Lunch can't meet its 120 s default (DR-07 Known). The per-room time limits that encode the designer's expected length span 120 s (all floors, src/sim/grade.ts:3) to 360–720 s (stations), a 6× spread. GAME_DESIGN's core loop says 5–10 min per level. The Playground tutorial in particular finishes before the player has had to wrap the cable round a pillar, see strain colour or try the slingshot: the clean route is a 15 m L-shaped walk (tests/routes.spec.ts:21-22), and the result card stamps triple A. The cable feel that every later floor relies on is never really exercised in the tutorial.

*qfn-play* — **The bench session is far longer than other rooms (about 40 inputs, 720 s limit), so room lengths are uneven.** The clean solve in tests/station-qfn.spec.ts and s2 is 10 part moves, 17 track strokes, 5 vias, 1 layer switch, 3 checks and 3 ships, plus a crate run. The reference board-3 route alone is 8 tracks and 5 vias (logic.ts:314-317), all at par with no slack. The station's own time limit is 720 s (station.ts:51), six times the 120 s cable-floor default (src/sim/grade.ts:3). A first-time player needs several CHECK/undo cycles per board, so a realistic clean solve is 6–12 minutes, more than twice the median room. It is also one unbroken stretch at one camera, with no walking or physical break between boards. The three boards are fun individually (see notes), but three in a row with escalating rules is a long, quiet stretch for a slapstick game. Manual-mode time can't measure bench seconds (s2 reports 9.25 s), so this needs a human timing.

Then set per-level limits from human-timed runs (see the grading finding), and bring the station limits down to about 1.3× median human time, so all jobs fall within about 2× of the median (DR-08).

*From qfn-play:* Break the session up with the room: after each SHIP the player stands up to carry the board to the oven (see the room-backdrop finding), which gives a 15–20 s physical break and a juicy moment per board. Give board 3 one slack cell of par (42→44) so 'elegant' needs understanding rather than exact replication. Measure real bench time with 3 playtesters (NEXT_STEPS §3) and set limits.time to the median clean time ×1.3.
